labs.expected_result: A segregation of duties conflict exists in Accounts Payable, with no mitigating control recorded. The affected user holds vendor master maintenance and payment run execution on a single ID, both unrestricted. The 38 mitigated conflicts are not concluded upon here — a recorded mitigation in GRC is an assertion, not evidence, and forms a separate population requiring its own risk-based sample before reliance can be placed on it. Recommendation: remediate the role design for the 3 unmitigated conflicts (split the conflicting authorizations into separate roles), and schedule a follow-up test of a risk-based sample of the 38 recorded mitigations to confirm each is a real, operating control rather than a label in GRC.
labs.objective: Verify that, at a defined point in time, no user in production holds both vendor-master-maintenance access and payment-run execution access without a recorded and substantiated mitigating control — across all relevant Thornfield company codes.
results: Forty-one (41) conflicts identified organisation-wide (unmitigated-excluded count vs. mitigated-included count, one checkbox apart, same system, same minute).
Thirty-eight (38) of the 41 carry a recorded mitigating control in GRC. Three (3) do not.
Of the 3 unmitigated conflicts, one (1) involves a user with the ability to both create/amend a vendor record and execute a payment run — the combination this control exists to prevent.
Independent trace of the flagged user confirmed the conflict originates from a single role holding both halves of the access — a role design issue, not two separate role assignments.

labs.reviewer_discussion: Management's initial framing was to treat only the 3 unmitigated conflicts as requiring action, on the basis that the other 38 are "already mitigated." This workpaper does not accept that framing outright — see Conclusion above for why the 38 remain a separate, untested population. This point is flagged here for reviewer discussion rather than resolved unilaterally by the preparer.

steps.narration:
CONTROL TESTING SCOPE
Verify that, at a defined point in time, no user in production holds both vendor-master-maintenance access and payment-run execution access without a recorded and substantiated mitigating control — across all relevant Thornfield company codes. I opened Lab 1 with one discipline: I wrote the control assertion in plain English before opening SAP. The question was not “Can I run the report?” It was whether the evidence could support this statement: Verify that, at a defined point in time, no user in production holds both vendor-master-maintenance access and payment-run execution access without a recorded and substantiated mitigating control — across all relevant Thornfield company codes. Priya: “Before you touch the system, tell me the population, the period, and what would count as an exception.” I wrote those three items at the top of my workpaper. That small habit prevents one of the most common failures in controls testing: allowing the available report to define the test instead of allowing the control objective to define the report. I then moved into the system. SAP GUI command field, then /nSUIM, then select the user/role report required by the procedure, then enter the defined scope, then Execute, then retain the selection criteria and result. SAP GUI command field, then /nPFCG, then enter the role, then Display, then review Menu and Authorizations, then Display Authorization Data; do not change the role. Before executing, record the system and client or source application, test period, population definition, report parameters, preparer and evidence date. If the configured menu path differs from the wording in this lab, document the actual client path used rather than guessing. If the menu path differed from the training wording, I documented the actual path rather than pretending the environment looked exactly like the manual. My execution notes read like a trail another consultant could follow: Re-read the objective and define the exact control assertion, population, period and exception condition before opening the report. steps.title: Step 1
steps.action: First execution with Include Mitigated Risks unchecked. Recorded the unmitigated conflict count.
steps.confirm: Thirty-eight (38) of the 41 carry a recorded mitigating control in GRC. Three (3) do not.
steps.narration: First execution with Include Mitigated Risks unchecked. Recorded the unmitigated conflict count. Second execution, changing only the Include Mitigated Risks setting to checked. Recorded the mitigated-inclusive count. Selected one flagged user from the unmitigated result and independently traced their access: /nSUIM (Roles then By User Assignment) to list every role held, then /nPFCG in Display mode on each returned role, opening Authorizations then Display Authorization Data to confirm which authorization objects actually grant vendor-master-maintenance and payment-run activity values. Determined, from the PFCG trace, whether the conflict sits in a single role holding both halves (a role design issue) or in two roles each holding one half (a role assignment issue). After the system work, I reconciled the extracted population to the defined scope, investigated differences rather than forcing the result to match the completed example, traced each exception to its underlying evidence, and completed the evidence index before drafting the conclusion. The first result was not the conclusion. It was the point where the case became interesting. Forty-one (41) conflicts identified organisation-wide (unmitigated-excluded count vs. mitigated-included count, one checkbox apart, same system, same minute). Thirty-eight (38) of the 41 carry a recorded mitigating control in GRC. Three (3) do not. Of the 3 unmitigated conflicts, one (1) involves a user with the ability to both create/amend a vendor record and execute a payment run — the combination this control exists to prevent.

steps.title: Step 2
steps.action: Second execution, changing only the Include Mitigated Risks setting to checked. Recorded the mitigated-inclusive count.
steps.confirm: Of the 3 unmitigated conflicts, one (1) involves a user with the ability to both create/amend a vendor record and execute a payment run — the combination this control exists to prevent.
steps.narration: Independent trace of the flagged user confirmed the conflict originates from a single role holding both halves of the access — a role design issue, not two separate role assignments. Maya: “So what does that actually tell us? Is this a failed control, a documentation problem, a design issue, or simply something we still need to investigate?” That question forced me to stop describing the screen and start analyzing the control. I separated the observed condition from management’s explanation, then asked what additional evidence would prove or disprove the explanation. Do not stop at the GRC result count. Trace at least the relevant exception to SUIM/PFCG or the underlying authorization evidence so you know whether you are looking at a role-design problem, an assignment problem, or a ruleset artifact. A second rookie mistake is to crop evidence too aggressively. A screenshot that proves the number but hides the system, date, user, parameters or surrounding context may look clean in a slide deck and still be weak audit evidence. I treated the evidence package as part of the test, not as administration after the test. My rule was simple: selection criteria first, result second, raw export preserved separately, analysis performed only on a working copy. steps.title: Step 3
steps.action: Selected one flagged user from the unmitigated result and independently traced their access: /nSUIM (Roles → By User Assignment) to list every role held, then /nPFCG in Display mode on each returned role, opening Authorizations → Display Authorization Data to confirm which authorization objects actually grant vendor-master-maintenance and payment-run activity values.
steps.confirm: Independent trace of the flagged user confirmed the conflict originates from a single role holding both halves of the access — a role design issue, not two separate role assignments.
steps.narration: THORNFIELD-B01-AC-01-PFCG-Authorizations PNG image — PFCG Display-mode Authorizations tab, object tree expanded, showing where each capability lives THORNFIELD-B01-AC-01-ConflictCount-Summary Excel file — Tab "Population" — both conflict counts and the role design vs. assignment determination For every file I recorded the source, system and client, period, extraction criteria, filename, preparer, date and workpaper cross-reference. That is what turns a folder of screenshots into an evidence trail. Elena: “Management's initial framing was to treat only the 3 unmitigated conflicts as requiring action, on the basis that the other 38 are "already mitigated." This workpaper does not accept that framing outright — see Conclusion above for why the 38 remain a separate, untested population. This point is flagged here for reviewer discussion rather than resolved unilaterally by the preparer.” I answered by going back to the source evidence rather than defending my first interpretation. Reviewer challenge is not an interruption to the work; it is part of the control-testing process. If the conclusion survives challenge, it becomes stronger. If it changes, the workpaper has done its job. A segregation of duties conflict exists in Accounts Payable, with no mitigating control recorded. The affected user holds vendor master maintenance and payment run execution on a single ID, both unrestricted. The 38 mitigated conflicts are not concluded upon here — a recorded mitigation in GRC is an assertion, not evidence, and forms a separate population requiring its own risk-based sample before reliance can be placed on it. Recommendation: remediate the role design for the 3 unmitigated conflicts (split the conflicting authorizations into separate roles), and schedule a follow-up test of a risk-based sample of the 38 recorded mitigations to confirm each is a real, operating control rather than a label in GRC. I deliberately avoided writing beyond the evidence. Where a cause had not been proven, I called it a reviewer question or an investigation item rather than turning an assumption into a finding. Access evidence is not just a list of roles. The tester must connect the access combination to the risk, determine whether the problem is design or assignment, and test whether any claimed mitigation actually operates. The technical transaction or report is only the visible part of the work. The professional skill is deciding what evidence is sufficient, recognizing when the population or control design makes a “clean” result misleading, and documenting the reasoning so that someone who was not in the room can follow it.

Define the exact control assertion, production population, test period, relevant Thornfield company codes, P2P ruleset, and exception condition. Record the system/client and evidence date before opening GRC. Start from the assigned lab scope, system/client and test period.

Open GRC Access Risk Analysis at USER level, set Report Type to DETAIL, select the Step 1 system/connector and P2P ruleset, set Include Mitigated Risks to UNCHECKED/OFF, verify the selection screen, then click Execute/Run. Record and export the unmitigated result population and conflict count. Start from the completed output of Step 1.

Return to the same ARA selection screen, change only Include Mitigated Risks to CHECKED/ON, verify that every other parameter matches Step 2, then click Execute/Run. Record and export the mitigated-inclusive result population and conflict count. Start from the completed output of Step 2.

Compare the Step 2 and Step 3 counts and retain both outputs. Return to the Step 2 UNMITIGATED result for user selection; do not select the investigation user from the mitigated-inclusive result. Start from the completed output of Step 3.

From the Step 2 unmitigated result, select one user with the required vendor-master-maintenance plus payment-run conflict. If several qualify, use the first qualifying user unless the instructor assigns another. Record the User ID, Risk ID, Function 1 and Function 2; do not invent a User ID. Start from the completed output of Step 4.

Enter /nSUIM and run Roles by User Assignment using the exact User ID recorded in Step 5. Click Execute (F8). Record/export every role returned for that user; these role names are the inputs to Step 7. Start from the completed output of Step 5.

Enter /nPFCG, take each relevant role name returned by Step 6, enter it in the Role field, click Display, then open Authorizations → Display Authorization Data. Record the authorization objects/activity values that support vendor-master-maintenance and payment-run capability. Start from the completed output of Step 6.

Using the PFCG evidence from Step 7, determine whether both conflict halves sit in one role (role-design issue) or in separate roles assigned to the same user (role-assignment issue). Record the role-to-function mapping. Start from the completed output of Step 7.
Reconcile the extracted population/result to the scope used in the completed example. Investigate differences; do not force your result to match the sample. Start from the completed output of Step 8.

For each exception, trace back to the underlying SAP/source evidence and distinguish a control failure, documentation gap, configuration/design issue, population problem, or reviewer question. Start from the completed output of Step 9.

Complete the workpaper and evidence index using the Step 2/3 ARA outputs, Step 5 selected-user record, Step 6 SUIM role list, Step 7 PFCG authorization evidence, and Steps 8–10 analysis before writing the final conclusion. Start from the completed output of Step 10.

labs.expected_result: The new-hire provisioning control did not operate for 2 of 20 sampled requests during the period, both tied to a single approver still using a retired role template. Recommendation: retire the legacy composite role from the approval interface entirely, and refresh the approver's understanding of current role design.
labs.objective: Verify that a sample of newly provisioned users in the period were assigned the correct, current role — not a legacy or deactivated role template — following a personnel change.
results: Sample of 20 new-hire access requests tested against the current role catalog.
18 of 20 requests matched current role design exactly.
2 of 20 were provisioned using a legacy composite role retired from the design six months earlier — both requests had been approved by the same manager.
Sample Exhibit — Access Request History — Search Results

Both mismatches show an approved request for the current-design role, but PFCG shows the retired "LEGACY" role template was actually provisioned — and both were approved by the same manager (MLINDQVIST).
labs.reviewer_discussion: Both exceptions were approved by the same manager, raising a question of whether the approver's own role list is out of date — flagged for reviewer discussion rather than treated as two isolated errors.

labs.expected_result: A previously untested SoD risk exists in Procurement, with 2 of 7 flagged users having exercised both conflicting capabilities, and the same role pattern present in two other departments. The PO release test also found 2 purchase orders above the release threshold created and released by the same user. Recommendation: extend the AP ruleset's risk logic to cover Procurement explicitly, remediate the 7 flagged roles, and re-run the analysis across all non-finance departments before closing this finding.

steps.narration:
CONTROL TESTING SCOPE
Verify that no user in Procurement holds both vendor master maintenance and purchase order approval access without a recorded and substantiated mitigating control, applying the same SoD methodology used for Accounts Payable to a different risk pairing, and confirm that purchase order release approval is independent of purchase order creation. I opened Lab 7 with one discipline: I wrote the control assertion in plain English before opening SAP. The question was not “Can I run the report?” It was whether the evidence could support this statement: Verify that no user in Procurement holds both vendor master maintenance and purchase order approval access without a recorded and substantiated mitigating control, applying the same SoD methodology used for Accounts Payable to a different risk pairing, and confirm that purchase order release approval is independent of purchase order creation. Priya: “Before you touch the system, tell me the population, the period, and what would count as an exception.” I wrote those three items at the top of my workpaper. That small habit prevents one of the most common failures in controls testing: allowing the available report to define the test instead of allowing the control objective to define the report. I then moved into the system. steps.title: Step 3
steps.action: Interviewed the affected business process owner (BPO), framing the discussion around what the access allows rather than what has happened.
steps.confirm: The same role design pattern was found in 2 other non-finance departments (Facilities, IT Procurement) during the population check.
steps.narration: PO release test: 2 of 46 purchase orders above the release threshold in the test period were created and released by the same user (HKOWALSKI) — the operating failure the flagged conflict makes possible. Maya: “So what does that actually tell us? Is this a failed control, a documentation problem, a design issue, or simply something we still need to investigate?” That question forced me to stop describing the screen and start analyzing the control. I separated the observed condition from management’s explanation, then asked what additional evidence would prove or disprove the explanation. Do not stop at the GRC result count. Trace at least the relevant exception to SUIM/PFCG or the underlying authorization evidence so you know whether you are looking at a role-design problem, an assignment problem, or a ruleset artifact. A second rookie mistake is to crop evidence too aggressively. A screenshot that proves the number but hides the system, date, user, parameters or surrounding context may look clean in a slide deck and still be weak audit evidence. I treated the evidence package as part of the test, not as administration after the test. My rule was simple: selection criteria first, result second, raw export preserved separately, analysis performed only on a working copy. steps.title: Step 4
steps.action: Documented the population of similarly structured roles across other non-finance departments before closing the finding.
steps.confirm: PO release test: 2 of 46 purchase orders above the release threshold in the test period were created and released by the same user (HKOWALSKI) — the operating failure the flagged conflict makes possible.
steps.narration: THORNFIELD-B07-AC-05-CrossDept-RoleSearch Excel file — role pattern check across non-finance departments THORNFIELD-B07-AC-05-EKKO-CreatorVsReleaser Excel file — purchase orders above the release threshold with creator and releaser compared For every file I recorded the source, system and client, period, extraction criteria, filename, preparer, date and workpaper cross-reference. That is what turns a folder of screenshots into an evidence trail. Elena: “Show me the exact evidence that supports the conclusion. If I remove management’s explanation from the workpaper, does the evidence still tell the same story?” I answered by going back to the source evidence rather than defending my first interpretation. Reviewer challenge is not an interruption to the work; it is part of the control-testing process. If the conclusion survives challenge, it becomes stronger. If it changes, the workpaper has done its job. A previously untested SoD risk exists in Procurement, with 2 of 7 flagged users having exercised both conflicting capabilities, and the same role pattern present in two other departments. The PO release test also found 2 purchase orders above the release threshold created and released by the same user. Recommendation: extend the AP ruleset's risk logic to cover Procurement explicitly, remediate the 7 flagged roles, and re-run the analysis across all non-finance departments before closing this finding. I deliberately avoided writing beyond the evidence. Where a cause had not been proven, I called it a reviewer question or an investigation item rather than turning an assumption into a finding. Access evidence is not just a list of roles. The tester must connect the access combination to the risk, determine whether the problem is design or assignment, and test whether any claimed mitigation actually operates. The technical transaction or report is only the visible part of the work. The professional skill is deciding what evidence is sufficient, recognizing when the population or control design makes a “clean” result misleading, and documenting the reasoning so that someone who was not in the room can follow it.

steps.narration:
CONTROL TESTING SCOPE
Verify that manual journal entries meeting the policy risk threshold were routed for, and received, independent review and approval before posting. I opened Lab 3 with one discipline: I wrote the control assertion in plain English before opening SAP. The question was not “Can I run the report?” It was whether the evidence could support this statement: Verify that manual journal entries meeting the policy risk threshold were routed for, and received, independent review and approval before posting. Priya: “Before you touch the system, tell me the population, the period, and what would count as an exception.” I wrote those three items at the top of my workpaper. That small habit prevents one of the most common failures in controls testing: allowing the available report to define the test instead of allowing the control objective to define the report. I then moved into the system. SAP GUI command field, then /nFBL3N, then enter company code/G/L account and period criteria, then Execute, then retain selection and result/export. steps.narration: Maya: “So what does that actually tell us? Is this a failed control, a documentation problem, a design issue, or simply something we still need to investigate?” That question forced me to stop describing the screen and start analyzing the control. I separated the observed condition from management’s explanation, then asked what additional evidence would prove or disprove the explanation. Do not write the conclusion while you are still collecting evidence. Finish the evidence index, reconcile the population, and separate facts from explanations before deciding what the result means. A second rookie mistake is to crop evidence too aggressively. A screenshot that proves the number but hides the system, date, user, parameters or surrounding context may look clean in a slide deck and still be weak audit evidence. I treated the evidence package as part of the test, not as administration after the test. My rule was simple: selection criteria first, result second, raw export preserved separately, analysis performed only on a working copy. Reviewer challenge is not an interruption to the work; it is part of the control-testing process. If the conclusion survives challenge, it becomes stronger. A clean sample cannot rescue a flawed population. First prove that the population contains the transactions that could actually violate the policy; only then does sampling mean anything. steps.narration:
CONTROL TESTING SCOPE
Reconstruct the full history and underlying support for a specific journal entry flagged by an anonymous tip, independent of the original tester's prior conclusion. I opened Lab 9 with one discipline: I wrote the control assertion in plain English before opening SAP. The question was not “Can I run the report?” It was whether the evidence could support this statement: Reconstruct the full history and underlying support for a specific journal entry flagged by an anonymous tip, independent of the original tester's prior conclusion. Priya: “Before you touch the system, tell me the population, the period, and what would count as an exception.” I wrote those three items at the top of my workpaper. That small habit prevents one of the most common failures in controls testing: allowing the available report to define the test instead of allowing the control objective to define the report. I then moved into the system. SAP GUI command field, then /nFBL3N, then enter company code/G/L account and period criteria, then Execute, then retain selection and result/export. SAP GUI command field, then /nSE16N, then enter the table named in the procedure, then set the exact filters/period, then Execute, then retain selection criteria and result/export. SAP GUI command field, then /nFB03, then enter document/company code/fiscal year, then Display, then review header, line items and available change/workflow references. Before execution, I recorded the system and client or source application, test period, population definition, report parameters, preparer and evidence date. If the menu path differed from the training wording, I documented the actual path rather than pretending the environment looked exactly like the manual. My execution notes read like a trail another consultant could follow: Re-read the objective and define the exact control assertion, population, period and exception condition before opening the report.

After the system work, I reconciled the extracted population to the defined scope, investigated differences rather than forcing the result to match the completed example, traced each exception to its underlying evidence, and completed the evidence index before drafting the conclusion. The first result was not the conclusion. It was the point where the case became interesting. steps.title: Step 3
steps.action: Independently obtained the underlying support directly from its source system/owner rather than accepting a prepared summary.
steps.confirm: The original preparer's supporting file was a summary spreadsheet, not the underlying source data referenced in it.
steps.narration: The original preparer's supporting file was a summary spreadsheet, not the underlying source data referenced in it. Maya: “So what does that actually tell us? Is this a failed control, a documentation problem, a design issue, or simply something we still need to investigate?” That question forced me to stop describing the screen and start analyzing the control. I separated the observed condition from management’s explanation, then asked what additional evidence would prove or disprove the explanation. Do not write the conclusion while you are still collecting evidence. Finish the evidence index, reconcile the population, and separate facts from explanations before deciding what the result means. A second rookie mistake is to crop evidence too aggressively. A screenshot that proves the number but hides the system, date, user, parameters or surrounding context may look clean in a slide deck and still be weak audit evidence. I treated the evidence package as part of the test, not as administration after the test. My rule was simple: selection criteria first, result second, raw export preserved separately, analysis performed only on a working copy. That is what turns a folder of screenshots into an evidence trail. Elena: “Whether the 14% variance and the two undisclosed post-posting changes constitute a reportable matter is a determination for Internal Audit/Legal — this workpaper documents the reconstruction and does not reach that conclusion itself.” I answered by going back to the source evidence rather than defending my first interpretation. Reviewer challenge is not an interruption to the work; it is part of the control-testing process. If the conclusion survives challenge, it becomes stronger. If it changes, the workpaper has done its job. Independent reconstruction found two undisclosed changes to the entry after posting and a 14% variance between the booked amount and an independent recomputation — neither visible in the original workpaper's summary-level support. Recommendation: escalate the reconstruction findings to Internal Audit for a determination on reportability, and require underlying source data (not summaries) as standard support going forward. I deliberately avoided writing beyond the evidence. Where a cause had not been proven, I called it a reviewer question or an investigation item rather than turning an assumption into a finding. A clean sample cannot rescue a flawed population. First prove that the population contains the transactions that could actually violate the policy; only then does sampling mean anything. The technical transaction or report is only the visible part of the work. The professional skill is deciding what evidence is sufficient, recognizing when the population or control design makes a “clean” result misleading, and documenting the reasoning so that someone who was not in the room can follow it. labs.expected_result: Two findings, one root cause. The automated monitoring control did not operate effectively from the date of the data source change. labs.objective: Verify that the automated monitoring rule executed as scheduled, evaluated its intended population, and correctly identified exceptions.
results: The rule's data source was changed during the period; from that date the rule evaluated an empty or incorrect population and returned a clean result for six consecutive weeks.
The injection test confirmed the rule did not flag a transaction independently known to meet its condition, following the data source change.
The change to the rule's configuration was not subject to documented review or approval.
Sample Exhibit — Continuous Monitoring — Rule Execution History (Rule ID: CCM-FI-018)

Job status reads "Completed" for all 8 cycles — execution was never the problem. The rule's own exception count silently dropped to zero for 4 cycles while independent recomputation found 8–11 exceptions each time.

navigation: I then moved into the system. labs.expected_result: One payment run bypassed segregation of duties (same creator and releaser) and one payment file was transmitted twice with no compensating cancellation on record. Recommendation: enforce a hard system block on same-user creation and release in F110, and add a transmission-count check to the standard payment run evidence package. The duplicate-invoice test also found 1 invoice pair paid twice, with the double-invoice check switched off on the vendor record; switch the check on for all active vendors.
labs.objective: Test whether the payment run process can produce — and would catch — a duplicate bank file transmission, and confirm proposal creation and release are performed by different people, and confirm duplicate invoices are caught before they reach a payment run.
labs.topic: Payment Run Duplicate and SoD Testing
results: 22 payment runs in the period; 1 run had the same person as both creator and releaser.
REGUH/REGUP-based population matched the F110 screen count — no runs were hidden from the standard view.
1 file showed 2 transmission records in the DMEE tree; SM37 confirmed a second execution of the transmission job 40 minutes after the first, with no cancellation of the first recorded.

Duplicate-invoice test: 4 pairs of invoices matched on vendor, reference number and amount; the double-invoice check was switched off on the vendor records for 3 of the 4 pairs, and 1 pair had been paid twice in separate payment runs.
Sample Exhibit — Proposal List / Payment Run Log
One run bypassed segregation of duties entirely (same creator/releaser); a separate run transmitted its payment file twice with no cancellation of the first recorded in SM37.
labs.reviewer_discussion: Whether the duplicate transmission resulted in a duplicate payment to the bank (versus a resubmission the bank itself deduplicated) could not be confirmed from SAP data alone — flagged for follow-up with Treasury and the bank directly.

labs.expected_result: The absolute tolerance limit has not blocked a single invoice all period while 41 invoices clustered just below it, concentrated in 2 vendors — an empty blocked-invoice list was the reason to test the configuration, not evidence the control worked. results: Absolute tolerance limit unchanged since original go-live, despite three price increases in the underlying commodity since then.

Block-release test: not applicable this period — with no invoices blocked, there were no releases to test. On a system where the tolerance does block invoices, this is the step that tests whether the releaser is independent of the person who posted the invoice.

labs.expected_result: A 14-day gap between the tax rate's documented policy-effective date and its actual production go-live date resulted in $38,600 of under-collected tax across 412 transactions, and the configuration change itself moved through transport two weeks after the business believed it was already live. Recommendation: align the change-request approval date to the actual planned transport date going forward, and require Tax and Basis to jointly confirm go-live before the policy-effective date is communicated externally.
labs.objective: Confirm that a change to a tax code's rate was tested, approved, and moved to production on schedule — and quantify what happened to transactions caught in the gap if it wasn't.
results: The tax rate change (7.5% to 8.25%) was approved with a policy-effective date of March 1; the transport moved to production on March 15 — a 14-day gap.
412 transactions posted between March 1 and March 14 using the old 7.5% rate, though policy required 8.25% from March 1.
The total under-collected tax across the 412 transactions was calculated at $38,600, based on independent recomputation via BSET.

All 4 flagged documents posted between the March 1 policy-effective date and the March 15 actual go-live, each under-collecting tax at the old 7.5% rate.

labs.expected_result: The hedge program itself is economically sound and effectiveness testing is being performed consistently — the finding is procedural: two hedges' designation memos were completed after the contemporaneous-documentation window IFRS 9 requires. Recommendation: build a designation-memo deadline (e.g., trade date + 1 business day) directly into the Hedge Management Cockpit workflow rather than relying on Treasury staff to remember.
labs.objective: Confirm that Thornfield's active FX hedge relationships carry complete, contemporaneous designation and effectiveness-testing documentation, not just a completed trade and a favorable outcome.
results: 12 of 14 hedges had designation memos dated at or before inception, with complete effectiveness-testing documentation.
2 hedges had designation memos created 9 and 14 days after trade inception respectively — after the window IFRS 9 treats as contemporaneous.
All 3 sampled accounting entries matched the documented cash-flow hedge treatment.
Sample Exhibit — FX Hedge Documentation Review — Q3 Fiscal Period

Both late-designated hedges still passed effectiveness testing — the gap is purely documentation timing, but it's exactly the gap an external auditor would use to challenge hedge accounting treatment for those two positions.

labs.objective: Understand the SAP landscape, in-scope systems, major business processes, control owners and the initial evidence request before testing begins.
labs.scenario: You have joined ABC Manufacturing as an independent SAP Controls/GRC/Security Assurance consultant. Your first task is to understand the environment and build a defensible PBC/evidence request and initial risk view.
labs.systems: SAP GUI; SAP Easy Access/System Status; SU01/SUIM where authorized; client architecture documents; GRC/Fiori only if in scope.

steps.title: Step 1
steps.action: Log on to the assigned SAP client and capture System > Status. Record SID/system, client, SAP product/release information visible, and your evidence date.
steps.confirm: Confirm this step is complete and retain the required evidence before continuing.
steps.narration: I walked into ABC Manufacturing on a Monday morning with a laptop, a notebook, and a mandate: understand the landscape before I test anything. “First things first,” I told myself. I never conclude on a system I haven’t verified. I logged into the assigned client through SAP GUI and immediately went to System, then Status. I captured the SID, client number, and release information, and wrote down the evidence date on the screenshot itself. That screenshot — my first artifact — became E01. Priya Nair, the IT Compliance Lead, handed me a landscape diagram showing DEV, QAS, and PRD plus a GRC box and a Fiori front end. I didn’t just accept it. I reconciled the diagram against what I could actually log into. “Where’s the GRC connector pointing?” I asked. Priya confirmed it, and I noted that a missing component in scope documentation is exactly the kind of gap that invalidates an audit later.

steps.title: Step 2
steps.action: Review the client-provided landscape diagram/system inventory. Reconcile DEV/QAS/PRD and any GRC/Fiori components to what you can actually access.
steps.confirm: Confirm this step is complete and retain the required evidence before continuing.
steps.narration: Then I did the real work of scoping: I listed the in-scope business processes — FI/CO, MM/Procurement, SD, HR, and Basis/Security — and for each critical area (user access, roles, SoD, emergency access, transports, background jobs), I demanded an evidence owner. No owner, no control — that’s my rule. I built my PBC (Provided-By-Client) request list in Excel: user population, role population, privileged IDs, GRC risk results, Firefighter logs, access requests, transport history. Every PBC item, I tied to a specific risk it would support. And I drafted an initial risk register. I checked myself before leaving: System and period documented? Components identified? PBC tied to risks? Files named W01-L01 with dates and indexed? Yes, all four. Scoping isn’t testing — I wrote in my workpaper explicitly: “No conclusion on control effectiveness at this stage.” What I knew, what I suspected, and what was still outstanding — all three, stated plainly.

steps.action: Identify the business processes in scope: FI/CO, MM/Procurement, SD, HR, Basis/Security, change management and interfaces as applicable.
steps.confirm: Confirm this step is complete and retain the required evidence before continuing.
steps.narration: Priya glanced at the clock. “The steering committee wants preliminary findings by Friday. Can we start with access testing today?” “I can start extracting,” I said, “but I will not call anything a finding until I know exactly which system, client, period, process, and control owner I am testing. Speed without scope only produces faster mistakes.” I indexed the evidence before writing the conclusion. My training-file convention for this lab was:

navigation: SAP GUI command field > SUIM > Users > choose the report that supports the population required (for example users by complex selection criteria / users by role).
SAP GUI command field > SU01 > enter selected User ID > Display > Logon Data / Roles / Profiles as needed.
labs.objective: Obtain a complete user/access population, identify high-risk or inappropriate access, investigate selected users and document conclusions.
labs.scenario: Perform a user access review over the assigned SAP production client and investigate dormant, terminated, privileged, generic/service and high-risk users.

steps.title: Step 1
steps.action: In SUIM choose the user population report appropriate to the control objective. Enter the client-relevant criteria and “as-of”/validity criteria; avoid filters that accidentally exclude users.
steps.confirm: Confirm this step is complete and retain the required evidence before continuing.
steps.narration: Tuesday, I pulled my first real population. I typed SUIM into the command field and paused. The most dangerous mistake in a user access review, I reminded myself, is the accidental exclusion. A filter that quietly drops locked users, service accounts, or system IDs can make a dirty population look clean. So I chose my report — users by complex selection criteria — and deliberately set no validity exclusions. I captured the selection screen before executing. That became E01. The result came back: 412 users. I exported the raw population to Excel first — no filtering, no analysis columns — because the raw file is my proof of completeness. I recorded the extraction date, time, criteria, and row count in my workpaper. Then I made a copy for analysis.

steps.title: Step 2
steps.action: Capture the SUIM selection screen before execution. Execute and record the result count.
steps.confirm: Confirm this step is complete and retain the required evidence before continuing.
steps.narration: I scanned for the classic red flags: terminated users still valid, dormant dialog users, SAP-ALL or SAP-NEW profiles, generic IDs with no owner, security admins who also hold business roles, expired temporary access still active. I found one: USER-RSHARMA — a dialog account, last logon 9 months ago, holding an MM purchasing role. I opened SU01, then Display, reviewed the Logon Data and Roles tabs, and cross-checked against the HR termination list Priya had provided. Elena’s HR extract confirmed he left in March. No approval. No owner.

steps.title: Step 3
steps.action: Review column headings and several records for reasonableness. Export the full population where permitted.
steps.confirm: Confirm this step is complete and retain the required evidence before continuing.
steps.narration: I wrote the finding in the structure I always use: Criteria, then Condition, then Evidence, then Risk, then Recommendation. Access removed, evidence ID E03, conclusion documented. And I noted carefully in my workpaper that I had addressed completeness — every one of the 412 users was in scope, locked or not. Priya asked, “Do you really need the locked IDs? They cannot log in.” “Maybe they cannot log in today,” I replied, “but exclusion is a conclusion, not a filter setting. First I preserve the complete population. Then I document why any category is out of scope.”

steps.title: Identify review attributes
steps.action: Identify review attributes: user type, validity, lock status, last logon if available in the chosen report, roles, privileged access indicators and ownership.
steps.confirm: Confirm this step is complete and retain the required evidence before continuing.
steps.narration: I indexed the evidence before writing the conclusion. My training-file convention for this lab was: E01-L02-SUIM-Selection, PNG image E02-L02-SUIM-UserPopulation-RAW, Excel file

steps.title: Step 5
steps.action: Select exceptions/high-risk users from the population. Open each selected user in SU01 Display mode.
steps.confirm: Confirm this step is complete and retain the required evidence before continuing.
steps.narration: E03-L02-USER-RSHARMA-SU01, PNG image E04-L02-HR-Termination-Corroboration, PDF file W01-L02-User-Access-Review, Excel file

steps.title: Step 6
steps.action: In SU01 review Logon Data, Roles and Profiles only as needed for the test. Reconcile terminated/dormant status to HR or approved source evidence where provided.
steps.confirm: Confirm this step is complete and retain the required evidence before continuing.
steps.narration: Elena challenged whether one dormant terminated user justified an exception. I showed the HR termination evidence, SU01 status, role assignment, and population methodology. The issue was not the age of the account; it was valid production access with no current owner or approval. Confirmed: selection criteria captured

steps.title: Step 7
steps.action: Document each exception and determine whether access is appropriate, should be removed, or requires further investigation.
steps.confirm: Confirm this step is complete and retain the required evidence before continuing.
steps.narration: Confirmed: raw population preserved Confirmed: sampled users investigated Confirmed: every exception evidence-linked

navigation: SAP GUI command field > PFCG > enter Role > Display.
Within PFCG review Description, Menu, Authorizations and User tabs.
SAP GUI command field > SUIM > Roles / Users reports to obtain role/user populations where required.
labs.objective: Review selected SAP roles for appropriate menu content, authorization design, organizational restrictions and user assignment.
labs.scenario: Assess high-risk or business-critical roles and determine whether their design introduces excessive or incompatible access.

steps.title: Step 1
steps.action: Identify the role sample from the lab workbook or SUIM role population.
steps.confirm: Confirm this step is complete and retain the required evidence before continuing.
steps.narration: “Show me the roles that matter most,” I told Sameer on Wednesday. He gave me a list of high-risk roles. I picked Z:MM:PURCHASER to start. I opened PFCG, then Display and began my four-part ritual: Description, Menu, Authorizations, User. The role description said “Purchasing — Create Purchase Requisitions.” The Menu showed ME21N, ME51N — fine. But then I went to the Authorizations tab, because here’s the truth I drill into every junior consultant: the menu is decoration; authorizations are the access. The menu had no goods receipt transactions — but the authorization data contained full MIGO rights with unrestricted plant and storage location values.

steps.title: Step 2
steps.action: Open the role in PFCG Display mode and capture the role name/description.
steps.confirm: Confirm this step is complete and retain the required evidence before continuing.
steps.narration: “Sameer,” I called over, “this role can receive goods, but the business thinks it’s only a requisitioner.” That’s a classic design deficiency: receiving combined with purchasing is an SoD conflict living inside one role, invisible to anyone who only reads the menu. I exported the role-user population from SUIM (17 users) rather than screenshotting — populations deserve exports, not pictures. For each issue I wrote the cross-reference: expected business purpose versus actual authorization content, with the critical object and field values recorded.

steps.title: Step 3
steps.action: Review Menu entries for transactions/apps/services relevant to the business purpose.
steps.confirm: Confirm this step is complete and retain the required evidence before continuing.
steps.narration: My workpaper captured the key distinction: a design deficiency (the role itself is wrong) is different from an assignment problem (right role, wrong user). Both can exist; I documented each separately. Sameer pointed to the role menu. “There is no goods receipt transaction there.” “That tells me what the user sees,” I said. “Now we test what SAP will actually allow.” When MIGO capability appeared in the authorization data, the room went quiet.

steps.title: Step 4
steps.action: Review Authorizations for critical objects/field values and organizational restrictions. Do not rely only on menu entries.
steps.confirm: Confirm this step is complete and retain the required evidence before continuing.
steps.narration: I indexed the evidence before writing the conclusion. My training-file convention for this lab was: E01-L03-PFCG-Description, PNG image E02-L03-PFCG-Menu, PNG image

steps.title: Step 5
steps.action: Review User assignments and validity. If the list is large, obtain the role-user population from SUIM rather than relying on screenshots.
steps.confirm: Confirm this step is complete and retain the required evidence before continuing.
steps.narration: E03-L03-PFCG-Authorizations-MIGO, PNG image E04-L03-SUIM-RoleUsers-RAW, Excel file W01-L03-Role-Design-QA, Excel file

steps.title: Step 6
steps.action: Compare role design to stated business purpose and identify incompatible functions, broad values such as unrestricted organizational access, or privileged technical capabilities.
steps.confirm: Confirm this step is complete and retain the required evidence before continuing.
steps.narration: The role owner argued that no one had complained about inappropriate receiving access. I separated usage from capability: the control question was whether the role design permitted an incompatible activity, not whether we had evidence someone abused it. Confirmed: purpose documented

steps.title: Step 7
steps.action: Document design observations and recommended remediation.
steps.confirm: Confirm this step is complete and retain the required evidence before continuing.
steps.narration: Confirmed: menu and authorizations reviewed Confirmed: user assignment considered Confirmed: every issue evidence-linked

labs.module: Week 2 — GRC ARA / SoD / Ruleset / Mitigation
navigation: GRC NWBC/Fiori/Portal > Access Management > Access Risk Analysis > User Level (or equivalent configured path).
Choose the target system/connector, analysis type, user/role and rule/risk options required by the lab.
labs.objective: Run or review Access Risk Analysis, investigate SoD/critical-access results and determine whether conflicts are real, false-positive, remediated or mitigated.
labs.scenario: Analyze assigned users/roles in GRC ARA and explain the business risk behind each material conflict.
labs.systems: SAP GRC Access Control - Access Risk Analysis; backend SAP evidence as needed.

steps.title: Step 1
steps.action: Open User Level Access Risk Analysis. Select the correct target system/connector and user(s).
steps.confirm: Confirm this step is complete and retain the required evidence before continuing.
steps.narration: Thursday morning, I logged into the GRC system through NWBC and navigated to Access Risk Analysis, then User Level. Sameer stood behind me. “Show me USER-MBROOKS,” I said. I selected the correct connector — PRD-100, not the QAS one, a mistake I’ve seen derail an entire analysis — set the options to include mitigated risks, and screenshotted the criteria before executing. Results: 14 violations. I screenshotted the summary, exported the raw list, and then drilled into the one that mattered: Risk ID SOD-AP-001 — Create Vendor versus Process Payments. The detail showed both functions, their underlying transactions (XK01/FK01 on one side, F110 on the other), and the roles feeding each side.

steps.title: Step 2
steps.action: Set analysis options required by the client/lab, including whether mitigated risks are included/displayed. Capture the criteria.
steps.confirm: Confirm this step is complete and retain the required evidence before continuing.
steps.narration: But here is the discipline: a GRC violation is an indicator, not a verdict. I opened each source role and confirmed both sides were actually effective for this user. They were. Real conflict. Then — and only then — I looked at mitigation. There was one attached. I screenshotted it but didn’t rely on it; the mitigation itself gets tested in a later lab. This lab is about understanding the raw conflict.

steps.title: Step 3
steps.action: Execute the analysis and record total risks/violations.
steps.confirm: Confirm this step is complete and retain the required evidence before continuing.
steps.narration: I wrote each material risk into my workpaper: risk ID, the business conflict in plain language (“this user could create a fictitious vendor and then pay it”), the access sources on each side, and my disposition: valid conflict, unresolved, recommend removal of the payment function. Business impact first, technical detail second — always. Sameer saw the red risk and said, “So that is a confirmed SoD failure.” “It is a lead,” I corrected. “GRC tells us where to investigate. We still prove the functions, transactions, role sources, and mitigation status before we conclude.”

steps.title: Step 4
steps.action: Drill into each material risk to identify risk ID, functions/actions and underlying transactions/permissions.
steps.confirm: Confirm this step is complete and retain the required evidence before continuing.
steps.narration: I indexed the evidence before writing the conclusion. My training-file convention for this lab was: E01-L04-ARA-UserLevel-Criteria, PNG image E02-L04-ARA-USER-MBROOKS-RAW, Excel file

steps.title: Step 5
steps.action: Determine whether both sides of the conflict are actually assigned/effective for the user.
steps.confirm: Confirm this step is complete and retain the required evidence before continuing.
steps.narration: E03-L04-SOD-AP-001-Detail, PNG image E04-L04-SourceRole-Validation, Excel file W01-L04-SoD-Investigation, Excel file

steps.title: Step 6
steps.action: Review mitigation status only after understanding the raw conflict.
steps.confirm: Confirm this step is complete and retain the required evidence before continuing.
steps.narration: Elena asked for the risk in business language. I translated SOD-AP-001 into the fraud scenario: one person could establish a fictitious vendor and participate in paying it. That translation made the technical result decision-useful. Confirmed: criteria captured

steps.title: Document business impact and proposed action
steps.action: Document business impact and proposed action: remove access, redesign role, mitigate with control, or investigate ruleset issue.
steps.confirm: Confirm this step is complete and retain the required evidence before continuing.
steps.narration: Confirmed: raw results saved Confirmed: material risks drilled down Confirmed: every conclusion explained in business terms

labs.objective: Use GRC simulation to determine the access risk created by a proposed role or role change before provisioning.
labs.scenario: Simulate a proposed role assignment/design change and determine whether it introduces new SoD or critical-access risks.
labs.systems: SAP GRC Access Control - Access Risk Analysis / Simulation; PFCG where role content needs validation.

steps.title: Step 1
steps.action: Identify the proposed user/role or role change from the lab case.
steps.confirm: Confirm this step is complete and retain the required evidence before continuing.
steps.narration: “Sameer, before anyone gets that new role, we’re going to break it in a sandbox first,” I said. Friday’s task: simulate the proposed assignment of Z:FI:AP-CLERK to USER-JCHOI. In GRC I opened Simulation, then Role Level (labels vary by version — I anchored on the function name, not the menu path, per my own rule). I selected the PRD-100 connector, entered the user and proposed role, screenshotted the criteria, and executed.

steps.title: Step 2
steps.action: Open the appropriate GRC simulation function and select target connector/system.
steps.confirm: Confirm this step is complete and retain the required evidence before continuing.
steps.narration: Then I did the comparison that matters: current risk state versus simulated risk state. The user had 3 existing risks; the simulation showed 5. Two were new — introduced by this role. One was SOD-FI-004, journal creation versus journal approval. I drilled into the new risk detail to see which functions caused it, and then opened the role in PFCG Display to confirm the authorization content driving the risk. Confirmed: FB50 and FB02 both present with broad company-code values. My recommendation to Elena: reject as designed, or redesign to remove approval capability, or approve only with a separately validated mitigation. Not “approve because the simulation is clean” — and equally not “reject because risks exist.” I weighed business need against the incremental risk the change creates.

steps.narration: Key lesson I wrote in the workpaper: no new SoD does not mean appropriate access. Critical access and business need still matter even when no conflict pair exists. “The user already has three risks,” Elena said. “Two more may not change much.”

steps.confirm: Confirm this step is complete and retain the required evidence before continuing.

Open selected Risk > Functions > Actions/Permissions mapping.
labs.objective: Assess whether the GRC ruleset adequately represents the organization’s current SAP transactions, permissions, functions and SoD risks.
labs.scenario: Review selected risk/function definitions and identify missing, obsolete or mis-mapped transactions/permissions.
labs.systems: SAP GRC Access Control - Access Risk Analysis configuration/rules; backend PFCG/SAP transaction knowledge as needed.

steps.title: Step 1
steps.action: Obtain the lab-selected risk IDs/functions.
steps.confirm: Confirm this step is complete and retain the required evidence before continuing.
steps.narration: Monday of Week 2, I turned to a question most consultants skip: Is the GRC ruleset itself trustworthy? I opened Rule Setup in GRC and pulled the risk definition for SOD-MM-002, then opened each of its paired functions and their action/permission mappings. Sameer watched as I compared the mapped transactions against the client’s actual S/4 process design. “Here’s the problem,” I said, pointing. “This function still maps to MB21 — a legacy ECC transaction. Your process migrated to the Fiori ’Create Purchase Requisition’ app months ago. Any user whose access comes through the new app path won’t trigger this risk at all.”

steps.title: Step 2
steps.action: Open the risk definition and record risk description, business process and paired functions.
steps.confirm: Confirm this step is complete and retain the required evidence before continuing.
steps.narration: That’s the silent killer of ARA programs: a ruleset that tests a world that no longer exists. I documented the issue precisely — current rule, expected rule, reason, impact — and classified it: obsolete mapping, missing replacement app path. I also flagged a permission-level rule that was overly broad (a wildcard on the activity field) and recommended the regression test that must follow any ruleset change.

steps.title: Step 3
steps.action: Open each function and review actions/transactions and permission-level rules.
steps.confirm: Confirm this step is complete and retain the required evidence before continuing.
steps.narration: And I held my own red line: I did not touch the production ruleset. This is an assurance engagement, not a remediation project. My deliverable is the documented issue and the recommended fix — not an unauthorized configuration change. Sameer frowned at the old MB21 mapping. “But the rule has been in production for years.” “That is the problem,” I said. “A stable rule can become wrong when the process changes. Controls age even when configuration does not.”

steps.title: Step 4
steps.action: Compare mapped transactions/permissions to the current SAP process and S/4/Fiori design supplied in the lab.
steps.confirm: Confirm this step is complete and retain the required evidence before continuing.
steps.narration: I indexed the evidence before writing the conclusion. My training-file convention for this lab was: E01-L06-RiskDefinition-SOD-MM-002, PNG image

steps.title: Step 5
steps.action: Identify obsolete legacy transactions, missing replacement transactions/apps, overly broad permission values or incorrect function mapping.
steps.confirm: Confirm this step is complete and retain the required evidence before continuing.

steps.action: Run a focused ARA test if permitted to see the practical impact of the suspected ruleset issue.
steps.confirm: Confirm this step is complete and retain the required evidence before continuing.
steps.narration: Elena asked whether I would correct the production rule while I was there. I declined. Assurance identifies and supports the issue; remediation requires authorized change governance and regression testing. Confirmed: risk/function mapping reviewed

steps.title: Step 7
steps.action: Document recommended ruleset change and regression-test requirement.
steps.confirm: Confirm this step is complete and retain the required evidence before continuing.
steps.narration: Confirmed: current S/4 process considered Confirmed: issues evidence-linked Confirmed: production untouched

navigation: GRC > Access Risk Analysis / Mitigation > Mitigating Controls / Assignments (menu varies).
Open the mitigation assigned to the selected user/role/risk.
labs.objective: Determine whether a mitigating control assigned to an SoD/critical-access risk is properly designed, assigned, performed and evidenced.
labs.scenario: Assess selected mitigated GRC risks and decide whether the mitigation genuinely reduces the stated risk.
labs.systems: SAP GRC Access Control - mitigation assignment/maintenance; client control evidence.

steps.title: Step 1
steps.action: Start from the selected ARA risk and identify the mitigation relied upon.
steps.confirm: Confirm this step is complete and retain the required evidence before continuing.
steps.narration: Sameer showed me a mitigated risk in ARA — a green “Mitigated” flag next to SOD-FI-001. “So it’s fine?” he asked. “No,” I said. “That’s an administrative status. We test whether the control actually works.” I opened the mitigation definition: control ID MC-1047, description “Monthly review of vendor master changes,” owner listed. Assignment: correct user, correct risk, expiry date — valid, not expired. Good so far.

steps.title: Step 2
steps.action: Open the mitigation definition and record control ID, description, owner/monitor, validity and frequency.
steps.confirm: Confirm this step is complete and retain the required evidence before continuing.
steps.narration: Then the real questions: Was it performed? Does the activity actually address the conflict? Elena’s team produced the evidence: three months of review sign-offs. I checked each against the test period, confirmed the reviewer was independent (not the person whose access created the conflict — I checked the reviewer against the SUIM population), and traced two exceptions from the review into follow-up documentation. One exception, a vendor bank account change, had a follow-up note; the other didn’t. My conclusion: partially effective. Definition and assignment sound; performance evidenced; but one exception lacked follow-up, and the control description was vague about which vendor changes counted as reportable.

steps.title: Step 3
steps.action: Confirm the mitigation is assigned to the correct user/role/risk and is not expired.
steps.confirm: Confirm this step is complete and retain the required evidence before continuing.
steps.narration: The lesson I wrote large in the workpaper: “Mitigated” in GRC is a label. Effectiveness is evidence. And risk acceptance is not a mitigating control — they are fundamentally different things. Sameer tapped the green flag. “This one is mitigated.” “The system says it has a mitigation record,” I said. “Now we find out whether a human actually performed a control capable of reducing the risk.”

steps.title: Step 4
steps.action: Obtain evidence that the control was actually performed during the test period.
steps.confirm: Confirm this step is complete and retain the required evidence before continuing.
steps.narration: I indexed the evidence before writing the conclusion. My training-file convention for this lab was: E01-L07-MC1047-Definition, PNG image

steps.title: Step 5
steps.action: Evaluate whether the control activity addresses the specific conflict, not merely a general manager awareness statement.
steps.confirm: Confirm this step is complete and retain the required evidence before continuing.
steps.narration: E02-L07-Mitigation-Assignment, PNG image E03-L07-Monthly-Review-Evidence, PDF file E04-L07-Reviewer-Independence, Excel file

steps.confirm: Confirm this step is complete and retain the required evidence before continuing.
steps.narration: E05-L07-Exception-Followup, Excel file The control owner wanted the missing follow-up treated as a documentation issue. I explained that unresolved exceptions go to the heart of the control’s purpose; sign-off without follow-through can make the mitigation ineffective. Confirmed: definition and assignment captured

steps.action: Conclude effective, partially effective, ineffective, expired, unsupported or not applicable.
steps.confirm: Confirm this step is complete and retain the required evidence before continuing.
steps.narration: Confirmed: performance evidence tested Confirmed: reviewer independence considered Confirmed: status versus effectiveness distinguished

navigation: GRC > Access Management > Access Request Management > Search/Manage Access Requests (labels vary).
Open request > Request Details / Risk Analysis / Approval or Audit Log / Provisioning Status.
SAP GUI > SU01 or SUIM only when the lab requires confirmation of effective access.
labs.objective: Test whether sampled access requests had valid business need, risk analysis, required approvals and provisioning only after approval.
labs.scenario: Review sampled joiner/mover/access-change requests and identify workflow or provisioning exceptions.
labs.systems: SAP GRC Access Request Management; backend SU01/SUIM for effective-access confirmation when required.

steps.title: Step 1
steps.action: Locate the sampled request by request number or user.
steps.confirm: Confirm this step is complete and retain the required evidence before continuing.
steps.narration: My test follows one chain, end to end: request, then risk analysis, then approvals, then provisioning, then effective access. Miss one link and you’ve proven nothing. The request header showed beneficiary, requested role, validity, and a justification: “Needed for month-end close support.” Two sentences — thin, but let’s see. The embedded risk analysis showed one violation, marked “accepted.” I screenshotted it. Who accepted it? The approval history answered: the role owner approved, with a timestamp. Good — that’s the right approver for a risk acceptance.

steps.title: Step 2
steps.action: Review beneficiary, requested roles/access, validity and business justification.
steps.confirm: Confirm this step is complete and retain the required evidence before continuing.
steps.narration: Then the moment of truth: provisioning timestamp versus final approval timestamp. Approved 14:32. Provisioned 14:29. Three minutes before approval. “Sameer, look at this.” The access landed before the workflow closed. That’s a control exception — the automated provisioning fired early, or a manual pre-provision happened outside the workflow. Either way, the “approve-then-provision” control did not operate. I confirmed effective access in SU01 — the role was there. Consistent with provisioning, contradicting the intended sequence.

steps.title: Step 3
steps.action: Review risk analysis associated with the request and note unresolved violations.
steps.confirm: Confirm this step is complete and retain the required evidence before continuing.
steps.narration: I documented the exception with both timestamps preserved, cross-referenced to the request screenshots. And I wrote the principle in my workpaper, because it’s the one auditors forget: an approved request is not proof of correct provisioning, and a provisioned role is not proof of proper approval. Test the whole chain. Sameer read the approval history and smiled. “Approved.” I put the provisioning timestamp beside it. “Provisioned at 14:29. Approved at 14:32. The workflow looks complete now, but the control sequence failed when it mattered.”

steps.title: Step 4
steps.action: Open workflow/approval history and identify required approvers and timestamps.
steps.confirm: Confirm this step is complete and retain the required evidence before continuing.
steps.narration: I indexed the evidence before writing the conclusion. My training-file convention for this lab was: E01-L08-AR2026-04471-Request, PNG image

steps.title: Step 5
steps.action: Review provisioning status/timestamp. Compare final approval time to provisioning time.
steps.confirm: Confirm this step is complete and retain the required evidence before continuing.
steps.narration: E02-L08-RiskAnalysis, PNG image E03-L08-ApprovalHistory, PNG image E04-L08-ProvisioningTimestamp, PNG image

steps.title: Step 6
steps.action: If the request is expected to be active, confirm effective access in SU01/SUIM.
steps.confirm: Confirm this step is complete and retain the required evidence before continuing.
steps.narration: E05-L08-SU01-EffectiveAccess, PNG image The process owner suggested three minutes was immaterial. I separated elapsed time from control logic: if approval is a preventive gate, provisioning before approval means the gate did not operate. Confirmed: request details

steps.title: Step 7
steps.action: Document exceptions such as provisioning before approval, missing owner approval, weak justification or unapproved extension.
steps.confirm: Confirm this step is complete and retain the required evidence before continuing.
steps.narration: Confirmed: risk and approvals Confirmed: sequence tested Confirmed: effective access confirmed

labs.objective: Test whether role creation/change followed the organization’s governed role lifecycle including ownership, risk analysis, approval, testing and backend alignment.
labs.scenario: Review selected business/technical roles and determine whether their lifecycle evidence supports controlled design and change.
labs.systems: SAP GRC Business Role Management; backend PFCG.

steps.title: Step 1
steps.action: Locate the selected GRC role and record role type, business process, owner and status.
steps.confirm: Confirm this step is complete and retain the required evidence before continuing.
steps.narration: Elena gave me a recently changed business role, BR:FI:GL-ACCOUNTANT, to review its governance lifecycle. In GRC BRM I pulled the role’s definition: type, business process, owner, status. Then the methodology — and here’s the critical first step: BRM is configurable, so I confirmed the client’s required stages for this role type before calling anything “missing.” Their methodology required: definition, then risk analysis, then approval, then testing, then generation. Status showed all stages complete. But I don’t trust green checkmarks. I opened the approval evidence — role owner signed off, dated. Testing evidence: a UAT sign-off document existed. Then I opened the backend role in PFCG Display and compared it against the approved GRC definition.

steps.title: Step 2
steps.action: Review the methodology/lifecycle stages configured by the client and identify which stages were required for this role/change.
steps.confirm: Confirm this step is complete and retain the required evidence before continuing.
steps.narration: Mismatch. The GRC definition specified company code 1000 only. The backend role carried 1000, 2000, and 3000. Someone broadened it after generation — or generated from a stale definition. Either way, the governed definition and the technical reality had diverged. I documented it as two separate findings, per my discipline: (1) a technical mismatch between BRM definition and PFCG content, and (2) a note that the lifecycle workflow itself completed — meaning workflow completion did not prevent the divergence. Never infer technical correctness from completed workflow. My remediation recommendation: regenerate from the approved definition, investigate how the broadening happened, and restrict the company code values.

steps.title: Step 3
steps.action: Review risk analysis and approvals attached to the lifecycle.
steps.confirm: Confirm this step is complete and retain the required evidence before continuing.
steps.narration: “All stages are green,” Sameer said. “Good,” I replied. “Now we compare governance reality with technical reality.” The extra company codes in PFCG turned a green lifecycle into a red reconciliation issue. I indexed the evidence before writing the conclusion. My training-file convention for this lab was:

steps.action: Review testing/UAT evidence if the methodology requires it.
steps.confirm: Confirm this step is complete and retain the required evidence before continuing.

I documented both dimensions separately: lifecycle stages completed, but governed definition and technical role diverged. Confirmed: owner and status captured

labs.module: Week 3 — ARM / BRM / EAM / Access Governance
navigation: GRC > Emergency Access Management > Firefighter Assignments / Logs / Controller Review (labels vary).
Locate Firefighter ID/role assignment and selected session.
Open session activity/transaction log and controller review.
labs.objective: Test emergency-access authorization, session activity, purpose alignment and controller review.
labs.scenario: Review selected Firefighter sessions and determine whether emergency access was appropriately approved, used and independently reviewed.
labs.systems: SAP GRC Emergency Access Management; target SAP system for corroboration when needed.

steps.title: Step 1
steps.action: Identify whether the client uses Firefighter IDs or Firefighter roles.
steps.confirm: Confirm this step is complete and retain the required evidence before continuing.
steps.narration: “Firefighter time,” I said. Sameer pulled up GRC EAM. I picked session FF-LOG-88213 — Firefighter ID FF-PRD-BASIS, used by a Basis admin at 02:14 on a Sunday. First: the assignment. FF-PRD-BASIS had an owner, a controller, a validity period, and an approved purpose on file: “Emergency: apply critical kernel patch per INC-2210.” I screenshotted the assignment — controller named, dates valid, purpose documented. Good design. Then the session: login 02:14, logout 02:47, reason code present. I exported the detailed activity log raw — every transaction executed during the session, unchanged.

steps.title: Step 2
steps.action: Locate the selected assignment and confirm owner/controller, validity and approved purpose.
steps.confirm: Confirm this step is complete and retain the required evidence before continuing.
steps.narration: Now the comparison that defines this lab. The approved purpose was kernel patching. The activity log showed: SPAM (patch tool — consistent), SM37 (job monitoring — plausible), and then SE16 table browsing on BSEG, 40 minutes of it. At 02:30 in the morning. On financial data. “That’s not patching,” Sameer said quietly. Correct. Out-of-purpose activity on a sensitive financial table. The final test — the one that separates a real EAM program from theater: the controller review. The controller had signed off. I checked the review date: four days after the session, with a comment of “OK.” The controller approved an activity log containing unexplained financial table access.

steps.title: Step 3
steps.action: Locate the selected session and record user, Firefighter ID/role, login/logout and reason.
steps.confirm: Confirm this step is complete and retain the required evidence before continuing.
steps.narration: Two findings: (1) out-of-purpose Firefighter usage, and (2) ineffective controller review. I noted the principle in the workpaper: controller assignment is not controller review, and emergency access can be legitimate while its monitoring control fails. Sameer looked at the SE16 activity. “Could that have been part of troubleshooting?” “Possibly,” I said. “That is why we do not accuse. We ask for the connection to the approved purpose. If nobody can explain it, the exception remains.”

steps.title: Step 4
steps.action: Review detailed activity/transactions performed during the session.
steps.confirm: Confirm this step is complete and retain the required evidence before continuing.
steps.narration: I indexed the evidence before writing the conclusion. My training-file convention for this lab was: E01-L10-FF-Assignment, PNG image

steps.title: Step 5

steps.title: List the in-scope ITGC domains
steps.action: List the in-scope ITGC domains: logical access, privileged access, change management and computer operations.
steps.confirm: Confirm this step is complete and retain the required evidence before continuing.
steps.narration: For every control I wrote eight things — and I refused to move on until all eight were filled: risk, control objective, control activity, frequency, owner, population, evidence source, test procedure. The discipline of this lab is specificity. “Review user access quarterly” is not a control — it’s a wish. My version: “Quarterly, the Security Lead runs SUIM, then Users by Complex Selection Criteria on PRD/100 with no validity exclusions, exports the full population, and documents review sign-off within 10 business days.” A stranger could reproduce it. That’s the standard.

steps.title: Step 2
steps.action: For each control write control objective, risk, control activity, frequency, owner, population and evidence source.
steps.confirm: Confirm this step is complete and retain the required evidence before continuing.
steps.narration: For change controls, the evidence source is STMS, then Import History for the target system, tied to change tickets. For operations, SM37 with defined selection criteria. I took one example screenshot of each — SUIM, STMS, SM37 — clearly labeled as evidence-source examples, not operating-effectiveness proof. I built the completeness cross-check: every control mapped to a reproducible evidence source. Any control whose evidence “cannot prove the assertion” got rewritten or flagged. Elena read “Review user access quarterly” and nodded.

steps.confirm: Confirm this step is complete and retain the required evidence before continuing.
