labs.objective: Perform and document a walkthrough that connects the stated control to actual SAP execution, evidence generation and reviewer action.
labs.scenario: Walk one selected SAP control from initiation through processing, evidence generation, review and exception handling.
labs.systems: SAP transaction/report relevant to selected control; examples include SUIM, ARM, STMS or SM37.

steps.title: Step 1
steps.action: Confirm control owner, frequency, trigger and expected evidence.
steps.confirm: Confirm this step is complete and retain the required evidence before continuing.
steps.narration: I sat down with Maria, the Security Lead, for a walkthrough of the quarterly access review control. “Show me last quarter’s review,” I asked, “as you actually did it. Not a demo. The real one.” She opened SUIM, showed me the selection criteria she’d used — I captured them — executed, got the population, and then showed me her review workbook and her sign-off email.

steps.title: Step 2
steps.action: Ask the owner to demonstrate one recent occurrence in SAP using the control-specific transaction/report.
steps.confirm: Confirm this step is complete and retain the required evidence before continuing.
steps.narration: I traced one item end to end: a contractor whose role had been flagged. Maria showed me the approval for the contractor’s extended access. Then I asked the question that exposes weak walkthroughs: “What do you actually check when you review?” Maria hesitated, then said honestly: “Honestly, I scan for names I don’t recognize and check terminations against HR.” That’s a design observation, not an insult: the review criteria weren’t precise enough to detect dormant access or SoD conflicts — only unfamiliar names. The control as described (“comprehensive review of user access”) was not the control as performed.

steps.title: Step 3
steps.action: Capture the selection criteria or source item used.
steps.confirm: Confirm this step is complete and retain the required evidence before continuing.
steps.narration: I documented who, what, when, how — and the gap between documented and observed. And I noted the boundary clearly: a walkthrough tells me the control is designed and understood; one occurrence does not prove a quarterly control operated all year. That’s what operating-effectiveness testing is for. Maria opened SUIM and began setting up a fresh report. “Before you run a demo,” I said, “show me last quarter’s actual review. I want to see what happened, not what could happen.”

steps.title: Step 4
steps.action: Follow the item from initiation to approval/processing/review as applicable.
steps.confirm: Confirm this step is complete and retain the required evidence before continuing.
steps.narration: I indexed the evidence before writing the conclusion. My training-file convention for this lab was: E01-L12-SUIM-Walkthrough-Criteria, PNG image

steps.confirm: Confirm this step is complete and retain the required evidence before continuing.

navigation: Open the SAP source identified in the RCM and walkthrough for this control.
Use the same transaction/report path as the actual control, not a generic substitute.
labs.objective: Determine whether the selected SAP control, if performed as designed, is capable of preventing or detecting the stated risk.
labs.scenario: Evaluate design using the walkthrough plus SAP configuration/process evidence.
labs.systems: SAP source relevant to the control; SUIM/PFCG/GRC/STMS/SM37 depending on control selected.

steps.title: Step 1
steps.action: Restate the risk and control objective.
steps.confirm: Confirm this step is complete and retain the required evidence before continuing.
steps.narration: Back at my desk, I evaluated the quarterly access review as a design. I restated the risk: inappropriate or excessive access accumulating between terminations and detection. Control objective: detect and remove inappropriate access quarterly. Then the design questions, one by one:

steps.title: Step 2
steps.action: Review control owner, frequency, population, precision, evidence and reviewer competence/independence.
steps.confirm: Confirm this step is complete and retain the required evidence before continuing.
steps.narration: Timing? The review happens monthly in their process — good, before too much risk accumulates. Population? Here’s the design flaw: Maria’s standard SUIM variant excluded locked users. So a terminated employee whose account was locked but not deleted would never appear. The population was incomplete by design — not by error. Precision? Review criteria were vague (“look for unfamiliar names”) — too imprecise to reliably detect dormant or over-privileged access. Reviewer? Maria is competent and independent of provisioning. Fine.

steps.title: Step 3
steps.action: Inspect the SAP source/configuration that enables the control.
steps.confirm: Confirm this step is complete and retain the required evidence before continuing.
steps.narration: Evidence? Sign-off email exists but doesn’t document what was reviewed. Doesn’t demonstrate performance. My conclusion: design gap — population incomplete, precision insufficient. I wrote it as a design conclusion only, explicitly not an operating-effectiveness opinion. And I flagged the downstream question: if design is deficient, operating-effectiveness testing has limited value — I explained why we would still sample (to size the problem) but that the design finding stands on its own. Elena asked, “If the review happens every month, isn’t that strong?”

steps.title: Step 4
steps.action: Determine whether the control covers the full relevant population and occurs at the right point in the process.
steps.confirm: Confirm this step is complete and retain the required evidence before continuing.
steps.narration: “Frequency cannot rescue an incomplete population,” I replied. “A monthly review that systematically excludes the wrong accounts can fail twelve times a year.” I indexed the evidence before writing the conclusion. My training-file convention for this lab was: E01-L13-Control-Design-Assessment, Excel file

steps.title: Step 5
steps.action: Assess whether review criteria are precise enough to detect material exceptions.
steps.confirm: Confirm this step is complete and retain the required evidence before continuing.
steps.narration: E02-L13-SUIM-Variant-Exclusion, PNG image E03-L13-Review-Criteria-Observation, Word document W03-L13-DE-Conclusion, Word document The reviewer asked why we would perform any OE work after identifying a design gap. I documented the reason: not to reverse the design conclusion, but to understand magnitude and support remediation prioritization.

steps.title: Step 6
steps.action: Conclude effective design, design gap, or unable to conclude due to missing evidence.
steps.confirm: Confirm this step is complete and retain the required evidence before continuing.
steps.narration: Confirmed: risk and objective restated Confirmed: design attributes assessed Confirmed: conclusion limited to design

labs.systems: SUIM/GRC for access; STMS for transports; SM37 for background jobs; supporting workflow/ticket evidence.

steps.title: Step 1
steps.action: Obtain the complete population for the control period using the control-specific SAP report. Capture criteria before execution.
steps.confirm: Confirm this step is complete and retain the required evidence before continuing.
steps.narration: Now the heavy lifting: three populations, three samples. Access control: I ran the corrected SUIM criteria (no exclusions), captured criteria and count first — 412 users. I recorded the population and reconciled against the license count as an independent expectation. Close enough, documented. Change control: STMS, then Import History on PRD for the quarter — 67 transports. Operations: SM37 for the critical job list — 1,240 executions across 38 jobs.

steps.title: Step 2
steps.action: Record population count and reconcile to an independent expectation where available.
steps.confirm: Confirm this step is complete and retain the required evidence before continuing.
steps.narration: I selected samples per the methodology and tested each item. Most passed. The ones that didn’t: Change sample number 7: Transport imported to production by the same developer who wrote the code. No segregation — developer self-imported. And the change ticket showed no independent approval.

steps.title: Step 3
steps.action: Select the sample using the lab workbook methodology.
steps.confirm: Confirm this step is complete and retain the required evidence before continuing.
steps.narration: Operations sample number 12: A cancelled job (the daily invoice extract) sat cancelled for two days with no investigation note anywhere. Both exceptions stayed in the sample. I wrote the rule in my workpaper that I never bend: a failed sample is not silently replaced, and a clean sample never excuses an incomplete population. Exception rate evaluated, conclusion written with the exceptions explicitly weighed. A junior analyst asked, “Should I replace the failed transport sample with another one so we can see whether the issue repeats?”

steps.action: For access samples inspect approval/effective access/review evidence as required.
steps.confirm: Confirm this step is complete and retain the required evidence before continuing.
steps.narration: “No,” I said. “You can expand the sample if methodology supports it. You never erase the failure by substitution.” I indexed the evidence before writing the conclusion. My training-file convention for this lab was:

I took the SUIM user population export from Lab 14 and interrogated it: Source? SUIM, PRD/100, extracted 14:22 on the test date — matches the criteria screenshot. Confirmed: Parameters? No validity exclusions, no user-type filters — matches the documented criteria. Confirmed: Completeness? Count reconciled to an independent license report. Confirmed: Accuracy? I picked three rows at random and traced each back to SU01 — user type, lock status, and role assignment all matched the export. Confirmed: Alteration? The raw file’s timestamp predates any analysis copy, and analysis lives only in the working copy. Confirmed:

My control conclusion is scoped accordingly. The principle I wrote in bold: “system generated” does not mean “reliable for every purpose.” Reliability is purpose-specific, and limitations get documented, not hidden.

labs.objective: Assess security/control risks created by ECC-to-S/4 role migration and redesign.
labs.scenario: Review migrated/retained roles and identify legacy, broad, obsolete or poorly redesigned access.
labs.systems: SAP GUI; PFCG; SUIM; GRC ARA if available.

steps.title: Step 1
steps.action: Obtain the migrated-role inventory and identify legacy vs redesigned roles.
steps.confirm: Confirm this step is complete and retain the required evidence before continuing.
steps.narration: I pulled the migrated-role inventory from Elena and used SUIM to export current role-to-user assignments for the flagged legacy roles. Raw file, criteria captured. Then PFCG, role by role. The pattern was familiar and ugly: Z:MM:LEGACY-FULL — an ECC-era role with 340 menu entries, retained “temporarily” in S/4, still holding obsolete transactions (ME21, MB52) alongside broad MIGO and MI20 authorizations. Assigned to 23 users. The migration mapping document said it should have been decommissioned in Wave 2. “Temporarily,” Sameer said, “is the most dangerous word in SAP security.”

steps.title: Step 2
steps.action: Use SUIM to obtain current role/user assignments for selected roles; capture criteria and export.
steps.confirm: Confirm this step is complete and retain the required evidence before continuing.
steps.narration: I ran ARA against the role: it generated 9 risks, several reflecting S/4 process changes the ECC ruleset era never anticipated. The S/4 process redesign had merged steps that ECC kept separate — so old role designs now combined newly incompatible duties. I separated my findings into two buckets, as always: migration governance gaps (no owner review, no UAT evidence, no decommissioning) and technical access risks (obsolete transactions, over-broad values). Remediation priorities ranked: remove legacy access first, redesign second, retest third.

steps.title: Step 3
steps.action: Open selected roles in PFCG Display and review Menu, Authorizations and User assignments.
steps.confirm: Confirm this step is complete and retain the required evidence before continuing.
steps.narration: Key line in the workpaper: a migrated role that technically works can still be dangerously over-privileged, and ECC-era controls don’t automatically survive process redesign. Sameer called Z:MM:LEGACY-FULL “temporary.” I smiled. “Temporary access becomes permanent when nobody owns the exit condition. Show me the Wave 2 decommissioning evidence.” There was none.

steps.action: Identify obsolete ECC transactions, broad technical/security roles and changed S/4 business functions.

steps.confirm: Confirm this step is complete and retain the required evidence before continuing.

I documented why migration changed the context: redesigned processes can turn historically separate permissions into new incompatible combinations. Confirmed: current assignments exported

labs.objective: Validate Fiori access end to end: assigned content, launch behavior, backend authorization and troubleshooting evidence.
labs.scenario: Test selected Fiori apps for expected positive and negative access and explain the authorization path.
labs.systems: Fiori Launchpad; PFCG/SUIM; SU53; STAUTHTRACE/ST01 if approved.

steps.title: Step 1
steps.action: Identify app, user, expected business action and expected allow/deny result.
steps.confirm: Confirm this step is complete and retain the required evidence before continuing.
steps.narration: “Tile visibility is not authorization,” I told Elena. “Let’s prove it.” Test case: USER-DCAMPOS should be able to view purchase requisitions in the Fiori app “Manage Purchase Requisitions — Professional” but should not be able to release (approve) them. I confirmed her content assignment in PFCG — the front-end role with the right catalog, and the back-end role carrying the OData authorizations. Then I launched the app as her.

steps.title: Step 2
steps.action: Confirm user-role/content assignment using PFCG/SUIM appropriate to the client architecture.
steps.confirm: Confirm this step is complete and retain the required evidence before continuing.
steps.narration: She could view PRs. I screenshotted it. Then I attempted the release action. Error. Exactly as designed — negative test passed. Then the reverse test with USER-TNGUYEN, who should be able to release. He launched, executed the release, success. Positive test passed, screenshots captured. But a third case broke: USER-KLEE could see the tile but got a backend error trying to open any PR. Tile visible, app broken — the classic distributed-authorization failure. Immediately after the error, I ran SU53 in the correct ABAP system (front-end versus back-end system confusion is the rookie mistake here). It showed a failed check on authorization object M-EINK-FRG with activity 02 missing from the backend role.

steps.title: Step 3
steps.action: Launch the app and execute the actual business action; do not stop at tile visibility.
steps.confirm: Confirm this step is complete and retain the required evidence before continuing.
steps.narration: I mapped that object back to the PFCG role content and found the backend role had the display authorization but not the release activity — while the catalog assignment suggested full access. The fix direction: align backend role values with intended business action. Trace tools? Not needed — SU53 answered it, and I only trace with approval, scoped tightly, stopped immediately. Elena pointed to the visible tile. “So KLEE has the app.”

steps.title: Step 4
steps.action: Capture success or error. If error, run SU53 immediately in the relevant ABAP system.
steps.confirm: Confirm this step is complete and retain the required evidence before continuing.
steps.narration: “He has the doorway,” I said. “Now we test whether the backend lets him through.” The SU53 failure proved the distinction immediately. I indexed the evidence before writing the conclusion. My training-file convention for this lab was: E01-L17-DCAMPOS-View-OK, PNG image

steps.title: Step 5
steps.action: Review failed authorization object/field values and map them to PFCG role content.
steps.confirm: Confirm this step is complete and retain the required evidence before continuing.
steps.narration: E02-L17-DCAMPOS-Release-Denied, PNG image E03-L17-TNGUYEN-Release-OK, PNG image

steps.title: Step 6
steps.action: If SU53 is insufficient, obtain approval, start STAUTHTRACE/ST01 for the relevant user/time, reproduce once, stop trace promptly and evaluate checks.
steps.confirm: Confirm this step is complete and retain the required evidence before continuing.
steps.narration: E04-L17-KLEE-BackendError, PNG image E05-L17-SU53-MEINKFRG, PNG image E06-L17-PFCG-BackendRole, PNG image

steps.title: Step 7
steps.action: Perform the required negative test with an unauthorized user/role where the lab case provides one.
steps.confirm: Confirm this step is complete and retain the required evidence before continuing.
steps.narration: The reviewer asked why I did not launch a trace. I documented proportionality: SU53 identified the failed object, so broader tracing was unnecessary. Use the least invasive diagnostic that answers the question. Confirmed: actual business action tested Confirmed: not just tiles

labs.objective: Identify privileged users/roles/profiles and determine whether access is restricted, justified, monitored and segregated.
labs.scenario: Assess high-privilege access including SAP_ALL/SAP_NEW, security administration, Basis/technical access and other critical authorizations.
labs.systems: SUIM; SU01; PFCG; GRC ARA/EAM where applicable.

steps.title: Define the privileged-access criteria for the lab
steps.action: Define the privileged-access criteria for the lab: profiles, roles, critical transactions/authorization objects.
steps.confirm: Confirm this step is complete and retain the required evidence before continuing.
steps.narration: I defined privilege explicitly before hunting it — because “admin” labels lie. My criteria: SAP-ALL/SAP-NEW profiles, security administration roles (S-USER-* objects with change activity), Basis/technical roles with production transport capability, and critical objects like S-TABU-NAM with broad table access. SUIM by profile: 6 users with SAP-ALL. Raw export saved. SU01 on the first: USER-ADMIN01 — a dialog account, interactive use, SAP-ALL with no expiry. Justification on file? None. Owner? Listed as “IT.” Monitoring? None found.

steps.title: Step 2
steps.action: Run SUIM report(s) that identify the relevant population. Capture criteria and export raw results.
steps.confirm: Confirm this step is complete and retain the required evidence before continuing.
steps.narration: The second one was worse: USER-DEV03, a developer, holding a role with production import authorization in STMS. Development plus production change capability in one pair of hands. I opened the role in PFCG and screenshotted the S-TRANSPRT object with activity 6 (import) against production — that’s the smoking gun, the value, and the role, all in one frame. Third pattern: a generic privileged ID, RFC-SUPER, no named owner, used by three interfaces. Standing privilege where emergency access should be the model — and no periodic review evidence anywhere.

steps.title: Step 3
steps.action: Select privileged users and inspect SU01 status/roles/profiles.
steps.confirm: Confirm this step is complete and retain the required evidence before continuing.
steps.narration: Elena’s team produced justification for two of the six; the rest had nothing. My finding: privileged access was not restricted, justified, or monitored to standard, with remediation split by pattern — emergency-only access via EAM for the standing privileges, removal for the rest, and a hard rule that developers never hold production import rights. “This role isn’t called administrator,” the owner said. “I’m not auditing names,” I replied. “I’m auditing capability.” The S-TRANSPRT activity value told the story more clearly than the role title ever could.

steps.title: Step 4
steps.action: Open the source role in PFCG and identify the critical authorization that creates privilege.
steps.confirm: Confirm this step is complete and retain the required evidence before continuing.
steps.narration: I indexed the evidence before writing the conclusion. My training-file convention for this lab was: E01-L18-SAPALL-Population-RAW, Excel file E02-L18-ADMIN01-SU01, PNG image

steps.title: Step 5
steps.action: Review business/technical justification, ownership and monitoring evidence.
steps.confirm: Confirm this step is complete and retain the required evidence before continuing.
steps.narration: E03-L18-DEV03-STRANSPRT, PNG image E04-L18-RFC-SUPER-Ownership, Excel file E05-L18-PrivilegedAccess-Assessment, Excel file

steps.title: Step 6
steps.action: If privilege is emergency-only, reconcile to EAM rather than accepting standing access without explanation.
steps.confirm: Confirm this step is complete and retain the required evidence before continuing.
steps.narration: Management produced justification for only two of six SAP-ALL users. I did not treat missing paperwork as the only issue; I also tested ownership, expiry, monitoring, and whether standing privilege should be replaced by controlled emergency access. Confirmed: privilege criteria documented

steps.action: Identify inappropriate combinations such as security administration plus business processing or development plus production change capability.
steps.confirm: Confirm this step is complete and retain the required evidence before continuing.
steps.narration: Confirmed: population exported Confirmed: users traced to source role/object Confirmed: justification and monitoring tested

labs.lab: Lab 19 — Independent QA/QC of Tester Workpapers
navigation: For each tester workpaper, return to the exact SAP transaction/report named in that workpaper.
Re-run or inspect the relevant population/detail using the same criteria, then independently assess the result.
labs.objective: Independently reperform key tester procedures and determine whether tester conclusions are supported by complete, accurate evidence.
labs.scenario: Review the capstone tester workpapers and identify missed exceptions, incomplete populations and unsupported conclusions.
labs.systems: Use the SAP source corresponding to each tester workpaper: SUIM/GRC/STMS/SM37/ARM/EAM as applicable.

steps.title: Step 1
steps.action: Select the tester workpaper and identify control objective, population, sample and conclusion.
steps.confirm: Confirm this step is complete and retain the required evidence before continuing.
steps.narration: I took the UAR workpaper first. Population stated: 412 users. The retained raw export: 411 rows. One row missing. I re-ran the SUIM criteria myself — 412. The tester had exported after applying a filter. An incomplete population invalidates a clean-sample conclusion, and I wrote exactly that in the QA note. Next: the change-management workpaper concluded “operating effectively.” I re-ran STMS for the same period and opened the transport the tester had sampled. Then I opened the one next to it — which the tester hadn’t sampled — and found it was the developer’s own production import, ticket unapproved. The tester missed it because the sample never touched it; but the workpaper’s population was also under-counted (67 transports tested against a stated population of 61 — the criteria screenshot showed a date range that cut six transports off).

steps.title: Step 2
steps.action: Check whether the tester retained selection criteria and raw population.
steps.confirm: Confirm this step is complete and retain the required evidence before continuing.
steps.narration: Third: the EAM workpaper — controller review accepted at face value. I reperformed: the controller review for the session in question was dated, but the activity log attached to the review showed unexplained SE16 usage that the review comment didn’t address. Missed exception. Each workpaper got a QA note: issue, evidence, impact, required correction. Ratings: revise, revise, fail. I preserved the original tester evidence untouched — read-only, always — and saved my re-performance evidence with QA prefixes. The principle, written in the log header: QA/QC is independent verification, not making the tester’s work pass.

steps.title: Step 3
steps.action: Reperform the critical SAP step using the same source.
steps.confirm: Confirm this step is complete and retain the required evidence before continuing.
steps.narration: The junior consultant said, “The conclusion is right; I just need help cleaning up the workpaper.” “My job is not to make it look right,” I said. “My job is to determine whether another reviewer can reach the same conclusion from the retained evidence.”

steps.title: Step 4
steps.action: Compare tester evidence to SAP source and look for contradictory facts or omitted exceptions.
steps.confirm: Confirm this step is complete and retain the required evidence before continuing.
steps.narration: I indexed the evidence before writing the conclusion. My training-file convention for this lab was: QA01-L19-UAR-Reperformance.xlsx QA02-L19-STMS-Reperformance.xlsx

steps.title: Step 5
steps.action: Verify sample items and reviewer notes.
steps.confirm: Confirm this step is complete and retain the required evidence before continuing.
steps.narration: QA03-L19-EAM-Reperformance.xlsx QA04-L19-Review-Log.xlsx

steps.title: Document QA review note
steps.action: Document QA review note: issue, evidence, impact and required correction.
steps.confirm: Confirm this step is complete and retain the required evidence before continuing.
steps.narration: Three QA results—revise, revise, fail—were tied to concrete defects: incomplete population, truncated transport period, and superficial EAM review. Each note stated issue, evidence, impact, and required correction. Confirmed: Conclusion is evidence-linked Confirmed: Raw evidence is preserved

steps.title: Step 7
steps.action: Do not edit the original tester evidence; record QA in the QA/QC review log.
steps.confirm: Confirm this step is complete and retain the required evidence before continuing.
steps.narration: Confirmed: Reviewer can reproduce the result Confirmed: Open questions and limitations are documented

labs.objective: Evaluate identified SAP control exceptions for risk, severity, root cause, scope and reporting impact.
labs.scenario: Assess capstone deficiencies including termination, privileged population, change segregation, Firefighter purpose, weak mitigation and Fiori backend access.
labs.systems: SAP/GRC source relevant to each deficiency; evidence already obtained in prior capstone testing may be reperformed as needed.

steps.title: Step 1
steps.action: Take one deficiency at a time and identify the failed criterion/control.
steps.confirm: Confirm this step is complete and retain the required evidence before continuing.
steps.narration: Now I took each exception and built a defensible deficiency. I started with the termination finding from Lab 2. Back to SUIM/SU01 — condition confirmed, evidence ID attached. Scope: was it one user or systemic? I re-ran the reconciliation of terminated employees against active SAP users: 11 of 43 terminations in the period still had valid access. Not isolated — systemic. Root cause: no automated deprovisioning trigger from HR; removal depended on a manual ticket nobody owned. Effect: ex-employees retained production access for weeks. Compensating controls asserted? A monthly review — but I tested it in Lab 13 and found its population excluded locked users, so it demonstrably didn’t catch these. Severity: significant deficiency, per the methodology criteria, because the control absence was systemic and the compensating control was ineffective.

steps.title: Step 2
steps.action: Return to the SAP/GRC source and confirm the condition is factual and evidence-supported.
steps.confirm: Confirm this step is complete and retain the required evidence before continuing.
steps.narration: The privileged-access finding: likelihood high, impact high, but scope smaller (6 users, now being remediated). Severity: high finding, not a significant deficiency. The Firefighter controller-review finding: I was careful — do not overstate. The emergency access itself was approved; the monitoring failed. Root cause: controller reviews treated as perfunctory sign-off, no criteria, no SLA. Management action: define review criteria, 48-hour review SLA, retraining. I wrote every one in the full structure: Criteria, then Condition, then Cause, then Effect/Risk, then Evidence, then Recommendation. And I flagged the trap explicitly in my notes: do not downgrade severity because management plans to fix it later, and do not upgrade it beyond what the evidence shows.

steps.title: Step 3
steps.action: Determine affected population/time period and whether the issue is isolated or systemic.
steps.confirm: Confirm this step is complete and retain the required evidence before continuing.
steps.narration: Elena asked, “Can we call the terminated-user issue isolated? We only found one in the original sample.” “Not until we scope it,” I said. The reconciliation found 11 of 43 terminations with valid access. The evidence changed the story from one bad account to a process failure.

steps.title: Step 4
steps.action: Assess likelihood/impact in the context of the control objective.
steps.confirm: Confirm this step is complete and retain the required evidence before continuing.
steps.narration: I indexed the evidence before writing the conclusion. My training-file convention for this lab was: E01-L20-Termination-Reconciliation, Excel file E02-L20-PrivilegedFinding-Assessment, Excel file

steps.title: Identify root cause
steps.action: Identify root cause: design, execution, evidence, configuration, governance or monitoring.
steps.confirm: Confirm this step is complete and retain the required evidence before continuing.
steps.narration: E03-L20-EAM-Deficiency-Assessment, Excel file W05-L20-Deficiency-Register, Excel file

steps.title: Step 6
steps.action: Consider compensating controls only if evidenced.
steps.confirm: Confirm this step is complete and retain the required evidence before continuing.
steps.narration: I challenged my own conclusions in both directions: do not minimize a systemic absence of control, and do not overstate a monitoring failure when the underlying emergency access was properly approved. Confirmed: conditions reconfirmed Confirmed: scope assessed

steps.confirm: Confirm this step is complete and retain the required evidence before continuing.
steps.narration: Confirmed: root causes identified Confirmed: severity rationale documented

labs.objective: Validate whether management’s claimed remediation actually resolves the SAP control deficiency and is operating as intended.
labs.scenario: Retest remediation claims and classify them as closed, partially remediated, risk accepted or still open.
labs.systems: SAP/GRC source corresponding to each remediated deficiency.

steps.title: Step 1
steps.action: Read the original deficiency and management remediation claim.
steps.confirm: Confirm this step is complete and retain the required evidence before continuing.
steps.narration: Elena’s team came back with remediation claims. My job: verify, not trust. Claim 1: “Terminated user access removed — ticket closed.” I went to SU01. USER-RSHARMA: locked, but the role assignments were still present, and the validity date was unchanged. Locked is not removed. Ticket said closed; the condition persisted. Classification: still open. The ticket was administrative closure, not remediation. Claim 2: “SoD conflict in Z:MM:PURCHASER redesigned.” I opened PFCG — MIGO removed from authorizations. Then I ran ARA on the role: conflict count dropped from 9 to 2. The 2 remaining were different risks than the original — I traced them and found they predated the change and weren’t part of this remediation’s scope. Classification: validated closed — for the specific condition. I documented that closure was scoped to the finding, not a claim that the role is now risk-free.

steps.title: Step 2
steps.action: Identify the exact condition that must change for closure.
steps.confirm: Confirm this step is complete and retain the required evidence before continuing.
steps.narration: Claim 3: “Firefighter review process strengthened — policy updated.” I asked for operating evidence. They produced the new policy document — and nothing else. No review performed under the new criteria since implementation. Classification: partial — design changed, operation not yet evidenced. Follow-up date set. Claim 4: One item was labeled “remediated” but the evidence was a signed risk-acceptance form. I reclassified it honestly: risk accepted, which is a governance decision, not technical remediation, and must never be reported as “closed/remediated.” Before closing each item I asked: does the fix address the root cause and the full population, or just the one user in the finding? labs.objective: Convert the completed SAP controls testing into an audit-ready evidence package, executive dashboard and management report.
labs.scenario: Prepare the final capstone reporting package for ABC Manufacturing using only conclusions supported by indexed evidence.
labs.systems: No new transaction is mandatory; return to SUIM/PFCG/GRC/STMS/SM37/Fiori only to resolve evidence gaps identified during final QA.

steps.title: Step 1
steps.action: Reconcile all planned capstone deliverables to completed workpapers.
steps.confirm: Confirm this step is complete and retain the required evidence before continuing.
steps.narration: Final week. No new transactions — my job now was to make the whole engagement survive an independent reviewer’s eyes. I started with the evidence index. Every file checked: named correctly, opens, criteria visible, cross-references intact. I found one broken reference — a finding cited E03 but the file was labeled E04 — and fixed the index, not the evidence. Then the findings register: every finding had criteria, condition, risk, cause, recommendation, owner, status, and evidence ID. One finding had no evidence ID attached. It went back to its source, evidence re-extracted as new dated evidence, index updated. No exceptions.

steps.title: Step 2
steps.action: Review evidence index for missing files, unclear filenames, missing criteria or broken cross-references.
steps.confirm: Confirm this step is complete and retain the required evidence before continuing.
steps.narration: Then the tie-out that executives trust and auditors verify: dashboard numbers must equal register numbers. Open deficiencies: 4. Remediation in progress: 3. Validated closed: 6. Risk accepted: 2. My dashboard said exactly that, and I traced each count back to the register line by line. I structured the audit-readiness assessment by domain — access, SoD/GRC, privileged/EAM, change, operations, S/4/Fiori, evidence quality — each rated with its evidence basis. And I ran my final reviewer test, the one I put at the top of the management report’s methodology section: could another consultant reproduce every conclusion from the evidence package without calling me? I handed the package to a colleague cold. She reproduced all four open-deficiency conclusions. Pass.

steps.title: Step 3
steps.action: Review findings register for consistent criteria, condition, risk, cause, recommendation, owner and status.
steps.confirm: Confirm this step is complete and retain the required evidence before continuing.
steps.narration: The final report went to Elena’s steering committee: scope, approach, key observations, risk themes, remediation priorities, limitations — including the open evidence requests and the items where scope was limited by access. Written in plain management language, every sentence traceable to a workpaper and evidence ID. Because here’s what I told the committee in the closing session, and it’s the sentence the whole eight weeks earned: “Audit readiness doesn’t mean you have no issues. It means every issue, every piece of evidence, and every remediation status is controlled, supportable, and reproducible. ABC Manufacturing isn’t perfect — but today, ABC Manufacturing is ready.”

steps.title: Step 4
steps.action: Tie executive dashboard counts to the detailed findings register.
steps.confirm: Confirm this step is complete and retain the required evidence before continuing.
steps.narration: Before the steering committee, Elena asked, “Are we ready?” “I know the answer only after the package survives someone who did not build it,” I said. I handed it to a colleague cold and watched what happened. I indexed the evidence before writing the conclusion. My training-file convention for this lab was:

Foundational — read before Module B1
Before starting B1–B10, get grounded in why SAP controls exist at all. Every module in this programme ties back to one or more of the seven goals below.

1. Regulatory Compliance SOX (Sarbanes-Oxley) — ICFR (Internal Control over Financial Reporting), ensuring financial statements are free of material misstatement Industry-specific mandates — GDPR (data privacy), HIPAA (healthcare), Basel III (banking), local statutory requirements External audit readiness — providing auditors with evidence controls operate effectively, avoiding audit findings/qualified opinions

2. Fraud Prevention & Detection Segregation of Duties (SoD) — no single user can execute conflicting steps in a process end-to-end (e.g., create vendor + post payment) Sensitive access controls — restricting powerful transactions (mass changes, direct table updates, debug/change access) to authorized, monitored users Detective controls — anomaly monitoring, exception reports, continuous controls monitoring (CCM) to catch fraud that preventive controls miss

3. Financial Statement Integrity Accuracy, completeness, and validity of transactions posted to the ledger Proper authorization hierarchies (approval limits, workflow release strategies) Reliable cutoff, valuation, and reconciliation processes

4. Operational Risk Management Protecting against unauthorized or erroneous transactions that disrupt business operations Business continuity — ensuring critical processes (O2C, P2P, R2R) aren't compromised by access or config errors Data integrity across master data (vendor, customer, material, GL accounts)

5. IT General Controls (ITGCs) — the technical backbone Change management — controlled transport path, no direct production changes Access management — provisioning/deprovisioning aligned to role, periodic access recertification Computer operations — job scheduling, batch monitoring, backup/recovery

6. Accountability & Traceability Audit trails (change documents, table logging) that answer "who did what, when, and was it authorized" Clear ownership of controls (control owners, risk owners) so failures have accountability
7. Stakeholder Confidence Investor and board assurance that governance is sound Reduced insurance/regulatory risk exposure Reputational protection — control failures often become public failures

steps.action: When you arrive on a new SAP engagement — whether it is a greenfield S/4HANA implementation, an operating effectiveness review, or a remediation programme — the first task is establishing the Risk Universe. What are all the things that could go wrong in this environment? Until you have that picture, you cannot design controls, scope tests, or give your client a credible view of their exposure. Risk classification is how we build that picture systematically.

steps.title: Financial risk arises when an error, omission, or deliberate manipulatio…
steps.action: Financial risk arises when an error, omission, or deliberate manipulation results in a financial statement that does not accurately reflect the organisation's true position. This is the category most directly linked to fraud, misstatement, and external audit findings — and it is the primary target of SAP GRC Access Control deployments.
steps.narration: Financial risk arises when an error, omission, or deliberate manipulation results in a financial statement that does not accurately reflect the organisation's true position. This is the category most directly linked to fraud, misstatement, and external audit findings — and it is the primary target of SAP GRC Access Control deployments.

steps.title: Consider a concrete SAP example. A user creates a fictitious vendor usin…
steps.action: Consider a concrete SAP example. A user creates a fictitious vendor using transaction XK01 — Vendor Master Create — and then processes a payment run to that vendor via F110 — Automatic Payment Programme. Because the same person can both create the payee and authorise the payment, no independent check exists. Cash leaves the organisation, accounts payable is misstated, and the external auditor will raise a material weakness finding under SOX Section 404.

steps.action: US Listed Companies SOX Section 404 Management must assess and external auditors must attest to the effectiveness of internal controls over financial reporting. SAP is the system of record — control gaps in SAP become SOX material weaknesses.

navigation_sections: Navigate to: Track 0 · Controls Theory → B1 — Risk Types
Risk Types in SAP Environments

Master the practitioner's starting question — what could go wrong? Classify Financial, Compliance, and Operational risk; understand inherent versus residual risk; and apply the risk-to-control cycle to real SAP scenarios.
10–12 min · 1,039 words · 3 sections · 5-question quiz · AI Tutor

Learning Objectives By the end of this module you will be able to identify and define the three primary risk categories — Financial, Compliance, and Operational — in SAP environments, and give a concrete example of each. By the end of this module you will be able to explain how risks drive the need for controls and describe the relationship between inherent risk and residual risk. By the end of this module you will be able to apply a risk classification framework to a real-world SAP scenario — such as a Procure-to-Pay process or period-end financial close — and identify the appropriate control response.
Section 1 · The Risk Universe

When you arrive on a new SAP engagement — whether it is a greenfield S/4HANA implementation, an operating effectiveness review, or a remediation programme — the first task is establishing the Risk Universe. What are all the things that could go wrong in this environment? Until you have that picture, you cannot design controls, scope tests, or give your client a credible view of their exposure. Risk classification is how we build that picture systematically.

The Practitioner's Starting Question Every controls engagement — regardless of industry, SAP version, or client size — begins with one question: what could go wrong? Your answer to that question is your Risk Universe. This module gives you the framework to answer it precisely and consistently.
1.1 · Financial Risk

Financial risk arises when an error, omission, or deliberate manipulation results in a financial statement that does not accurately reflect the organisation's true position. This is the category most directly linked to fraud, misstatement, and external audit findings — and it is the primary target of SAP GRC Access Control deployments.

Consider a concrete SAP example. A user creates a fictitious vendor using transaction XK01 — Vendor Master Create — and then processes a payment run to that vendor via F110 — Automatic Payment Programme. Because the same person can both create the payee and authorise the payment, no independent check exists. Cash leaves the organisation, accounts payable is misstated, and the external auditor will raise a material weakness finding under SOX Section 404.

HIGH SoD Conflict — Vendor Creation + Payment Run Function A XK01 Create / Maintain Vendor Master Function B F110 Automatic Payment Run Risk One user can create a fictitious vendor and pay it — no independent authorisation required Control SoD Ruleset in SAP GRC Access Control · MSMP workflow approval for exceptions COSO Obj. Operations · Financial Reporting

GRC Connection Financial risk is the primary driver for deploying SAP GRC Access Control. The GRC Ruleset is essentially a codified library of financial risks expressed as SoD conflict rules. When GRC surfaces a conflict, it is surfacing an elevated inherent risk awaiting a control response.
1.2 · Compliance Risk

Compliance risk is the risk that the organisation fails to meet an external regulatory obligation. In SAP environments, this covers a wide spectrum of requirements depending on the organisation's sector and geography:

US Listed Companies SOX Section 404 Management must assess and external auditors must attest to the effectiveness of internal controls over financial reporting. SAP is the system of record — control gaps in SAP become SOX material weaknesses.

EU / Global GDPR Personal data stored and processed in SAP — HR records, customer data, supplier contacts — must be handled per GDPR Article requirements. Inadequate access controls or audit logging creates compliance exposure.

Life Sciences FDA 21 CFR Part 11 Electronic records and electronic signatures in SAP must meet FDA validation standards. Failure to maintain compliant audit trails is a direct regulatory violation with enforcement consequences.

All Sectors IFRS / Local GAAP SAP is the system of record for financial reporting. Configuration errors in chart of accounts, consolidation settings, or posting period controls can create IFRS / GAAP non-compliance.

The System of Record Multiplier Because SAP is the system of record, weaknesses in configuration, access controls, or change management can translate directly into regulatory non-compliance. The consequences extend beyond financial penalties to reputational damage that controls remediation cannot easily reverse.
1.3 · Operational Risk

Operational risk arises from weaknesses in day-to-day processes, system configuration, or human behaviour that impair the organisation's ability to operate accurately and efficiently. A key SAP example is the three-way match tolerance setting in Materials Management.
In a correctly configured Procure-to-Pay process, the system automatically compares three documents before posting an invoice:
ME21N
Purchase Order
Agreed price & quantity for goods or services
MIGO
Goods Receipt
Physical confirmation goods were received
MIRO
Vendor Invoice
Supplier's invoice — must match PO & GR within tolerance
FAIL
Invoice Posts
Tolerance too wide — discrepancy ignored

If the tolerance threshold is configured too loosely — or not configured at all — the system will post and pay invoices with significant discrepancies between purchase order value, goods receipt quantity, and vendor invoice amount. This is not necessarily fraud: it may simply be a configuration weakness. But it costs the organisation money and erodes the reliability of its financial data — a textbook operational risk with direct financial impact.

Operational risk also includes inadequate training (users bypassing standard process steps), unclear process ownership (no one reviews exception reports), and system availability failures. In the context of controls audit work, we focus primarily on process-level operational risks that can be mitigated by automated or manual controls.
1.4 · The Overlap — Risks Are Not Independent Silos

The three categories do not operate independently. A single control weakness can simultaneously create Financial, Compliance, and Operational risk. This overlap is one of the most important insights for practitioners — and the reason risk classification must identify the primary risk driver rather than simply listing all affected categories.

Section 2
Section 2 · From Risk to Control

Now that we have our Risk Universe mapped, the question becomes: what do we do about it? The answer is a control. A control is an activity to mitigate or manage a risk — something put in place to address the risks we have identified. That definition is simple. Making it operational requires one additional concept.
2.1 · Inherent Risk and Residual Risk
Inherent Risk The level of risk present before any controls are applied. Your baseline when you first assess a client environment.
Controls The gap-filler. Your primary deliverable on an engagement. Moves the organisation from inherent to residual.
Residual Risk What remains after controls are implemented and operating. Must fall within the organisation's defined risk tolerance.

Conceptual Formula Residual Risk = Inherent Risk − Control Effectiveness This is a conceptual model, not a literal arithmetic equation. In practice, practitioners use risk ratings (High / Medium / Low) adjusted by the degree of reliance placed on each control, informed by design and operating effectiveness testing results.

Your job on an engagement is to help your client move from an elevated inherent-risk position to an acceptable residual-risk position. That gap is filled by controls. This is why risk identification and control design always move together. Risk identification without control design is just a problem list. Control design without risk identification is a set of activities with no anchor.
2.2 · The SAP GRC Ruleset — The Risk-to-Control Cycle

SAP GRC Access Control's Ruleset is the most direct example of the risk-to-control cycle in an SAP context. Each rule in the Ruleset says: if a single user can perform Function A and Function B, a Segregation of Duties conflict exists. The Ruleset is a codified Risk Universe for access-related financial risks.
How the Risk-to-Control Cycle Works in GRC AC
01 Run SoD Analysis The GRC Ruleset scans all user roles and identifies combinations of transactions that create SoD conflicts. Each conflict is a flagged inherent risk.
02 Classify the Risk Each conflict is rated High, Medium, or Low based on the financial exposure of the conflicting functions. XK01 + F110 is typically High — direct payment fraud potential.

03 Design the Control Response Options: (a) remove conflicting access from the role, (b) implement a compensating control such as an MSMP approval workflow, or (c) formally accept the risk with documented business justification and enhanced monitoring.

04 Measure Residual Risk Re-run the SoD analysis. Remaining unmitigated conflicts represent residual risk. Test compensating controls for operating effectiveness. Document the outcome in the Risk and Controls Matrix.

Case Study: PetroNova S.A. — Risk Mapping on a Greenfield S/4HANA

PetroNova S.A., a mid-size hydrocarbon producer headquartered in Port Meridian, Arcadia, commissioned a 37-week SAP S/4HANA implementation with TIB Systems as the QA/QC partner. During Phase 0 — Blueprint & Governance, the controls audit team produced a Risk Universe document covering all three risk categories for each process area.

Key finding in Accounts Payable: A single user role combined vendor master maintenance (XK01, XK02) with payment run authorisation (F110). The inherent risk rating was High — direct payment fraud potential. The recommended control was a workflow-enforced dual approval in SAP, implemented in MSMP. Post-control, residual risk was reduced to Low, subject to annual operating effectiveness testing.

This single finding — surfaced in Blueprint, remediated in Design, tested in UAT — prevented a potential control failure from reaching production on Day 1 of Go-Live. That is the value proposition of a controls-first implementation approach.

Section 3 · Classification in Practice — The RCM

Risk Types in SAP Environments

Master the practitioner's starting question — what could go wrong? Classify Financial, Compliance, and Operational risk; understand inherent versus residual risk; and apply the risk-to-control cycle to real SAP scenarios.

10–12 min · 1,039 words · 3 sections · 5-question quiz · AI Tutor

Learning Objectives By the end of this module you will be able to identify and define the three primary risk categories — Financial, Compliance, and Operational — in SAP environments, and give a concrete example of each. By the end of this module you will be able to explain how risks drive the need for controls and describe the relationship between inherent risk and residual risk. By the end of this module you will be able to apply a risk classification framework to a real-world SAP scenario — such as a Procure-to-Pay process or period-end financial close — and identify the appropriate control response.

Section 1 · The Risk Universe

When you arrive on a new SAP engagement — whether it is a greenfield S/4HANA implementation, an operating effectiveness review, or a remediation programme — the first task is establishing the Risk Universe. What are all the things that could go wrong in this environment? Until you have that picture, you cannot design controls, scope tests, or give your client a credible view of their exposure. Risk classification is how we build that picture systematically.

The Practitioner's Starting Question Every controls engagement — regardless of industry, SAP version, or client size — begins with one question: what could go wrong? Your answer to that question is your Risk Universe. This module gives you the framework to answer it precisely and consistently.

1.1 · Financial Risk

Financial risk arises when an error, omission, or deliberate manipulation results in a financial statement that does not accurately reflect the organisation's true position. This is the category most directly linked to fraud, misstatement, and external audit findings — and it is the primary target of SAP GRC Access Control deployments.

Consider a concrete SAP example. A user creates a fictitious vendor using transaction XK01 — Vendor Master Create — and then processes a payment run to that vendor via F110 — Automatic Payment Programme. Because the same person can both create the payee and authorise the payment, no independent check exists. Cash leaves the organisation, accounts payable is misstated, and the external auditor will raise a material weakness finding under SOX Section 404.

HIGH SoD Conflict — Vendor Creation + Payment Run Function A XK01 Create / Maintain Vendor Master Function B F110 Automatic Payment Run Risk One user can create a fictitious vendor and pay it — no independent authorisation required Control SoD Ruleset in SAP GRC Access Control · MSMP workflow approval for exceptions COSO Obj. Operations · Financial Reporting

GRC Connection Financial risk is the primary driver for deploying SAP GRC Access Control. The GRC Ruleset is essentially a codified library of financial risks expressed as SoD conflict rules. When GRC surfaces a conflict, it is surfacing an elevated inherent risk awaiting a control response.

1.2 · Compliance Risk

Compliance risk is the risk that the organisation fails to meet an external regulatory obligation. In SAP environments, this covers a wide spectrum of requirements depending on the organisation's sector and geography:

US Listed Companies SOX Section 404 Management must assess and external auditors must attest to the effectiveness of internal controls over financial reporting. SAP is the system of record — control gaps in SAP become SOX material weaknesses.

EU / Global GDPR Personal data stored and processed in SAP — HR records, customer data, supplier contacts — must be handled per GDPR Article requirements. Inadequate access controls or audit logging creates compliance exposure.

Life Sciences FDA 21 CFR Part 11 Electronic records and electronic signatures in SAP must meet FDA validation standards. Failure to maintain compliant audit trails is a direct regulatory violation with enforcement consequences.

All Sectors IFRS / Local GAAP SAP is the system of record for financial reporting. Configuration errors in chart of accounts, consolidation settings, or posting period controls can create IFRS / GAAP non-compliance.

The System of Record Multiplier Because SAP is the system of record, weaknesses in configuration, access controls, or change management can translate directly into regulatory non-compliance. The consequences extend beyond financial penalties to reputational damage that controls remediation cannot easily reverse.

1.3 · Operational Risk

Operational risk arises from weaknesses in day-to-day processes, system configuration, or human behaviour that impair the organisation's ability to operate accurately and efficiently. A key SAP example is the three-way match tolerance setting in Materials Management.

In a correctly configured Procure-to-Pay process, the system automatically compares three documents before posting an invoice:

ME21N

Purchase Order

Agreed price & quantity for goods or services

→

MIGO

Goods Receipt

Physical confirmation goods were received

→

MIRO

Vendor Invoice

Supplier's invoice — must match PO & GR within tolerance

⚠

FAIL

Invoice Posts

Tolerance too wide — discrepancy ignored

If the tolerance threshold is configured too loosely — or not configured at all — the system will post and pay invoices with significant discrepancies between purchase order value, goods receipt quantity, and vendor invoice amount. This is not necessarily fraud: it may simply be a configuration weakness. But it costs the organisation money and erodes the reliability of its financial data — a textbook operational risk with direct financial impact.

Operational risk also includes inadequate training (users bypassing standard process steps), unclear process ownership (no one reviews exception reports), and system availability failures. In the context of controls audit work, we focus primarily on process-level operational risks that can be mitigated by automated or manual controls.

1.4 · The Overlap — Risks Are Not Independent Silos

The three categories do not operate independently. A single control weakness can simultaneously create Financial, Compliance, and Operational risk. This overlap is one of the most important insights for practitioners — and the reason risk classification must identify the primary risk driver rather than simply listing all affected categories.

Risk Category Overlap — The Venn Model Financial
Misstatement
Fraud · SoD Compliance
SOX · GDPR
FDA · GAAP Operational
Process failure
Config weakness SoD Conflict XK01 + F110 in a single user's role creates financial risk (fictitious payments), compliance risk (SOX 404 material weakness), and operational risk (broken payment process integrity) — simultaneously.

Section 2

Section 2 · From Risk to Control

Now that we have our Risk Universe mapped, the question becomes: what do we do about it? The answer is a control. A control is an activity to mitigate or manage a risk — something put in place to address the risks we have identified. That definition is simple. Making it operational requires one additional concept.

2.1 · Inherent Risk and Residual Risk

Inherent Risk The level of risk present before any controls are applied. Your baseline when you first assess a client environment.

Controls The gap-filler. Your primary deliverable on an engagement. Moves the organisation from inherent to residual.

Residual Risk What remains after controls are implemented and operating. Must fall within the organisation's defined risk tolerance.

Conceptual Formula Residual Risk = Inherent Risk − Control Effectiveness This is a conceptual model, not a literal arithmetic equation. In practice, practitioners use risk ratings (High / Medium / Low) adjusted by the degree of reliance placed on each control, informed by design and operating effectiveness testing results.

Your job on an engagement is to help your client move from an elevated inherent-risk position to an acceptable residual-risk position. That gap is filled by controls. This is why risk identification and control design always move together. Risk identification without control design is just a problem list. Control design without risk identification is a set of activities with no anchor.

2.2 · The SAP GRC Ruleset — The Risk-to-Control Cycle

SAP GRC Access Control's Ruleset is the most direct example of the risk-to-control cycle in an SAP context. Each rule in the Ruleset says: if a single user can perform Function A and Function B, a Segregation of Duties conflict exists. The Ruleset is a codified Risk Universe for access-related financial risks.

How the Risk-to-Control Cycle Works in GRC AC

01 Run SoD Analysis The GRC Ruleset scans all user roles and identifies combinations of transactions that create SoD conflicts. Each conflict is a flagged inherent risk.

02 Classify the Risk Each conflict is rated High, Medium, or Low based on the financial exposure of the conflicting functions. XK01 + F110 is typically High — direct payment fraud potential.

03 Design the Control Response Options: (a) remove conflicting access from the role, (b) implement a compensating control such as an MSMP approval workflow, or (c) formally accept the risk with documented business justification and enhanced monitoring.

04 Measure Residual Risk Re-run the SoD analysis. Remaining unmitigated conflicts represent residual risk. Test compensating controls for operating effectiveness. Document the outcome in the Risk and Controls Matrix.

Common High-Risk SoD Conflicts in SAP S/4HANA

Risk | Function A | Function B | Exposure
HIGH | XK01 Create Vendor | F110 Payment Run | Fictitious vendor fraud
HIGH | FB01 Post Journal | FB03 Approve Journal | Unauthorised journal entry
MED | ME21N Create PO | MIRO Post Invoice | Bypass PO approval workflow
MED | PA30 Maintain HR Master | PC00 Run Payroll | Ghost employee / payroll fraud
MED | SE16N Table Browse | SM30 Table Maintain | Direct table manipulation

Case Study: PetroNova S.A. — Risk Mapping on a Greenfield S/4HANA

PetroNova S.A., a mid-size hydrocarbon producer headquartered in Port Meridian, Arcadia, commissioned a 37-week SAP S/4HANA implementation with TIB Systems as the QA/QC partner. During Phase 0 — Blueprint & Governance, the controls audit team produced a Risk Universe document covering all three risk categories for each process area.

Key finding in Accounts Payable: A single user role combined vendor master maintenance (XK01, XK02) with payment run authorisation (F110). The inherent risk rating was High — direct payment fraud potential. The recommended control was a workflow-enforced dual approval in SAP, implemented in MSMP. Post-control, residual risk was reduced to Low, subject to annual operating effectiveness testing.

This single finding — surfaced in Blueprint, remediated in Design, tested in UAT — prevented a potential control failure from reaching production on Day 1 of Go-Live. That is the value proposition of a controls-first implementation approach.

steps.action: A preventive control is one that stops an undesirable event from occurring in the first place. It operates upstream — before the error, before the fraud, before the non-compliant transaction. In SAP environments, preventive controls are your first and most powerful line of defence.

steps.title: Reference table
steps.action: The Practitioner's Definition A preventive control is stopping the activity from even happening. This is the gold standard in control design — you are not waiting for something to go wrong and then reacting. You are making it structurally impossible for the adverse event to occur in the first place.

steps.title: Reference table
steps.action: 01 Access Restriction via Role Design Preventive By configuring roles and authorisations so that users can only perform the transactions required for their job function, you prevent Segregation of Duties conflicts from materialising. A user who cannot access XK01 (Vendor Create) and F110 (Payment Run) in the same role simply cannot commit vendor fraud — the system will not permit it. SAP Mechanism: Authorisation object-level role design Detection tool: SAP GRC Access Control Ruleset

steps.title: Reference table
steps.action: GRC Detects, Role Design Prevents The SAP GRC Ruleset is an analytical engine — it tells you whether access restrictions are working. But it is the role design itself, enforced at the authorisation object level, that is the preventive control. In an RCM, the control is "Vendor Create and Payment Run access segregated in role design." GRC Access Control is the test procedure.

Control Types — Preventive, Detective & Beyond

Master the two fundamental control types, understand the practitioner's control-nature hierarchy, and internalise Ronnie's field insight on the critical difference between configured and inherent automated controls.
10–12 min · 3 sections · 6 SAP examples · 5-question quiz · AI Tutor

Learning Objectives By the end of this module you will be able to distinguish between preventive controls and detective controls and give three concrete SAP examples of each. By the end of this module you will be able to explain Ronnie's automated versus configured distinction — why a configured control requires a configuration review but an inherent automated control requires a "not disabled" check. By the end of this module you will be able to apply a control-type classification to a real engagement scenario, selecting the appropriate control type given the risk and the process constraints.
Section 1 · Preventive Controls

A preventive control is one that stops an undesirable event from occurring in the first place. It operates upstream — before the error, before the fraud, before the non-compliant transaction. In SAP environments, preventive controls are your first and most powerful line of defence.

The Practitioner's Definition A preventive control is stopping the activity from even happening. This is the gold standard in control design — you are not waiting for something to go wrong and then reacting. You are making it structurally impossible for the adverse event to occur in the first place.
1.1 · Access Restriction

01 Access Restriction via Role Design Preventive By configuring roles and authorisations so that users can only perform the transactions required for their job function, you prevent Segregation of Duties conflicts from materialising. A user who cannot access XK01 (Vendor Create) and F110 (Payment Run) in the same role simply cannot commit vendor fraud — the system will not permit it. SAP Mechanism: Authorisation object-level role design Detection tool: SAP GRC Access Control Ruleset

GRC Detects, Role Design Prevents The SAP GRC Ruleset is an analytical engine — it tells you whether access restrictions are working. But it is the role design itself, enforced at the authorisation object level, that is the preventive control. In an RCM, the control is "Vendor Create and Payment Run access segregated in role design." GRC Access Control is the test procedure.
1.2 · Workflow Enforcement

02 Workflow Enforcement — MSMP Approval Preventive SAP's workflow engine can be configured to require sequential approvals before a transaction completes. In Procure-to-Pay, a purchase order above a defined threshold cannot be released unless an authorised approver has electronically confirmed it. The process literally cannot advance without the approval — the system enforces the control, not a person's memory or goodwill. SAP Mechanism: MSMP — Multi-Step Multi-Process workflow in SAP GRC
PO Created
ME21N Requester submits PO above threshold
MSMP Triggers
Workflow initiated — approval request sent
Approver Reviews
Authorised approver confirms electronically
PO Released
ME29N Only after approval recorded
1.3 · System Configuration Validation

03 Three-Way Match — OMR6 Tolerance Configuration Preventive The three-way match in Materials Management is a configured preventive control. The system automatically compares the purchase order, goods receipt, and vendor invoice amounts. If the discrepancy exceeds the configured tolerance in OMR6, the system blocks the invoice from posting. No human intervention is required — it operates consistently on every single transaction, every time. Configuration: OMR6 tolerance key settings Process: ME21N → MIGO → MIRO

Audit Testing Implication When testing a configured preventive control like the three-way match, you must inspect the OMR6 settings and verify the tolerance parameters are set appropriately — not just confirm the control "exists." A tolerance of 99% means the control provides almost no protection. This is the audit implication of Ronnie's distinction, covered in Section 3.
Section 2
Section 2 · Detective Controls

Preventive controls are the ideal. But we cannot prevent everything. Some risks are too complex to fully prevent through system configuration alone, some involve human judgement that cannot be automated, and some control gaps are only discovered after the fact. This is where detective controls come in.

A detective control does not stop an event from occurring. Instead, it identifies that something has gone wrong after the fact, enabling corrective action to be taken. Think of detective controls as your second line of defence — a fail-safe for situations where prevention was not possible or did not hold.
2.1 · Management Review of Exception Reports

01 Exception Report Review Detective At the end of a defined period, a responsible manager reviews a system-generated report of unusual or potentially erroneous transactions. The event has already occurred — the control's purpose is to identify it and trigger a corrective response. In SAP, this typically covers journal entries posted after period-end cutoff, vendor master changes in the prior month, or payment runs that bypassed standard approval workflows. SAP Reports: FB03 · FK04 · F110 log Frequency: Weekly / Monthly / Quarterly
2.2 · User Access Review

02 User Access Review (UAR) Detective On a quarterly or annual cycle, business process owners review active users and their assigned roles. Inappropriate access — due to role change, leavers, or SoD policy violations — is flagged for removal. The UAR does not prevent the access from existing during the period under review. But it is a critical second fail-safe: if access provisioning controls failed, the UAR will surface the problem before it becomes a sustained exposure or an audit finding. Tool: SAP GRC Access Control — user access certification Frequency: Quarterly or Annual One of the most commonly tested controls in a SOX 404 engagement
2.3 · Reconciliation

03 Reconciliation Controls Detective Reconciliation compares two independent data sets and identifies discrepancies. A discrepancy signals that something happened upstream — a posting error, an unauthorised journal entry, or a process breakdown — that must be investigated and corrected. In SAP, reconciliation controls frequently run through the Financial Closing Cockpit and are supported by automated variance reports, making most of them ITDM controls (see Section 3). Types: Bank recon · Subledger-to-GL · Intercompany SAP: FF67 · FBL3N · FBU3
Preventive vs. Detective — Side-by-Side Framework

Dimension | Preventive | Detective
Timing | Before the event occurs | After the event has occurred
Objective | Stop the error, fraud, or non-compliance | Identify and trigger corrective action
SAP Examples | Role design · MSMP workflow · OMR6 tolerance | Exception reports · User Access Review · Reconciliation
Test Approach | Inspect configuration / role design / workflow setup | Verify report completeness + evidence of review + action taken
Reliance Level | High — blocks every transaction automatically | Medium — depends on review frequency and quality

Design Rule Design preventive first. Detective is your second line of defence — not a substitute. On every engagement, push clients toward preventive controls wherever the process allows. When prevention is not feasible, implement detective controls with defined frequency, clear ownership, and documented evidence of review.
Section 3
Section 3 · Ronnie's Distinction — Automated vs. Configured

Within the broader category of automated or configured controls, there is a meaningful difference between two sub-types that practitioners frequently conflate. A colleague, Ronnie, flagged this distinction in a field session — and it is one of those insights that separates experienced practitioners from entry-level candidates.

🔑 Ronnie's Field Insight "An automated control could be based on system configuration, or that control could be inherent to the system — an out-of-the-box standard control. There is a distinction." — Ronnie, SAP GRC Practitioner · Source Session AUD-20260602-WA0018
Configured Automated Control — requires a configuration review

A configured control is enabled by deliberate system configuration — someone has set it up. It only works if the parameters are set correctly. The three-way match tolerance in OMR6 is the canonical example: powerful, but only if the tolerance threshold is set appropriately. A tolerance of 99% technically means the control is configured, but operationally it provides almost no protection.

Audit Testing Implication Configured controls require a configuration review. You must inspect the OMR6 settings and verify the tolerance parameters are appropriate. Simply confirming "three-way match is turned on" is insufficient evidence.
Inherent Automated Control — verify it has not been disabled

An inherent automated control is active by default — it operates regardless of whether the client has done anything special. SAP's built-in duplicate invoice check in MIRO posting is a clear example: the system automatically checks for duplicate document numbers and vendor-invoice combinations on every posting, out-of-the-box.

Audit Testing Implication Inherent controls do not require configuration verification. But you must confirm the standard functionality has not been switched off — check the relevant system switches. Some clients disable standard checks to accommodate a workaround; that disablement is a control gap requiring a compensating control.
3.1 · The ITDM Control — IT-Dependent Manual

Between fully automated controls and fully manual controls sits the IT-Dependent Manual (ITDM) control. An ITDM leverages the system to generate data — a report, a log, an exception list — but requires a human to review that output and take action.
System Component
IT-Generated Data
The system generates the report, log, or exception list. Examples: SAP exception report, GRC SoD conflict list, Financial Closing Cockpit variance output.
Human Component
Manual Review & Action
A competent person reviews the output, investigates exceptions, and takes documented corrective action. Both steps must be evidenced for the control to be considered effective.

ITDM Testing Requirement — Both Elements When testing an ITDM, you must test both elements: (1) verify the report is complete and accurate, and (2) verify that a competent person reviewed it and took documented action on exceptions. Missing either element renders the ITDM control ineffective.
3.2 · The Control Nature Hierarchy

① Highest Reliability Configured / Automated System enforces on every transaction automatically. No human action required in normal operation. Examples: OMR6 tolerance · MSMP workflow · Role design · Duplicate invoice check First Design Choice

② Medium Reliability IT-Dependent Manual (ITDM) System generates data; human must review and act. Reliability depends on review quality and frequency. Examples: Exception report review · UAR · Reconciliation Second Choice

③ Lowest Reliability Manual Control Fully human — no system component. Most costly to test, maintain, and rely upon. Subject to human error. Examples: Paper invoice review · Physical inventory count · Verbal approval Last Resort

The Practitioner's Value-Add Wherever possible, encourage clients to move up the hierarchy during system implementation. A manual control converted to a configured automated control is not just a compliance improvement — it is an operational efficiency gain and a long-term reduction in audit cost. That is a direct contribution to their controls maturity.

steps.title: Reference table

Failure Mode | Mechanism | Audit Implication
Person forgets | No system prompt or reminder — control simply does not occur | No evidence of performance for the period; control gap
Person rushes | Review completed superficially — exceptions not investigated | Evidence of review exists but effectiveness cannot be confirmed
Staff turnover | Control knowledge not documented; successor unaware | Invisible gap — may persist across multiple audit periods
Evidence manipulation | Paper easier to falsify than system-generated logs | Auditor must consider documentary integrity, not just existence

Control Nature — The Descending Scale

Understand how the degree of system reliance determines what a control is worth, how to test it, and how to advise clients to improve it. From fully automated at the top to fully manual at the bottom — with the ITDM in between.
10–12 min · 3 sections · B2 cross-link · 5-question quiz · AI Tutor

Learning Objectives By the end of this module you will be able to describe all three control nature types — configured automated, ITDM, and manual — with a concrete SAP example of each. By the end of this module you will be able to explain how your audit testing approach shifts as you move down the scale from automated (config review) to ITDM (two-element evidence) to manual (physical artefacts). By the end of this module you will be able to connect the control nature hierarchy to Ronnie's B2 distinction, explaining why configured controls require a configuration review but inherent controls require a "not disabled" check.

Related Module B2 — Control Types: Ronnie's Distinction This module extends Ronnie's configured vs. inherent insight from B2 into its full audit testing implications. Revisit B2 if you need a refresher. ← Review B2
Section 1 · Configured Automated Controls

In Module B2 we established that preventive controls are the gold standard — they stop adverse events before they occur. But not all preventive controls are equally reliable. Control nature answers the question: how much does this control depend on the system versus a human being? The answer places every control on a descending scale of system reliance, from fully automated at the top through to fully manual at the bottom.

Configured Automated
