1.1 · Configured Automated — Deep Dive

The source session's exact words: "this is your best bet — the system is automatically going to be set up to prevent something." The three-way match is the canonical example. The system automatically compares the purchase order (ME21N), goods receipt (MIGO), and vendor invoice (MIRO). If the discrepancy exceeds the configured tolerance in OMR6, the system blocks the invoice — automatically, consistently, on every single transaction, every time.

Why This is the Highest Reliability Level Configured automated controls do not depend on anyone remembering to perform a check. They do not weaken when staff are absent, busy, or under pressure. They enforce the same rule on the first transaction of the day and the last. This consistency is exactly why they attract the highest audit reliance rating — and why audit sample sizes for these controls are typically small.
1.2 · Ronnie's B2 Distinction — Applied to Testing

🔑 Extending Ronnie's B2 Insight "An automated control could be based on system configuration, or that control could be inherent to the system — an out-of-the-box standard control. There is a distinction." — Ronnie · Source Session AUD-20260602-WA0018
In B2, Ronnie flagged the distinction between configured and inherent automated controls. In B3, we make that distinction operationally concrete — because it changes your test procedure:

Configured Automated Requires a Configuration Review Enabled by deliberate setup. OMR6 three-way match tolerance. Test step: inspect the OMR6 settings and verify the tolerance parameters are set appropriately — not just confirm "three-way match is enabled."

A tolerance of 99% technically means the control is configured, but operationally it provides almost no protection.

Inherent Automated Requires a "Not Disabled" Check Active by default — no configuration required. MIRO duplicate invoice check (document number + vendor combination). Test step: confirm the standard SAP functionality has not been switched off in system settings.

Some clients disable standard checks to accommodate workarounds — that disablement is itself a control gap.
1.3 · Writing a Complete Test Procedure
The most common weakness in configured automated control testing is an incomplete test procedure. Here is what the difference looks like in practice:

❌ Insufficient — Not Acceptable as Audit Evidence "Confirm three-way match is enabled in the system."

This evidences existence, not effectiveness. It says nothing about whether the tolerance is appropriate, whether the configuration has been overridden, or whether the system actually blocked any discrepant invoices during the test period.

✅ Complete — Three-Component Test 1. Configuration inspection: Navigate to OMR6; confirm tolerance key is set to ≤3% or per approved policy.

 2. Parameter verification: Confirm no user-specific or vendor-specific exceptions override the standard tolerance.

 3. Sample test: Select 25 MIRO postings from the test period; confirm the system blocked invoices where discrepancy exceeded tolerance and generated a blocking reason code.
Section 2
Section 2 · IT-Dependent Manual (ITDM) Controls

Where we cannot have everything be configured and automated, we leverage the IT-Dependent Manual (ITDM) control. The source session defined it precisely: it does require human interaction, but you are at least leveraging the system to a certain extent. The canonical example is a monthly review: generate a report from the system, then require somebody to review that report, identify the discrepancies, and take action.
System Component
IT-Generated Data

SAP generates the report, log, or exception list automatically. Examples: monthly vendor master change report (FK04), GRC SoD conflict list, Financial Closing Cockpit variance output, payment run exception report (F110 log).
Human Component
Manual Review & Action

A competent person reviews the output, investigates exceptions, and takes documented corrective action. The control's effectiveness depends entirely on the quality and consistency of this human element.

The Core Reliance Risk An ITDM is only as strong as the quality and consistency of the human review. The system component is reliable — it generates the report on schedule. The human component is where control quality degrades: reviewers who rush, miss exceptions, or fail to document their follow-up. This is why ITDM controls attract medium reliance ratings, not high.
2.1 · Testing an ITDM — Both Elements Required
Testing an ITDM requires evidence of both elements. This is the most common source of ITDM audit deficiencies — practitioners test one element and miss the other.
Element 1 — System Component: Report Completeness & Accuracy
01 Coverage Check Does the report cover all relevant transactions for the test period? Verify the date range, entity scope, and transaction type filters are correctly configured.
02 Data Source Verification Is the report pulling from the correct system table or data source? Trace the report logic to the underlying SAP data.
03 Accuracy Sample Select 5–10 transactions from the underlying data and agree them to the report output. Confirm no exceptions are missing from the population.
Element 2 — Human Component: Review Evidence & Action on Exceptions
01 Evidence of Review Is there documented evidence the reviewer examined the report — a sign-off, date stamp, or email approval? Oral confirmation ("we always review it") is not audit evidence.

02 Exception Follow-Up For each exception flagged in the period: is there documented follow-up and corrective action? A signed-off report with no exception follow-up is evidence that a review occurred — not that it was effective.

03 Reviewer Competence Was the reviewer competent and appropriately independent? Check the reviewer's role against the process being reviewed — a reviewer approving their own transactions is not independent.

This distinction drives some of the most common ITDM audit findings in SOX engagements. Control owners who sign reports without investigating or documenting exception resolution create a paper trail that looks like a working control but evidences nothing about effectiveness.
Section 3
Section 3 · Manual Controls & The Uplift Imperative

At the bottom of the scale sits the fully manual control — no IT component at all. The source session is direct: these are going to be the least effective, and you want to leverage the more configured and ITDM controls as much as we can. But manual controls are a reality on every engagement, particularly in current-state assessments of legacy environments.
3.1 · Manual Control Nature

A manual control depends entirely on human behaviour — on memory, consistency, diligence, and the integrity of the individual performing it. There is no system prompt, no automated flag, no configuration enforcement. If the person forgets, the control fails. If the person rushes, the control is weakened.

Failure Mode | Mechanism | Audit Implication
Person forgets | No system prompt or reminder — control simply does not occur | No evidence of performance for the period; control gap
Person rushes | Review completed superficially — exceptions not investigated | Evidence of review exists but effectiveness cannot be confirmed
Staff turnover | Control knowledge not documented; successor unaware | Invisible gap — may persist across multiple audit periods
Evidence manipulation | Paper easier to falsify than system-generated logs | Auditor must consider documentary integrity, not just existence
3.2 · Testing Manual Controls

Testing manual controls requires physical artefacts of the control having been executed — signed forms, dated approval stamps, email confirmations, documented inspection records. The physical record must exist, be complete, and cover the period under review.

Oral Confirmation is Not Evidence "We always do it this way" is not audit evidence for a manual control. The physical record of the control having been performed is evidence. Auditors must also consider documentary integrity: manual evidence is easier to falsify than system-generated logs, which is why manual controls attract the largest sample sizes and, where evidence manipulation is a concern, may require corroborating evidence from independent sources.
3.3 · The Uplift Imperative — From Manual to Automated

On every S/4HANA implementation engagement, one of the highest-value contributions you can make is to identify manual controls in the current state and recommend their conversion to configured automated or ITDM controls in the future state. Interim State ITDM SAP generates weekly goods receipt exception report. Manager reviews and signs off in the system. Better than manual — but still dependent on review quality.

That is a direct contribution to the client's long-term controls maturity. This is the practitioner's value-add during an S/4HANA transformation.

Control Nature — The Descending Scale

Understand how the degree of system reliance determines what a control is worth, how to test it, and how to advise clients to improve it. From fully automated at the top to fully manual at the bottom — with the ITDM in between.

10–12 min · 3 sections · B2 cross-link · 5-question quiz · AI Tutor

Learning Objectives By the end of this module you will be able to describe all three control nature types — configured automated, ITDM, and manual — with a concrete SAP example of each. By the end of this module you will be able to explain how your audit testing approach shifts as you move down the scale from automated (config review) to ITDM (two-element evidence) to manual (physical artefacts). By the end of this module you will be able to connect the control nature hierarchy to Ronnie's B2 distinction, explaining why configured controls require a configuration review but inherent controls require a "not disabled" check.

Related Module B2 — Control Types: Ronnie's Distinction This module extends Ronnie's configured vs. inherent insight from B2 into its full audit testing implications. Revisit B2 if you need a refresher. ← Review B2

Section 1 · Configured Automated Controls

In Module B2 we established that preventive controls are the gold standard — they stop adverse events before they occur. But not all preventive controls are equally reliable. Control nature answers the question: how much does this control depend on the system versus a human being? The answer places every control on a descending scale of system reliance, from fully automated at the top through to fully manual at the bottom.

①Highest

Configured Automated

The system enforces the control automatically on every transaction, every time. No human action required in normal operation.

OMR6 Three-way match tolerance

Highest RelianceTest: Config inspection + sample postings

②Medium

IT-Dependent Manual (ITDM)

The system generates data; a human must review that output and take action. Both elements must be evidenced.

FK04 Monthly vendor master change report review

Medium RelianceTest: Report accuracy + review evidence

③Lowest

Manual

No IT component at all. Entirely dependent on human behaviour, memory, and consistency. Highest failure risk; largest testing sample required.

📄 Paper inspection form — physical inventory count

Lowest RelianceTest: Physical artefacts of performance

1.1 · Configured Automated — Deep Dive

The source session's exact words: "this is your best bet — the system is automatically going to be set up to prevent something." The three-way match is the canonical example. The system automatically compares the purchase order (ME21N), goods receipt (MIGO), and vendor invoice (MIRO). If the discrepancy exceeds the configured tolerance in OMR6, the system blocks the invoice — automatically, consistently, on every single transaction, every time.

Why This is the Highest Reliability Level Configured automated controls do not depend on anyone remembering to perform a check. They do not weaken when staff are absent, busy, or under pressure. They enforce the same rule on the first transaction of the day and the last. This consistency is exactly why they attract the highest audit reliance rating — and why audit sample sizes for these controls are typically small.

1.2 · Ronnie's B2 Distinction — Applied to Testing

🔑 Extending Ronnie's B2 Insight "An automated control could be based on system configuration, or that control could be inherent to the system — an out-of-the-box standard control. There is a distinction." — Ronnie · Source Session AUD-20260602-WA0018

In B2, Ronnie flagged the distinction between configured and inherent automated controls. In B3, we make that distinction operationally concrete — because it changes your test procedure:

Configured Automated Requires a Configuration Review Enabled by deliberate setup. OMR6 three-way match tolerance. Test step: inspect the OMR6 settings and verify the tolerance parameters are set appropriately — not just confirm "three-way match is enabled."

A tolerance of 99% technically means the control is configured, but operationally it provides almost no protection.

Inherent Automated Requires a "Not Disabled" Check Active by default — no configuration required. MIRO duplicate invoice check (document number + vendor combination). Test step: confirm the standard SAP functionality has not been switched off in system settings.

Some clients disable standard checks to accommodate workarounds — that disablement is itself a control gap.

1.3 · Writing a Complete Test Procedure

The most common weakness in configured automated control testing is an incomplete test procedure. Here is what the difference looks like in practice:

❌ Insufficient — Not Acceptable as Audit Evidence "Confirm three-way match is enabled in the system."

This evidences existence, not effectiveness. It says nothing about whether the tolerance is appropriate, whether the configuration has been overridden, or whether the system actually blocked any discrepant invoices during the test period.

✅ Complete — Three-Component Test 1. Configuration inspection: Navigate to OMR6; confirm tolerance key is set to ≤3% or per approved policy.

 2. Parameter verification: Confirm no user-specific or vendor-specific exceptions override the standard tolerance.

 3. Sample test: Select 25 MIRO postings from the test period; confirm the system blocked invoices where discrepancy exceeded tolerance and generated a blocking reason code.

Section 2 · IT-Dependent Manual (ITDM) Controls

The source session defined it precisely: it does require human interaction, but you are at least leveraging the system to a certain extent. System Component

IT-Generated Data

SAP generates the report, log, or exception list automatically. Examples: monthly vendor master change report (FK04), GRC SoD conflict list, Financial Closing Cockpit variance output, payment run exception report (F110 log).

+

Human Component

Manual Review & Action

A competent person reviews the output, investigates exceptions, and takes documented corrective action. The control's effectiveness depends entirely on the quality and consistency of this human element.

At go-live, they expect the system to work and they expect to run their business with confidence the very next morning. Now consider what happens if controls are not embedded before go-live. A controls failure discovered post-live is not an abstract risk — it is rework, cost, and potential regulatory exposure at exactly the moment when an organisation is most vulnerable.

What the Source Session Says The transcript is direct: "if they don't have their risks and controls right, there may be consequences — financial misstatements or loss, or they may have to end up redesigning their processes after go-live." Three concrete consequences: misstatements, post-live rework, and the inability to unlock the new value that S/4HANA was intended to deliver.
Compliant on Day One

The source session identifies the primary objective precisely: clients should be compliant on day one of go-live. That phrase captures the essential value proposition. When you embed controls during implementation, you are not creating compliance overhead — you are eliminating a far more expensive problem: discovering control gaps after the system is live, after real transactions have been processed, after external auditors have begun their review.

6 months – 3 years
Go-Live
Controls must be ready
External Audit
Post go-live

❌ Without Controls at Go-Live Gaps discovered after real transactions have been processed — remediation at maximum cost External auditor raises material weakness findings — reputational and regulatory exposure Post-live process redesign costs multiples of implementation-phase design cost S/4HANA investment fails to deliver intended ROI — lift-and-shift mentality persists

✅ With Controls Embedded at Go-Live Compliant on day one — no post-live remediation sprint; operations start cleanly External audit reliance increases; annual testing cost falls; fewer findings Controls designed right the first time — automation captured during implementation S/4HANA value realised — new capabilities unlocked, not just old process replicated
Section 2
Section 2 · Four Value Drivers

The source session identifies four value drivers that justify a controls workstream in an S/4HANA transformation programme. These are the arguments that land with a programme sponsor, a CFO, or an audit committee — because they are framed in business outcomes, not in controls taxonomy.

Value Driver 01 Issues Prevented from Go-Live The preventive measure — every financial, operational, and regulatory risk identified before go-live is a risk that cannot manifest as a live-system failure. Every SoD conflict resolved during design is a conflict that cannot generate a payment fraud or a material weakness finding in the live system. Outcome: Fewer post-live findings

Value Driver 02 Designing the Process Right the First Time Counter the lift-and-shift instinct. The source session is direct: "that is not the mindset we should be going with." The moment of transformation is the cheapest possible time to redesign a process — far cheaper than redesigning it post-live. Build compliance in, not on. Outcome: No re-engineering post-live

Value Driver 03 Reduced Cost of Compliance Controls designed, documented, and tested from day one require less auditor testing time than controls hastily assembled to address findings. Higher audit reliance means smaller sample sizes, lower external audit fees, and fewer audit hours consumed each year over the life of the programme. Outcome: Lower annual audit cost

Value Driver 04 Integration and Efficiency Controls fully embedded and operationalised in the client's environment — not delivered as a document set and left. The goal is controls the business owns, automates where possible, and can continuously improve over time. A controls workstream that leaves behind sustainable processes delivers value long after the engagement closes. Outcome: Sustainable controls maturity
Section 3
Section 3 · The External Audit Connection

The source session makes the external audit connection explicit: controls are the inputs for external auditors to conduct their annual audit. When control gaps surface during pre-go-live, the programme team can detect them, fix them, and address them so that once the actual audit starts, the client faces less cost and governs their controls framework more effectively.

The Direct Line to Audit Cost A control that is designed, documented, tested, and operating from go-live requires far less auditor testing than a control assembled post-finding. The difference is not marginal — it compounds over multiple audit cycles. The controls workstream is, in effect, reducing the client's external audit cost every year for the life of the S/4HANA system.

🎯 The Practitioner's Frame "Value Protection, Not Compliance Overhead" When you enter a client engagement, you are not there to build documents and run reports. You are there to protect the client's investment in their transformation. Every risk you identify, every control you design, every test you execute contributes to the four value drivers. That framing — value protection, not compliance overhead — is how you speak to senior stakeholders, and it is the language that unlocks the access and the buy-in you need to do the work effectively.

steps.action: 1 Assessment & Recommendation Advisory The practitioner reviews the client's current risk and controls environment — their existing framework, SAP configuration, process design — and provides an independent assessment of gaps and opportunities. steps.title: Reference table
steps.action: 2 S/4HANA Transformation Full Lifecycle The controls team is embedded from the beginning of the programme, working through all four phases: solution confirmation → design and build → testing → go-live. Activities shift in each phase: risk assessment and preliminary RCM drafting in solution confirmation; controls design and business validation in design and build; operating effectiveness testing in the testing phase. The primary deliverable — the Risk and Controls Matrix (RCM) — is progressively refined from a preliminary draft at solution confirmation to a fully validated, tested document by go-live. Scope Full transformation lifecycle — all four phases Deliverable Progressively refined RCM: preliminary → validated → tested Key Relationship Programme manager · Functional leads · System integrator Timing Solution Confirmation → Design & Build → Testing → Go-Live

steps.title: Reference table
steps.action: 3 Controls Testing DEF + OEF The client already has a controls framework in place. The controls workstream joins specifically to test whether controls are designed effectively (DEF) and operating effectively (OEF). The key activity is working with the programme's testing team to identify which test scripts are relevant from a controls perspective, then reviewing system testing results to confirm controls work as designed. This is common during SIT and UAT phases. Scope Existing controls framework — test DEF and OEF Deliverable Test results · Evidence packages · Gap findings Key Relationship Testing lead · Programme test manager Timing System integration testing (SIT) · UAT phase

steps.action: 4 Remediation Time-Sensitive Time is of essence. The practitioner is working against a deadline, with documented audit findings that define exactly what must be addressed — and a hard stop at the next external audit. steps.title: Reference table
steps.action: ⚠️ Field Insight — Controls-Security Integration Point The source session explicitly flags this: practitioners should connect the dots between how security roles are designed and how those roles affect the risk and controls framework. A role that creates a SoD conflict is not just a security issue — it is a financial risk. A control that relies on restricted system access must be coordinated with the security team. The security workstream designs SAP user roles and authorisation objects. The controls workstream identifies SoD conflicts in that role design and maps them to the financial risk framework. These two workstreams are not independent — failure to coordinate them is one of the most common delivery failures on large S/4HANA programmes.

2 S/4HANA Transformation Full Lifecycle The controls team is embedded from the beginning of the programme, working through all four phases: solution confirmation → design and build → testing → go-live. Activities shift in each phase: risk assessment and preliminary RCM drafting in solution confirmation; controls design and business validation in design and build; operating effectiveness testing in the testing phase. The primary deliverable — the Risk and Controls Matrix (RCM) — is progressively refined from a preliminary draft at solution confirmation to a fully validated, tested document by go-live. Scope Full transformation lifecycle — all four phases Deliverable Progressively refined RCM: preliminary → validated → tested Key Relationship Programme manager · Functional leads · System integrator Timing Solution Confirmation → Design & Build → Testing → Go-Live

3 Controls Testing DEF + OEF The client already has a controls framework in place. The controls workstream joins specifically to test whether controls are designed effectively (DEF) and operating effectively (OEF). The key activity is working with the programme's testing team to identify which test scripts are relevant from a controls perspective, then reviewing system testing results to confirm controls work as designed. This is common during SIT and UAT phases. Scope Existing controls framework — test DEF and OEF Deliverable Test results · Evidence packages · Gap findings Key Relationship Testing lead · Programme test manager Timing System integration testing (SIT) · UAT phase

4 Remediation Time-Sensitive Time is of essence. Clients who have received significant deficiency or material weakness findings from their external auditor need the controls team to overhaul the affected areas before the next audit cycle. The scope is defined by the findings. The practitioner is working against a deadline, with documented audit findings that define exactly what must be addressed — and a hard stop at the next external audit. Scope Deficiency / material weakness areas from external auditor Deliverable Remediated controls · Re-test evidence · Audit-ready packages Key Relationship External auditor · CFO · Audit committee Timing Post-audit-finding — before the next audit cycle
Section 3
Section 3 · Stakeholders, Integration & The Practitioner's Frame

Understanding your engagement type does more than clarify your scope — it tells you who your most important stakeholder is. In an assessment engagement, it is Internal Audit or the Compliance function. In a transformation engagement, it is the programme manager and the functional leads. In a testing engagement, it is the test manager. In a remediation engagement, it is the external auditor and the CFO.

⚠️ Field Insight — Controls-Security Integration Point The source session explicitly flags this: practitioners should connect the dots between how security roles are designed and how those roles affect the risk and controls framework. A role that creates a SoD conflict is not just a security issue — it is a financial risk. A control that relies on restricted system access must be coordinated with the security team. The security workstream designs SAP user roles and authorisation objects. The controls workstream identifies SoD conflicts in that role design and maps them to the financial risk framework. These two workstreams are not independent — failure to coordinate them is one of the most common delivery failures on large S/4HANA programmes.

Section 1 · The Degree-of-Engagement Spectrum

The first question to answer on any engagement is: how hands-on are we? The source session describes a spectrum from light-touch advising at one end — assessing and recommending without directly designing or testing — through to fully embedded delivery at the other, where the controls team is deeply involved in design, validation, testing, and implementation across all phases.

Degree-of-Engagement Spectrum

Advisory / AssessDesign & ValidateTest & Implement

Advisory End

• Assess client's controls environment • Identify gaps and opportunities • Provide recommendations • Primary relationship: Internal Audit • Deliverable: Assessment report

Design & Validate

• Embedded from programme start • Design controls and RCM • Validate with business process owners • Primary relationship: Programme mgr • Deliverable: Validated RCM

Hands-On End

• Test DEF and OEF • Review system artefacts • Confirm controls work as designed • Primary relationship: Test manager • Deliverable: Test results + evidence

S/4HANA Lifecycle — Phase by Phase

Map the controls workstream across all four phases of a full S/4HANA transformation — from Solution Confirmation through Design and Build, Testing, and Cutover and Deploy — tracking the RACM from preliminary draft to go-live-ready document.
14–16 min · 4 phases · Interactive timeline · RACM iteration narrative · 5-question quiz · AI Tutor

Learning Objectives By the end of this module you will be able to describe the specific controls activities and deliverables in each of the four phases — Solution Confirmation, Design and Build, Testing, and Cutover and Deploy. By the end of this module you will be able to explain how the RACM evolves across the lifecycle — from a preliminary draft in SolCon to a tested, go-live-ready document at Cutover and Deploy. By the end of this module you will be able to apply the key coordination strategies — the testing captain approach, AI agent integration points, and the external auditor relationship at each phase.
The S/4HANA Transformation Lifecycle

The S/4HANA transformation engagement is the most complex context for a controls practitioner — and the most important. The controls workstream runs across four distinct phases, each with different activities, different deliverables, and different primary coordination points. Click any phase below to explore its activities, or read through the full accordion that follows.

Phase 1 Solution Confirmation RACM: Preliminary Draft
Establish the Risk Universe

Review programme scope and business processes. Produce a preliminary risk assessment across financial, operational, and compliance risk categories. This is the foundation — without it, the RACM has no anchor.
Draft the Preliminary RACM
Not a finished document — a starting point. The source session: "it will not be perfect, but it sets the ground and foundation." Every subsequent phase refines it.
Make Friends
Build relationships with SI functional leads, testing team, security team, data team, cybersecurity team. These relationships will be called upon in every subsequent phase. Invest in them now.
Influence the Future State Design

Peak influence window. Identify processes that are currently manual but could be automated in S/4HANA. Raise them now — once Key Design Decisions are finalised, influencing the design becomes progressively harder and more expensive.
AI Agent Opportunity

AI agents can perform current-state to future-state gap analysis and propose preliminary controls from programme artefacts. The practitioner's role shifts from information processing to judgement — validating, challenging, contextualising.
Phase 2 Design and Build RACM: Refined & Validated
Read Functional Design Documents — Risk First

Three-step approach: (1) What risk am I concerned about? (2) Does this FD affect that risk? (3) If yes — what are the data frequency, direction, and error handling details? The error handling mechanism is typically the control.
Design Controls, Validate with Business

Translate FD analysis into specific controls. Hold working sessions with business process owners to validate — the business must agree to perform these controls on go-live. Update the RACM with specific, validated control descriptions.
Maintain Scope Boundary

The controls team consumes programme artefacts — we do not configure anything in SAP and do not perform design work. That is the SI's role. Our deliverable is the RACM. Keeping this scope boundary clear protects independence and audit credibility.
AI Agent Opportunity

AI agents can accelerate FD analysis across hundreds of documents — extracting risk-relevant sections and proposing draft controls. The practitioner validates and refines. Volume challenge in Design and Build is the clearest ROI case for AI assistance.
Phase 3 Testing RACM: Test Evidence Captured
Configuration Testing
Validate system settings that implement a control — OMR6 tolerance keys, workflow thresholds, approval routing. Confirm parameters are set correctly, not just that the control exists.
Transactional Testing

Execute real or simulated transactions to confirm the control responds as designed — run a payment to a fictitious vendor to confirm the SoD block fires, post an invoice exceeding tolerance to confirm the system blocks it.
Report Testing
Confirm exception reports are complete, accurate, and cover the right population. Run the UAR report and verify it captures all relevant user-role combinations. Agree to the underlying system data.
Testing Captain Strategy

From a major energy company engagement: integrate controls requirements into programme test cases before testing begins. Find the testing captain — the person coordinating a group of testers — and make them your key contact. Route all evidence requests and rework through one coordinator.
SIT vs UAT Scope Decision

Configuration controls (automated, no human intervention) → System Integration Testing. Workflow-driven and report-driven controls (require human review) → User Acceptance Testing. This distributes effort and aligns each control type with the most appropriate environment.
Phase 4 Cutover and Deploy RACM: Final — Go-Live Ready
Finalise the RACM

Every control has an assigned owner. Descriptions reflect the tested final state. RACM is formally approved and distributed to all post-go-live stakeholders. This is the finished version of a document that began as a preliminary draft in SolCon.
Train the Control Owners

Every person responsible for a control must understand: what to do, how often, what evidence to produce, and how to escalate exceptions — especially for ITDM and manual controls, where the human element is the control.
External Auditor Confirmation Gate

The auditor must confirm the controls designed and tested are the controls they will rely on in the annual audit. This confirmation is the final gate before go-live. Touchpoint frequency increases significantly in this phase.
Maintain RACM Traceability

The RACM is not a point-in-time document — it is an iterated artefact that has been through multiple versions since SolCon. The ability to trace from the final go-live control back to the original risk assessment is important for audit credibility and future engagements.
The RACM Iteration Narrative
The Risk and Controls Matrix is not a one-time build. It begins as a preliminary draft and is progressively refined through every phase of the transformation.
SolCon
Preliminary Draft
Risk Universe → initial risk list → placeholder controls based on early process understanding
Design & Build
Refined & Validated
FD review → specific controls → business process owner validation and sign-off
Testing
Evidence Captured
Test results → DEF/OEF conclusions → findings logged and control design updated if needed
Cutover & Deploy
Final — Go-Live Ready
Ownership assigned · Trained · Auditor confirmed · Formally approved and distributed
Phase-by-Phase Detail
Expand each phase for the full controls workstream narrative.
SC Phase 1 — Solution ConfirmationFoundation, relationships, preliminary RACM, peak influence window Preliminary Draft

Solution Confirmation is the first phase of the S/4HANA transformation. At this stage the client and their system implementer are defining the future state — what the new system will look like, what processes will change, and what key design decisions will be made. For the controls team, this is the most important phase of the entire engagement — not because the heaviest work happens here, but because the foundation you lay in Solution Confirmation determines everything that follows.
Three Core Activities

1. Establish the Risk Universe. Before a single control is designed, you need to understand what could go wrong in the future state. Review the programme scope, understand the business processes being transformed, and produce a preliminary risk assessment.

2. Draft the Preliminary RACM. Not a finished document — a starting point. The source session is clear: it will not be perfect, but it sets the ground and foundation for what the client's risk and controls landscape will look like. Every subsequent phase refines it.

3. Make friends. You need relationships with the system implementer's functional leads, the testing team, the security team, the data team, and the cybersecurity team. These relationships will be called upon in every subsequent phase. Invest in them now, when the programme is still in planning mode.

Peak Influence Window Solution Confirmation is your best opportunity to influence the future state design. If you identify a process that is currently manual but could be automated in S/4HANA, raise it now. Once the Key Design Decisions are finalised and the system is being configured, influencing the design becomes progressively harder and more expensive. The source session notes: it is better to have a workflow designed and built now than to try to get it built later in the programme.

🤖 AI Agent Callout — Solution Confirmation AI agents are beginning to add value in Solution Confirmation — performing current-state to future-state gap analysis, processing programme artefacts, and proposing preliminary controls. In a phase where the team is consuming large volumes of process documentation with limited bandwidth, the efficiency gain from AI-assisted analysis can be significant. The practitioner's role shifts from raw information processing to judgement: validating, challenging, and contextualising what the agent proposes.
DB Phase 2 — Design and BuildHeavy lifting — FD analysis, control design, business validation Refined & Validated

Design and Build is the phase of heavy lifting. The client's system implementer is now configuring the system, building workflows, and producing the functional design documents and configuration rationale that define exactly how the future state will work. The controls team's role is to consume those artefacts and translate them into controls.
Reading Functional Design Documents — Risk First
When you receive a functional design document, your job is not to read it word for word. Your job is to identify the risk relevant to your RACM. The three-step approach:
Step 1 — What risk am I concerned about? Financial, operational, or regulatory. Define this before opening the document — it is your filter.
Step 2 — Does this FD affect that risk? If a failed interface could cause a financial misstatement or a compliance exposure, the FD is relevant. If not, move on.

Step 3 — If relevant: extract the key parameters. For interface controls: data direction and frequency, source and target systems, and critically — the error handling mechanism. Does the system detect interface errors, alert someone, and trigger resolution? That error handling mechanism is the control.

Scope Boundary — Critical The controls team does not configure anything in SAP and does not perform design work. That is the system implementer's role. The controls team consumes the programme's design artefacts and produces the RACM. Keeping these roles distinct protects independence and audit credibility — the controls team reviewing the SI's design work is only meaningful if they are genuinely independent of that design.

🤖 AI Agent Callout — Design and Build Design and Build presents the clearest ROI case for AI assistance in the controls workstream. The team may be working through hundreds of functional design documents across multiple business processes, multiple team members, and a compressed timeline. AI agents can accelerate initial FD analysis — identifying risk-relevant sections, extracting error handling language, and proposing draft control descriptions. The practitioner validates and refines. The work shifts from document triage to control judgement.
TS Phase 3 — TestingThree test categories, testing captain coordination, SIT vs UAT scope Evidence Captured

Testing is the phase where you find out whether the controls you designed will actually work. The source session describes this as the best and last chance to see if the controls will operate as expected. Three test categories define the controls testing approach.

Configuration Testing What it tests System settings that implement a control — confirms parameters are set correctly, not just that the control exists. 🔍 Example: Inspect OMR6 tolerance keys; confirm threshold ≤3%; verify no vendor-specific overrides.

Transactional Testing What it tests Control responds as designed when a transaction is executed — positive and negative scenarios. 🔍 Example: Run payment to fictitious vendor — confirm SoD block fires. Post invoice exceeding tolerance — confirm system blocks.

Report Testing What it tests Exception reports are complete, accurate, and include the right data population. 🔍 Example: Run UAR report — verify all relevant user-role combinations are captured; agree to underlying system data.

🏭 Field Example — Major Energy Company Engagement The strategy that worked on a major energy company engagement: map controls to the programme's existing test cases before testing begins. Do not wait until the testing team has written their scripts — review the test case steps and add controls testing requirements directly. When a tester opens the test case, they see the programme requirement and the controls requirement in the same document. Also: find the testing captain — the person coordinating a group of testers — and make them your key contact. Routing evidence requests and rework through one coordinator is far more efficient than chasing individual testers across thousands of emails.
SIT vs UAT Scope Decision
System Integration Testing: Configuration controls — those that operate without human intervention — belong here, where the system itself is being validated.

User Acceptance Testing: Workflow-driven and report-driven controls — those requiring human review and action — belong here, where business users are in the system. This distributes the testing workload across cycles and aligns each control type with the most appropriate testing environment.
CD Phase 4 — Cutover and DeployRACM finalised, control owners trained, external auditor gate Final — Go-Live Ready

Cutover and Deploy is the final phase before go-live. The system has been configured, controls have been designed, and testing has confirmed they work. Now the question is: is the organisation ready to operate those controls from day one?
Three Go-Live Readiness Activities

1. Finalise the RACM. Confirm every control has an assigned owner. Descriptions reflect the tested final state. The RACM is formally approved and distributed to everyone who will need it post-go-live. This is the completed version of a document that began as a preliminary draft in Solution Confirmation.

2. Train the control owners. Every person responsible for a control — particularly ITDM and manual controls — must understand what they need to do, how often, what evidence to produce, and how to escalate exceptions. The source session is explicit: people must know how to execute the controls before the system goes live.

3. External auditor confirmation gate. Across the transformation, the external auditor has been a periodic touchpoint. At Cutover and Deploy, the frequency of those touchpoints increases significantly. The auditor must confirm that the controls the programme designed and tested are the controls they will rely on in their annual audit. That confirmation is the final gate before go-live.

RACM Traceability — The Final Principle The RACM is not a point-in-time document — it is an iterated artefact that has been through multiple versions since the preliminary draft in Solution Confirmation. The ability to trace from the final tested control back to the original risk assessment that motivated it is important for audit credibility, for programme retrospectives, and for future engagements with the same client. Maintain version control on the RACM from day one.

Click any phase below to explore its activities, or read through the full accordion that follows.

Phase 1 Solution Confirmation RACM: Preliminary Draft

Establish the Risk Universe

Review programme scope and business processes. Produce a preliminary risk assessment across financial, operational, and compliance risk categories. This is the foundation — without it, the RACM has no anchor.

Draft the Preliminary RACM

Not a finished document — a starting point. The source session: "it will not be perfect, but it sets the ground and foundation." Every subsequent phase refines it.

Make Friends

Build relationships with SI functional leads, testing team, security team, data team, cybersecurity team. These relationships will be called upon in every subsequent phase. Invest in them now.

Influence the Future State Design

Peak influence window. Identify processes that are currently manual but could be automated in S/4HANA. Raise them now — once Key Design Decisions are finalised, influencing the design becomes progressively harder and more expensive.

AI Agent Opportunity

AI agents can perform current-state to future-state gap analysis and propose preliminary controls from programme artefacts. The practitioner's role shifts from information processing to judgement — validating, challenging, contextualising.

Phase 2 Design and Build RACM: Refined & Validated

Read Functional Design Documents — Risk First

Three-step approach: (1) What risk am I concerned about? (2) Does this FD affect that risk? (3) If yes — what are the data frequency, direction, and error handling details? The error handling mechanism is typically the control.

Design Controls, Validate with Business

Translate FD analysis into specific controls. Hold working sessions with business process owners to validate — the business must agree to perform these controls on go-live. Update the RACM with specific, validated control descriptions.

Maintain Scope Boundary

The controls team consumes programme artefacts — we do not configure anything in SAP and do not perform design work. That is the SI's role. Our deliverable is the RACM. Keeping this scope boundary clear protects independence and audit credibility.

AI Agent Opportunity

AI agents can accelerate FD analysis across hundreds of documents — extracting risk-relevant sections and proposing draft controls. The practitioner validates and refines. Volume challenge in Design and Build is the clearest ROI case for AI assistance.

Phase 3 Testing RACM: Test Evidence Captured

Configuration Testing

Validate system settings that implement a control — OMR6 tolerance keys, workflow thresholds, approval routing. Confirm parameters are set correctly, not just that the control exists.

Transactional Testing

Execute real or simulated transactions to confirm the control responds as designed — run a payment to a fictitious vendor to confirm the SoD block fires, post an invoice exceeding tolerance to confirm the system blocks it.

Report Testing

Confirm exception reports are complete, accurate, and cover the right population. Run the UAR report and verify it captures all relevant user-role combinations. Agree to the underlying system data.

Testing Captain Strategy

From a major energy company engagement: integrate controls requirements into programme test cases before testing begins. Find the testing captain — the person coordinating a group of testers — and make them your key contact. Route all evidence requests and rework through one coordinator.

SIT vs UAT Scope Decision

Configuration controls (automated, no human intervention) → System Integration Testing. Workflow-driven and report-driven controls (require human review) → User Acceptance Testing. This distributes effort and aligns each control type with the most appropriate environment.

Phase 4 Cutover and Deploy RACM: Final — Go-Live Ready

Finalise the RACM

Every control has an assigned owner. Descriptions reflect the tested final state. RACM is formally approved and distributed to all post-go-live stakeholders. This is the finished version of a document that began as a preliminary draft in SolCon.

Train the Control Owners

Every person responsible for a control must understand: what to do, how often, what evidence to produce, and how to escalate exceptions — especially for ITDM and manual controls, where the human element is the control.

External Auditor Confirmation Gate

The auditor must confirm the controls designed and tested are the controls they will rely on in the annual audit. This confirmation is the final gate before go-live. Touchpoint frequency increases significantly in this phase.

Maintain RACM Traceability

The RACM is not a point-in-time document — it is an iterated artefact that has been through multiple versions since SolCon. The ability to trace from the final go-live control back to the original risk assessment is important for audit credibility and future engagements.

The RACM Iteration Narrative

The Risk and Controls Matrix is not a one-time build. It begins as a preliminary draft and is progressively refined through every phase of the transformation.

Testing

Cutover & Deploy

SC Phase 1 — Solution ConfirmationFoundation, relationships, preliminary RACM, peak influence window Preliminary Draft

Solution Confirmation is the first phase of the S/4HANA transformation. At this stage the client and their system implementer are defining the future state — what the new system will look like, what processes will change, and what key design decisions will be made. For the controls team, this is the most important phase of the entire engagement — not because the heaviest work happens here, but because the foundation you lay in Solution Confirmation determines everything that follows.

Three Core Activities

1. Establish the Risk Universe. Before a single control is designed, you need to understand what could go wrong in the future state. Review the programme scope, understand the business processes being transformed, and produce a preliminary risk assessment.

2. Draft the Preliminary RACM. Not a finished document — a starting point. The source session is clear: it will not be perfect, but it sets the ground and foundation for what the client's risk and controls landscape will look like. Every subsequent phase refines it.

3. Make friends. You need relationships with the system implementer's functional leads, the testing team, the security team, the data team, and the cybersecurity team. These relationships will be called upon in every subsequent phase. Invest in them now, when the programme is still in planning mode.

Peak Influence Window Solution Confirmation is your best opportunity to influence the future state design. If you identify a process that is currently manual but could be automated in S/4HANA, raise it now. Once the Key Design Decisions are finalised and the system is being configured, influencing the design becomes progressively harder and more expensive. The source session notes: it is better to have a workflow designed and built now than to try to get it built later in the programme.

🤖 AI Agent Callout — Solution Confirmation AI agents are beginning to add value in Solution Confirmation — performing current-state to future-state gap analysis, processing programme artefacts, and proposing preliminary controls. In a phase where the team is consuming large volumes of process documentation with limited bandwidth, the efficiency gain from AI-assisted analysis can be significant. The practitioner's role shifts from raw information processing to judgement: validating, challenging, and contextualising what the agent proposes.

DB Phase 2 — Design and BuildHeavy lifting — FD analysis, control design, business validation Refined & Validated

Design and Build is the phase of heavy lifting. The client's system implementer is now configuring the system, building workflows, and producing the functional design documents and configuration rationale that define exactly how the future state will work. The controls team's role is to consume those artefacts and translate them into controls.

Reading Functional Design Documents — Risk First

When you receive a functional design document, your job is not to read it word for word. Your job is to identify the risk relevant to your RACM. The three-step approach:

Step 1 — What risk am I concerned about? Financial, operational, or regulatory. Define this before opening the document — it is your filter.

Step 2 — Does this FD affect that risk? If a failed interface could cause a financial misstatement or a compliance exposure, the FD is relevant. If not, move on.

Step 3 — If relevant: extract the key parameters. For interface controls: data direction and frequency, source and target systems, and critically — the error handling mechanism. Does the system detect interface errors, alert someone, and trigger resolution? That error handling mechanism is the control.

Scope Boundary — Critical The controls team does not configure anything in SAP and does not perform design work. That is the system implementer's role. The controls team consumes the programme's design artefacts and produces the RACM. Keeping these roles distinct protects independence and audit credibility — the controls team reviewing the SI's design work is only meaningful if they are genuinely independent of that design.

🤖 AI Agent Callout — Design and Build Design and Build presents the clearest ROI case for AI assistance in the controls workstream. The team may be working through hundreds of functional design documents across multiple business processes, multiple team members, and a compressed timeline. AI agents can accelerate initial FD analysis — identifying risk-relevant sections, extracting error handling language, and proposing draft control descriptions. The practitioner validates and refines. The work shifts from document triage to control judgement.

TS Phase 3 — TestingThree test categories, testing captain coordination, SIT vs UAT scope Evidence Captured

Testing is the phase where you find out whether the controls you designed will actually work. The source session describes this as the best and last chance to see if the controls will operate as expected. Three test categories define the controls testing approach.

Configuration Testing What it tests System settings that implement a control — confirms parameters are set correctly, not just that the control exists. 🔍 Example: Inspect OMR6 tolerance keys; confirm threshold ≤3%; verify no vendor-specific overrides.

Transactional Testing What it tests Control responds as designed when a transaction is executed — positive and negative scenarios. 🔍 Example: Run payment to fictitious vendor — confirm SoD block fires. Post invoice exceeding tolerance — confirm system blocks.

Report Testing What it tests Exception reports are complete, accurate, and include the right data population. 🔍 Example: Run UAR report — verify all relevant user-role combinations are captured; agree to underlying system data.

🏭 Field Example — Major Energy Company Engagement The strategy that worked on a major energy company engagement: map controls to the programme's existing test cases before testing begins. Do not wait until the testing team has written their scripts — review the test case steps and add controls testing requirements directly. When a tester opens the test case, they see the programme requirement and the controls requirement in the same document. Also: find the testing captain — the person coordinating a group of testers — and make them your key contact. Routing evidence requests and rework through one coordinator is far more efficient than chasing individual testers across thousands of emails.

SIT vs UAT Scope Decision

System Integration Testing: Configuration controls — those that operate without human intervention — belong here, where the system itself is being validated.

User Acceptance Testing: Workflow-driven and report-driven controls — those requiring human review and action — belong here, where business users are in the system. This distributes the testing workload across cycles and aligns each control type with the most appropriate testing environment.

CD Phase 4 — Cutover and DeployRACM finalised, control owners trained, external auditor gate Final — Go-Live Ready

Cutover and Deploy is the final phase before go-live. The system has been configured, controls have been designed, and testing has confirmed they work. Now the question is: is the organisation ready to operate those controls from day one?

Three Go-Live Readiness Activities

1. Finalise the RACM. Confirm every control has an assigned owner. Descriptions reflect the tested final state. The RACM is formally approved and distributed to everyone who will need it post-go-live. This is the completed version of a document that began as a preliminary draft in Solution Confirmation.

2. Train the control owners. Every person responsible for a control — particularly ITDM and manual controls — must understand what they need to do, how often, what evidence to produce, and how to escalate exceptions. The source session is explicit: people must know how to execute the controls before the system goes live.

3. External auditor confirmation gate. Across the transformation, the external auditor has been a periodic touchpoint. At Cutover and Deploy, the frequency of those touchpoints increases significantly. The auditor must confirm that the controls the programme designed and tested are the controls they will rely on in their annual audit. That confirmation is the final gate before go-live.

RACM Traceability — The Final Principle The RACM is not a point-in-time document — it is an iterated artefact that has been through multiple versions since the preliminary draft in Solution Confirmation. The ability to trace from the final tested control back to the original risk assessment that motivated it is important for audit credibility, for programme retrospectives, and for future engagements with the same client. Maintain version control on the RACM from day one.

steps.title: Reference table
steps.action: 1 Business Purpose "What is this interface supposed to do — and what is the business consequence if it fails?" Business purpose connects the technical specification to the financial or operational risk. A procurement interface that stops working means purchase orders cannot be raised. A financial posting interface that fails means the general ledger is incomplete. FD-MM-INT-027 → Section 2: Transfers approved PRs from VANTAGE ERP to SAP S/4HANA MM. Failure: no POs raised → procurement stops or goes off-system.
steps.narration: 1 Business Purpose "What is this interface supposed to do — and what is the business consequence if it fails?" Business purpose connects the technical specification to the financial or operational risk. A procurement interface that stops working means purchase orders cannot be raised. A financial posting interface that fails means the general ledger is incomplete. FD-MM-INT-027 → Section 2: Transfers approved PRs from VANTAGE ERP to SAP S/4HANA MM. Failure: no POs raised → procurement stops or goes off-system.

steps.title: Reference table
steps.action: 2 Direction "Is this unidirectional or bidirectional?" Direction determines where failure must be detected. For a unidirectional interface, all failure detection must happen at the receiving system — the sending system has no visibility of what happened after it transmitted. The monitoring control must sit at the receiver. FD-MM-INT-027 → Section 3.2: UNIDIRECTIONAL — VANTAGE sends, SAP receives. VANTAGE receives no confirmation. All detection on the SAP side.
steps.narration: 2 Direction "Is this unidirectional or bidirectional?" Direction determines where failure must be detected. For a unidirectional interface, all failure detection must happen at the receiving system — the sending system has no visibility of what happened after it transmitted. The monitoring control must sit at the receiver. FD-MM-INT-027 → Section 3.2: UNIDIRECTIONAL — VANTAGE sends, SAP receives. VANTAGE receives no confirmation. All detection on the SAP side.

steps.title: Reference table
steps.action: 3 Frequency "How often does the interface run?" Frequency sets the maximum exposure window — the period during which undetected errors can accumulate. A daily monitoring report is not sufficient for an interface that runs every hour. The control design must match the frequency. FD-MM-INT-027 → Section 3.3: Every 4 hours during business hours (normal operations). Exposure window = 4 hours per cycle.
steps.narration: 3 Frequency "How often does the interface run?" Frequency sets the maximum exposure window — the period during which undetected errors can accumulate. A daily monitoring report is not sufficient for an interface that runs every hour. The control design must match the frequency. FD-MM-INT-027 → Section 3.3: Every 4 hours during business hours (normal operations). Exposure window = 4 hours per cycle.

steps.title: Reference table
steps.action: 4 Error Handling ⚠ "How does the system detect, alert, and resolve transfer failures?" This is where most interface controls live. You need: automatic error detection, an alert mechanism, a defined resolution procedure with a timeline, and a reconciliation to confirm the data was recovered. If any of these is missing, that is a control gap. FD-MM-INT-027 → Section 5: Hard Errors → /PNS/INT_ERR → email alert within 15 min → 4-hour resolution SLA → re-submission log → daily sign-off report.

Reading FD Documents — The Question Sequence

Master the four-parameter extraction sequence that turns a functional design document into a well-formed RACM control. Business purpose, direction, frequency, error handling — in that order, every time.
9–11 min · 3 sections · Screen-recording format · Interactive FD checklist · FD excerpt quiz · AI Tutor

Learning Objectives By the end of this module you will be able to apply the risk-first question sequence — business purpose, direction, frequency, error handling — to any functional design document before extracting control parameters. By the end of this module you will be able to identify the controls-critical sections of an interface FD and use the interactive checklist to navigate them systematically. By the end of this module you will be able to translate FD parameters into a formed RACM control with a control type, nature classification, and a two-element ITDM test procedure.
Section 1 · What Is an FD and the Risk Filter

A functional design document is a programme artefact produced by the system implementer. It describes how a specific function will work in the future-state system — an interface between two systems, a workflow that automates an approval, a custom report, or a configuration rationale. The source session is direct: the idea is not to read word for word, but to understand what specific types of details you need to draft an appropriate control.
The One Question Before You Open the Document

Before reading a single page of an FD, answer this question: What risk am I trying to control? This is your filter. Without it you will read everything and extract nothing. Define the risk — financial, operational, or regulatory — then assess whether this FD is relevant. If the answer is yes, proceed to parameter extraction.
FD received
Interface / workflow / report / config rationale
Name the risk
Financial / operational / regulatory — define it before opening
Relevance test
What could go wrong if this process or interface failed?
Yes → Extract
Proceed to four-parameter extraction

PetroNova S.A. Scenario — FD-MM-INT-027 This module uses FD-MM-INT-027 — a purchase requisition interface from VANTAGE ERP into SAP S/4HANA MM — as the running example. The risk: if PRs are not transferred completely and accurately, PetroNova cannot raise purchase orders in SAP. That is an operational risk (procurement stops) and a financial risk (purchases made off-system create unrecorded liabilities). The FD is relevant. Proceed to extraction.
Section 2 · The Four Extraction Parameters

Once you have confirmed the FD is relevant to your risk, move into extraction mode. For an interface FD — the most common type in a Materials Management or Finance transformation — four parameters generate your control design.

1 Business Purpose "What is this interface supposed to do — and what is the business consequence if it fails?" Business purpose connects the technical specification to the financial or operational risk. A procurement interface that stops working means purchase orders cannot be raised. A financial posting interface that fails means the general ledger is incomplete. FD-MM-INT-027 → Section 2: Transfers approved PRs from VANTAGE ERP to SAP S/4HANA MM. Failure: no POs raised → procurement stops or goes off-system.

2 Direction "Is this unidirectional or bidirectional?" Direction determines where failure must be detected. For a unidirectional interface, all failure detection must happen at the receiving system — the sending system has no visibility of what happened after it transmitted. The monitoring control must sit at the receiver. FD-MM-INT-027 → Section 3.2: UNIDIRECTIONAL — VANTAGE sends, SAP receives. VANTAGE receives no confirmation. All detection on the SAP side.

3 Frequency "How often does the interface run?" Frequency sets the maximum exposure window — the period during which undetected errors can accumulate. A daily monitoring report is not sufficient for an interface that runs every hour. The control design must match the frequency. FD-MM-INT-027 → Section 3.3: Every 4 hours during business hours (normal operations). Exposure window = 4 hours per cycle.

4 Error Handling ⚠ "How does the system detect, alert, and resolve transfer failures?" This is where most interface controls live. You need: automatic error detection, an alert mechanism, a defined resolution procedure with a timeline, and a reconciliation to confirm the data was recovered. If any of these is missing, that is a control gap. FD-MM-INT-027 → Section 5: Hard Errors → /PNS/INT_ERR → email alert within 15 min → 4-hour resolution SLA → re-submission log → daily sign-off report.
Interactive FD Review Checklist
Use this checklist while reviewing FD-MM-INT-027 (or any interface FD). Tick each item as you confirm it. Stateless — resets on page reload.
Section A · Business Purpose & Scope
Param 1
☐ I can state what data this interface transfers and between which systems.
☐ I can describe the business consequence if the interface fails (operational or financial impact).
☐ I have noted any explicit in-scope / out-of-scope boundaries that affect the control population.
Section B · Interface Direction
Param 2
☐ I have confirmed whether the interface is unidirectional or bidirectional.
☐ For unidirectional: I have confirmed the monitoring control must sit at the receiving system.
Section C · Transfer Frequency
Param 3
☐ I have recorded the interface frequency (e.g. every 4 hours, daily, real-time).
☐ I have assessed whether the monitoring control frequency is aligned to the transfer frequency.
Section D · Error Handling & Monitoring ⚠ Controls-Critical
Param 4
☐ I have confirmed the system detects errors automatically (hard errors, soft warnings, interface failures).
☐ I have confirmed there is a notification mechanism (email alert, system message) when errors occur.
☐ I have recorded the resolution SLA (e.g. hard errors resolved within 4 hours).
☐ I have confirmed there is a reconciliation or sign-off mechanism to evidence the control was performed.
☐ I have identified any gaps in error handling that represent a control design deficiency.
All sections reviewed — you have everything you need to draft the control.
Section 3 · Deriving the Control
With all four parameters extracted, the control design follows directly. Using the PetroNova S.A. FD-MM-INT-027 scenario:
RACM Control Output — FIN-P2P-028
Control Reference
FIN-P2P-028
Control Type
Detective
Control Nature
ITDM — IT-Dependent Manual
Risk
Incomplete/inaccurate PR transfer → no POs in SAP → off-system procurement → unrecorded liabilities
Control Description

The P2P Interface Monitor reviews the daily SAP monitoring report (/PNS/INT_RPT_DAILY) by 09:00 WAT each business day. For each Hard Error flagged, the Monitor investigates the root cause, resolves it, and re-submits the affected records within 4 hours of notification. The signed-off monitoring report and re-submission log are retained as evidence.
Why This Is an ITDM Control

The system component: SAP automatically generates the monitoring report and populates the error log. The human component: the P2P Interface Monitor reviews the report, investigates exceptions, documents corrective action, and signs off. Both elements must be present and evidenced — a report that is generated but not reviewed is evidence that a control exists, not that it is effective. This is the B3 ITDM pattern applied to an interface control scenario.
Test Procedure — Two-Element ITDM Pattern
Element 1 — System Component: Report Completeness & AccuracyVerify the monitoring report is complete and covers the right population
01 Coverage Check Confirm the daily monitoring report covers all batch cycles for the test period. Verify the report is generated from the correct SAP table (/PNS/INT_ERR and /PNS/INT_WARN).

02 Accuracy Sample Select 3 batch cycles from the test period. For each, agree the Hard Error count in the report to the records in /PNS/INT_ERR. Confirm there are no gaps — every hard error in the table should appear in the report.
03 Reconciliation Verification Confirm the end-of-day PR count reconciliation was performed — total approved PRs in VANTAGE matches total PR records received by SAP for the same day.
Element 2 — Human Component: Review Evidence & Exception ResolutionVerify the P2P Monitor reviewed, investigated, and documented exceptions

01 Review Evidence Is there a signed-off monitoring report for each business day in the test period? Confirm sign-off is by the P2P Process Lead (not a subordinate or IT). Confirm sign-off occurred by 09:00 WAT the following business day per the SLA.

02 Exception Follow-Up For each Hard Error flagged in the period: is there a re-submission record in /PNS/INT_RESUBMIT with a timestamp within 4 hours of the original alert? Is there a documented root cause and resolution sign-off?

03 Effectiveness Assessment A monitoring report that is signed off with no exception investigation documented — despite hard errors in the log — is evidence that a review occurred, not that it was effective. Flag as ITDM deficiency if exception follow-up is absent.

All Sections Complete You have worked through the FD question sequence, the interactive checklist, and the control derivation. Proceed to Key Concepts for a structured recall review, or go directly to the Knowledge Check. A passing score of 60% marks this module complete and unlocks Module B8.

steps.action: Testing is the best and last chance to see if the controls will actually work as expected. The evidence standard determines whether your test result is defensible — to your client, to an external auditor, and to your own quality review. Each test category has a different evidence standard.

steps.title: Reference table
steps.action: 🏭 Field Example — Major Energy Sector Engagement On a major energy sector engagement, the three-way match configuration test involved navigating to SPRO → the tolerance key path → confirming the tolerance limits were set. The design specified a 3% threshold. What the system showed: 2% for both quantity and price variance. More restrictive than designed — test result: Pass. But the value-add came next: reviewing all company codes, not just one. Most showed 2–3%. One showed 10%. That exception needed a policy justification or a correction. A practitioner who checked only the first company code would have missed it.

Option:   Screenshot ASAP screen showing "Tolerance Key active" — no path, no value displayed Option:   Screenshot BSPRO path screenshot + OMR6 screen showing 2% quantity and price variance for one company code Option:   Screenshot CPositive test scenario: invoice within tolerance posted successfully — system log shown Option:   Screenshot DPositive scenario (invoice passed) + negative scenario (invoice blocked + blocking reason code) ❌ Insufficient This screenshot proves existence — the tolerance key is active — but not appropriateness. You cannot tell from this screen what the tolerance value is, whether it matches the control design, or whether any company code exceptions exist. You also need: The SPRO navigation path screenshot, the specific tolerance percentage values (quantity variance and price variance), and a cross-check across all company codes. ⚠️ Partially Sufficient — Missing Company Code Cross-Check Good progress — the SPRO path establishes navigation and the OMR6 screen shows the specific tolerance values (2% quantity and price). This is better than Screenshot A and covers two of the three required components. You also need: A cross-check across all company codes. If most show 2% but one shows 10%, that exception must be investigated and either justified by policy or corrected before go-live. Checking one company code is not sufficient. ❌ Insufficient — Missing Negative Scenario A positive scenario confirms the control does not block valid transactions — it rules out false positives. But it does not prove the control actually fires when it should. You also need: A negative scenario — a transaction that exceeds the tolerance — resulting in a system block and a blocking reason code. Without this, you have not tested the control's core function. ✅ Sufficient — for Transactional Testing Both scenarios are present: a positive scenario (compliant transaction processes without a block) and a negative scenario (non-compliant transaction triggers the system block with a blocking reason code).
