Testing Phase — Three Decisions

Testing is where controls earn their credibility — or expose their gaps. Three decisions determine how effective your testing phase will be: what counts as sufficient evidence, how to scope SIT versus UAT, and how to anchor your coordination through the testing captain.
10–12 min · 3 decisions · Advanced · Evidence sufficiency checker · 4 MCQs · AI Tutor

Learning Objectives By the end of this module you will be able to define sufficient evidence for config, transactional, and ITDM controls testing — including the company-code cross-check and why positive scenarios alone are not enough. By the end of this module you will be able to apply the SIT vs UAT scope split based on control nature and explain why automated controls tested in SIT do not need to be re-run in UAT. By the end of this module you will be able to set up and use the testing captain model — identifying the anchor, integrating controls requirements into test cases before testing starts, and managing re-test requests efficiently.
Decision 1 · What Counts as Sufficient Evidence?

Testing is the best and last chance to see if the controls will actually work as expected. The evidence standard determines whether your test result is defensible — to your client, to an external auditor, and to your own quality review. Each test category has a different evidence standard.

🏭 Field Example — Major Energy Sector Engagement On a major energy sector engagement, the three-way match configuration test involved navigating to SPRO → the tolerance key path → confirming the tolerance limits were set. The design specified a 3% threshold. What the system showed: 2% for both quantity and price variance. More restrictive than designed — test result: Pass. But the value-add came next: reviewing all company codes, not just one. Most showed 2–3%. One showed 10%. That exception needed a policy justification or a correction. A practitioner who checked only the first company code would have missed it.
Evidence Standard by Test Category
⚙️ Configuration TestingSPRO path · tolerance values · company code cross-check
Insufficient: A screenshot showing "three-way match active" or "workflow enabled." This proves existence — not appropriateness.
Sufficient: Three components required:
01 Navigation path Screenshot showing the exact SPRO or transaction path taken to reach the configuration setting. Not just the result screen — the path to it.
02 Value confirmation Screenshot showing the specific tolerance or threshold value — e.g. 2% for quantity variance and 2% for price variance. Compared against the design threshold in the RACM.

03 Company code cross-check All relevant company codes reviewed. Any exception to the standard value is documented. If one company code has 10% where all others have 3%, that exception requires a policy justification or correction before go-live.
💳 Transactional TestingPositive AND negative scenario — both required
The rule: Every transactional test requires a positive scenario AND a negative scenario. A test plan with only positive scenarios does not prove a control blocks what it should block.
✅ POSITIVE SCENARIO
Compliant transaction processes correctly. For three-way match: invoice within 2% tolerance is posted — no block fired.
Purpose: confirms no false positives.
❌ NEGATIVE SCENARIO
Non-compliant transaction is blocked. For three-way match: invoice exceeding 2% tolerance — system blocks posting and generates blocking reason code.
Purpose: confirms the control actually blocks what it should.

The Most Common Transactional Testing Deficiency Test plans that contain only positive scenarios. When this happens: push back. "We do not want to just see the happy path. We want to see what happens when it works and what happens when it does not work as expected."

🔍 Interactive Tool Evidence Sufficiency Checker Select a screenshot type to see whether it constitutes sufficient audit evidence — and why. Option:   Screenshot ASAP screen showing "Tolerance Key active" — no path, no value displayed Option:   Screenshot BSPRO path screenshot + OMR6 screen showing 2% quantity and price variance for one company code Option:   Screenshot CPositive test scenario: invoice within tolerance posted successfully — system log shown Option:   Screenshot DPositive scenario (invoice passed) + negative scenario (invoice blocked + blocking reason code) ❌ Insufficient This screenshot proves existence — the tolerance key is active — but not appropriateness. You cannot tell from this screen what the tolerance value is, whether it matches the control design, or whether any company code exceptions exist. You also need: The SPRO navigation path screenshot, the specific tolerance percentage values (quantity variance and price variance), and a cross-check across all company codes. ⚠️ Partially Sufficient — Missing Company Code Cross-Check Good progress — the SPRO path establishes navigation and the OMR6 screen shows the specific tolerance values (2% quantity and price). This is better than Screenshot A and covers two of the three required components. You also need: A cross-check across all company codes. If most show 2% but one shows 10%, that exception must be investigated and either justified by policy or corrected before go-live. Checking one company code is not sufficient. ❌ Insufficient — Missing Negative Scenario A positive scenario confirms the control does not block valid transactions — it rules out false positives. But it does not prove the control actually fires when it should. You also need: A negative scenario — a transaction that exceeds the tolerance — resulting in a system block and a blocking reason code. Without this, you have not tested the control's core function. ✅ Sufficient — for Transactional Testing Both scenarios are present: a positive scenario (compliant transaction processes without a block) and a negative scenario (non-compliant transaction triggers the system block with a blocking reason code). This is sufficient evidence that the control is operating as designed for transactional testing purposes. Remember: This covers transactional testing only. A complete test package for a configured automated control also requires the configuration evidence (Screenshot B + company code cross-check) as a separate test step.
Decision 2 · SIT vs UAT Scope
Which controls belong in System Integration Testing, and which belong in User Acceptance Testing? The split is based on control nature — not risk rating, not design ownership.

⚙️ SIT — System Integration Testing Rule: Configuration and automated controls — those that operate without human intervention. The system itself is being validated. Technical testers are executing functional test cases. Controls requirements are integrated into the programme test scripts — testers execute and produce the required evidence in one pass. SIT EXAMPLES Three-way match tolerance (OMR6) · Vendor master workflow configuration · Duplicate invoice block · Payment run SoD restriction

👤 UAT — User Acceptance Testing Rule: ITDM and manual controls — those that require human review and action. Business users are in the system. They can demonstrate they can perform the required review steps — generate the report, investigate exceptions, sign off. Both the IT component and the human component are evidenced. UAT EXAMPLES PR Interface Monitoring Report Review · Vendor Change Report Review · Period-End Close Checklist · Emergency PO Authorisation Review

Why Automated Controls Don't Need to Be Re-Run in UAT Configuration controls validated in SIT do not change between SIT and UAT — the system configuration is the same. Re-running them in UAT consumes business user time and testing programme capacity without adding audit value. The efficiency gain from the SIT/UAT split is real — on a programme with 300 controls, it can eliminate dozens of unnecessary UAT test cycles.
Decision 3 · The Coordination Anchor — Testing Captain
How do you maintain evidence quality across a testing programme with dozens of testers, hundreds of test cases, and multiple coordination layers? The testing captain is the answer.
Controls Team
↓ single channel
Testing Captain
↓ coordinates
Tester 1
Tester 2
Tester 3
🎯 Why the Testing Captain Model WorksWithout it: thousands of email threads. With it: one channel, consistent standards.

A testing captain is the coordinator for a group of testers in the programme's testing structure. They are not necessarily senior — they may be a test coordinator or team lead from the system integrator's testing organisation. What they provide is a single point of contact for evidence requests, rework, and re-execution.

Without the testing captain model: the controls team chases each individual tester directly. Each tester may interpret evidence requirements differently. Re-test requests are managed across hundreds of separate email threads. Evidence quality is inconsistent.

With the testing captain model: evidence requests go to one person. The captain enforces consistent standards across their tester group. Re-test requests are coordinated through one channel. The controls team's time is spent reviewing evidence, not chasing individuals.
📋 Integration Before Testing Starts — Four StepsSet up in Design and Build. Pay back in Testing.
01 Map controls to test cases Before testing begins, review each programme test case and identify which controls it exercises. Add the RACM control reference to the test case metadata.

02 Add controls requirements to test scripts For each mapped test case, add the specific controls testing requirements as additional steps. When a tester opens the test case, they see both the programme requirement and the controls requirement in the same document.

03 Specify evidence requirements upfront Publish the evidence requirements before testing starts — exactly which screenshots, system logs, or outputs are needed for each control test. Agree with the testing captain before the first test is executed.

04 Define the re-test mechanism Define in advance: who decides if evidence is insufficient, who communicates the re-test request, and what the SLA is. The testing captain is the communication channel. Setting this up before testing starts eliminates the friction of chasing re-executions mid-programme.
The Practitioner's Payoff Setting this up takes effort in Design and Build. It pays back in the Testing phase every time you do not have to chase a re-execution.

AI in Controls — Augment, Not Replace

AI agents are already showing up in the controls workstream. This module gives you a grounded picture of where they add real value, where practitioner judgement remains irreplaceable, and how the "augment not replace" frame applies to how you work.
9–11 min · 3 sections · Advanced · 5 MCQs · Self-referential AI Tutor

Learning Objectives By the end of this module you will be able to describe where AI agents add measurable value in the controls workstream — gap analysis in SolCon, control proposal in Design & Build, test coverage analysis in Testing. By the end of this module you will be able to explain the clear limits of AI capability and identify the three practitioner judgements that remain irreplaceable. By the end of this module you will be able to apply the augment-not-replace frame — understanding how attention shifts without the practitioner's role disappearing.
Section 1 · What AI Agents Do in the Controls Workstream

An agent, in the controls context, is a software system that can be given a task, access relevant information, and produce a structured output — without requiring a human to do each step manually. The tasks agents handle best involve processing large volumes of structured or semi-structured information to produce a preliminary output that a practitioner then reviews and refines.

SolCon Gap Analysis 🤖 Agent: Ingests current-state process docs + future-state programme artefacts. Surfaces which controls exist today with no future-state equivalent — and which risks are new. Practitioner role shifts to Reviewing the first-cut gap analysis. Validating what the agent found. Challenging what it missed. Applying programme context and professional scepticism.

Design & Build Control Proposal 🤖 Agent: Ingests functional design documents. Proposes a control description, suggested type/nature classification, and a draft RACM entry for each FD. Practitioner role shifts to Reviewing each proposal. Accepting well-formed drafts. Reworking those that missed a nuance — wrong classification, overlooked error handling, manual where automated is possible.

Testing Test Coverage Analysis 🤖 Agent: Cross-references the RACM against the test case library. Flags controls with no test coverage and test cases with evidence requirements inconsistent with the control type. Practitioner role shifts to Reviewing flagged gaps. Confirming whether missing coverage is intentional or an oversight. Directing the testing captain to address gaps before the testing cycle closes.

The Value Is Not That the Agent Replaces Review The value is that the practitioner starts from a structured draft rather than a blank page. On a programme with hundreds of FDs, that shift — from blank-page creation to structured review — is where the efficiency gain actually materialises. The judgement work remains. The information-processing work is accelerated.
Section 2 · The Limits of AI Capability
There are three practitioner judgements that AI agents cannot make — not as a matter of current capability, but as a matter of what the judgement requires.

⚖️ Professional Judgement Whether a test result constitutes sufficient evidence for a specific client and engagement context. An agent can flag that evidence exists — it cannot assess whether it is appropriate for this client, this auditor, this risk level.

🔗 Client Context Why one company code has a tolerance exception — and whether the explanation is credible. An agent can identify the exception. It cannot assess the business rationale, the relationship history, or whether the client's answer makes sense.

🧐 Professional Scepticism Recognising when a monitoring report was signed off without any investigation of the exceptions it flagged. An agent can see the sign-off. It cannot sense the absence of substantive review behind a clean-looking form.
These assessments require a practitioner who knows the client, knows the programme, and has the professional accountability that comes with signing off on the work.
Section 3 · Augment, Not Replace — The Frame That Matters
The framing that matters is simple: AI agents propose. Practitioners decide. What changes is where in the process your attention is most needed.
Where Your Attention Shifts
Information Processing
Initial triage, first-draft analysis, volume cross-referencing — agent accelerates this
Less
Judgement
Validating, challenging, contextualising agent outputs — this grows in importance
More
Relationship Work
Client credibility, stakeholder conversations, trust — AI cannot substitute here
More
Accountability
Professional sign-off cannot be delegated to an agent — this stays with you
Same
The Capstone Line of the Advanced Section "The practitioner's core skill set is not going away. It is becoming more valuable. That is a good place to be."

steps.title: Reference table
steps.action: Tip 01 · Starting Right Always start with pain points. Before you walk into your first meeting with a business process team, find out what is keeping them up at night. If you have heard there are problems with the manual journal entry threshold, lead with that. Say: I heard you have been having trouble with this — let us talk about it. The room will change. They have a hundred obligations competing for their attention. Controls is rarely at the top of that list. But when you connect to something they are already worried about, you become relevant immediately. You have something they want to talk about. The conversation you planned becomes one they want to have.

steps.title: Reference table
steps.action: Tip 02 · Starting Right Establish your approach before you start — and hold to it consistently. On a complex programme, you will be working with multiple business process teams at the same time. If you tell the P2P team one thing and the Record-to-Report team something different, word will travel. They will compare notes. Inconsistency creates noise that you will then have to manage on top of everything else. Set your standard approach for how you work, what you deliver, and what you ask of them — and apply it consistently across every team from day one. Consistency is a form of credibility.

steps.title: Reference table
steps.action: Tip 03 · Communicating Well Over-communicate, and integrate early. The most common reason testing phases go badly is not technical — it is that the controls requirements were not visible to the testing team until it was too late to address them properly. Tell people what you are doing and what you need from them before you need it. Integrate your controls testing requirements into the programme test cases before testing starts. Agree the evidence requirements before the first test is executed. The testing captain relationship only works if you have established it before testing begins. Over-communication is not a weakness — it is how you prevent the avoidable surprises.

steps.title: Reference table
steps.action: Tip 04 · Communicating Well Tailor every conversation to the person in the room. Not everyone you work with will be literate in controls. The P2P business user who owns the three-way match control needs a different conversation than the external auditor who is going to rely on it. The CFO needs a different framing than the implementation partner's functional lead. You will have third-party vendors, external auditors, internal stakeholders, and SAP consultants — all in the same programme, all with different frames of reference. Your job is not to deliver the same explanation repeatedly until they understand it. Your job is to translate what matters into a language that makes sense for each specific person.

steps.title: Reference table
steps.action: Tip 05 · Maintaining Rigour Trace everything. Version your RACM from day one. The Risk and Controls Matrix is a living document. It will go through multiple iterations from the preliminary draft in Solution Confirmation to the final version at go-live. The ability to trace from the control you tested back to the risk assessment that motivated it — and back to the original programme scope that defined the risk universe — is not just good hygiene. It is audit credibility. When the external auditor asks why a particular control exists, or why it was designed a specific way, the answer should be traceable in the RACM version history. Maintain version control from the first draft. That traceability is part of the value you deliver.

steps.title: Reference table
steps.action: Tip 06 · Maintaining Rigour Know your artefact landscape — and what you do when it is incomplete. Programmes do not always give you what you need. Some clients will have business process diagrams but not functional design documents. Some will have FDs but nothing that gives you an end-to-end view of the process. When that happens, your job is to figure out how much you have to work with and what you need to get from them. Put the pieces together yourself. Build a preliminary stance on the end-to-end. Do not wait for complete documentation before forming a view — you will wait indefinitely. Work with what you have, identify the gaps explicitly, and pursue them.

steps.title: Reference table
steps.action: Tip 07 · Maintaining Rigour Be strategic about scope — especially in testing. On a programme with hundreds of controls, you cannot test everything in every cycle without burning out the testing team and yourself. Apply the SIT/UAT split. Scope automated and configuration controls for system integration testing. Scope ITDM and manual controls for user acceptance testing. Be deliberate about which controls are key and which are non-key — and use the go-live period to finalise that determination based on what you have seen in testing. A rationalised, well-evidenced set of forty key controls is more valuable than three hundred controls with inconsistent evidence.

steps.title: Reference table
steps.action: Tip 08 · Knowing Your Audience Master the tools your programme uses — better than the implementers do. Every programme uses some kind of tool to track testing, manage defects, and report progress. If you know how to use it better than the people running it, you get to lead the workflow instead of fitting into someone else's. That is a real advantage. It also sends a signal — that you are not just the controls person who shows up with requirements and then waits for the testing team to produce evidence. You are a full participant in how the programme runs. Whatever the tool is — learn it properly before testing starts.

Practitioner Capstone

Ten insights from practitioners who have done this work across multiple engagements and multiple industries. Less framework, more reflection. This is a letter from someone who has been where you are going.
12–14 min · 10 practitioner tips · Capstone · Knowledge check · Certificate generator · Programme complete

What This Module Is This is not a framework module. It is a reflection on what experienced practitioners have learned — the hard way, across real engagements. Ten insights across five themes: starting right, communicating well, maintaining rigour, knowing your audience, and building lasting value. After the knowledge check, generate your programme completion certificate.

"You have covered the frameworks. You know the vocabulary. You can read an FD, write a control, and navigate a testing cycle. What the frameworks do not teach you — what nobody can teach you before you have done the work — is what I am going to try to write down here. Consider this a letter from someone who has been where you are going."

Tip 01 · Starting Right Always start with pain points. Before you walk into your first meeting with a business process team, find out what is keeping them up at night. If you have heard there are problems with the manual journal entry threshold, lead with that. Say: I heard you have been having trouble with this — let us talk about it. The room will change. They have a hundred obligations competing for their attention. Controls is rarely at the top of that list. But when you connect to something they are already worried about, you become relevant immediately. You have something they want to talk about. The conversation you planned becomes one they want to have.

Tip 02 · Starting Right Establish your approach before you start — and hold to it consistently. On a complex programme, you will be working with multiple business process teams at the same time. If you tell the P2P team one thing and the Record-to-Report team something different, word will travel. They will compare notes. Inconsistency creates noise that you will then have to manage on top of everything else. Set your standard approach for how you work, what you deliver, and what you ask of them — and apply it consistently across every team from day one. Consistency is a form of credibility.

Tip 03 · Communicating Well Over-communicate, and integrate early. The most common reason testing phases go badly is not technical — it is that the controls requirements were not visible to the testing team until it was too late to address them properly. Tell people what you are doing and what you need from them before you need it. Integrate your controls testing requirements into the programme test cases before testing starts. Agree the evidence requirements before the first test is executed. The testing captain relationship only works if you have established it before testing begins. Over-communication is not a weakness — it is how you prevent the avoidable surprises.

Tip 04 · Communicating Well Tailor every conversation to the person in the room. Not everyone you work with will be literate in controls. The P2P business user who owns the three-way match control needs a different conversation than the external auditor who is going to rely on it. The CFO needs a different framing than the implementation partner's functional lead. You will have third-party vendors, external auditors, internal stakeholders, and SAP consultants — all in the same programme, all with different frames of reference. Your job is not to deliver the same explanation repeatedly until they understand it. Your job is to translate what matters into a language that makes sense for each specific person.

Tip 05 · Maintaining Rigour Trace everything. Version your RACM from day one. The Risk and Controls Matrix is a living document. It will go through multiple iterations from the preliminary draft in Solution Confirmation to the final version at go-live. The ability to trace from the control you tested back to the risk assessment that motivated it — and back to the original programme scope that defined the risk universe — is not just good hygiene. It is audit credibility. When the external auditor asks why a particular control exists, or why it was designed a specific way, the answer should be traceable in the RACM version history. Maintain version control from the first draft. That traceability is part of the value you deliver.

Tip 06 · Maintaining Rigour Know your artefact landscape — and what you do when it is incomplete. Programmes do not always give you what you need. Some clients will have business process diagrams but not functional design documents. Some will have FDs but nothing that gives you an end-to-end view of the process. When that happens, your job is to figure out how much you have to work with and what you need to get from them. Put the pieces together yourself. Build a preliminary stance on the end-to-end. Do not wait for complete documentation before forming a view — you will wait indefinitely. Work with what you have, identify the gaps explicitly, and pursue them.

Tip 07 · Maintaining Rigour Be strategic about scope — especially in testing. On a programme with hundreds of controls, you cannot test everything in every cycle without burning out the testing team and yourself. Apply the SIT/UAT split. Scope automated and configuration controls for system integration testing. Scope ITDM and manual controls for user acceptance testing. Be deliberate about which controls are key and which are non-key — and use the go-live period to finalise that determination based on what you have seen in testing. A rationalised, well-evidenced set of forty key controls is more valuable than three hundred controls with inconsistent evidence.

Tip 08 · Knowing Your Audience Master the tools your programme uses — better than the implementers do. Every programme uses some kind of tool to track testing, manage defects, and report progress. If you know how to use it better than the people running it, you get to lead the workflow instead of fitting into someone else's. That is a real advantage. It also sends a signal — that you are not just the controls person who shows up with requirements and then waits for the testing team to produce evidence. You are a full participant in how the programme runs. Whatever the tool is — learn it properly before testing starts.

Tip 09 · Building Lasting Value Do the change management that nobody else is doing. A go-live is not the end of a controls engagement — it is the beginning of an operational reality for the client. The people who will execute these controls from day one may have never heard of the RACM. They may not know what they are supposed to do, how often, or what happens if they miss it. You do not need to run a full change management programme — that is not your scope. But you do need to make sure the control owners know what is changing, what their responsibilities are, and what a compliant execution looks like. At minimum: clear training for ITDM and manual control owners before go-live. If they are not ready on day one, the controls are not operating on day one.

Tip 10 · Building Lasting Value Go beyond the engagement — position yourself as a trusted advisor. Your primary job on an engagement is to build the controls. But there is more value you can deliver than that. During the programme, surface the risks and improvement opportunities that your position in the workstream uniquely lets you see. After the programme, stay connected. What else could the controls workstream do to better support the client going forward — a more streamlined framework, a rationalised control set, an ongoing monitoring approach? The practitioners who become trusted advisors are not the ones who delivered a clean RACM and moved on. They are the ones who stayed curious about the client's situation, communicated clearly, and made themselves useful beyond the original scope.
Ten tips. Some of them will feel obvious after you have been on a few engagements. Some of them will only land when you have seen what happens when you ignore them. That is how it goes.

The work is real. The clients are real. The risks you are designing controls against are real. And the practitioner who does this work well — who understands the frameworks, communicates clearly, builds relationships, maintains rigour, and stays curious — genuinely makes organisations safer. That is worth something.
Go do good work.
Isaac Babson Managing Partner & Principal Consultant TIB Systems Inc. | academy@tib-systems.com

steps.title: 49 questions pooled from all 10 modules. A score of 60% or higher passes…
steps.action: 49 questions pooled from all 10 modules. A score of 60% or higher passes and marks this prerequisite complete. In the app, questions are presented in random order and the exam can be retaken at any time. The answer key with explanations follows this section.

steps.title: B1 — Risk Types
steps.action: B1 — Risk Types

steps.title: Q1. A user in Accounts Payable has authorisation to create vendors using…
steps.action: Q1. A user in Accounts Payable has authorisation to create vendors using XK01 and also run the automated payment programme via F110. Which risk category does this conflict primarily represent?

steps.title: A. Operational Risk — the Accounts Payable process is poorly designed.
steps.action: A. Operational Risk — the Accounts Payable process is poorly designed.

steps.title: B. Financial Risk — a Segregation of Duties conflict exists that enables…
steps.action: B. Financial Risk — a Segregation of Duties conflict exists that enables payment fraud.

steps.title: C. Compliance Risk — the organisation is in breach of GDPR requirements.
steps.action: C. Compliance Risk — the organisation is in breach of GDPR requirements.

steps.title: D. Change Risk — an unauthorised system configuration change was made.
steps.action: D. Change Risk — an unauthorised system configuration change was made.

steps.title: Q2. An organisation's board states: "We will not tolerate any unmitigate…
steps.action: Q2. An organisation's board states: "We will not tolerate any unmitigated High-risk SoD conflicts in our Financial Accounting module." This statement is best described as:

steps.title: A. An inherent risk assessment.
steps.action: A. An inherent risk assessment.

steps.title: B. A risk tolerance threshold.
steps.action: B. A risk tolerance threshold.

steps.title: C. A residual risk rating.
steps.action: C. A residual risk rating.

steps.title: D. A control objective.
steps.action: D. A control objective.

steps.title: Q3. After controls are implemented and tested in a Procure-to-Pay proces…
steps.action: Q3. After controls are implemented and tested in a Procure-to-Pay process, the payment run still carries a Medium risk rating. This remaining exposure is referred to as:

steps.title: A. Inherent risk.
steps.action: A. Inherent risk.

steps.title: B. Control risk.
steps.action: B. Control risk.

steps.title: C. Residual risk.
steps.action: C. Residual risk.

steps.title: D. Detection risk.
steps.action: D. Detection risk.

steps.title: Q4. The three-way match in Materials Management (ME21N → MIGO → MIRO) is…
steps.action: Q4. The three-way match in Materials Management (ME21N → MIGO → MIRO) is configured with a tolerance of 95%, allowing invoices to post with up to a 5% discrepancy. A vendor consistently invoices 4.8% above the PO value. This scenario is primarily an example of:

steps.title: A. Financial Risk — the vendor is committing invoice fraud.
steps.action: A. Financial Risk — the vendor is committing invoice fraud.

steps.title: B. Compliance Risk — the configuration violates GDPR Article 5.
steps.action: B. Compliance Risk — the configuration violates GDPR Article 5.

steps.title: C. Operational Risk — a configuration weakness allows material discrepan…
steps.action: C. Operational Risk — a configuration weakness allows material discrepancies to post undetected.

steps.title: D. Change Risk — the tolerance was altered without approval.
steps.action: D. Change Risk — the tolerance was altered without approval.

steps.title: Q5. In building a Risk and Controls Matrix (RCM), a practitioner classif…
steps.action: Q5. In building a Risk and Controls Matrix (RCM), a practitioner classifies a risk as Compliance Risk rather than Financial Risk. What is the most significant practical consequence of this classification decision?

steps.title: A. The risk will be assigned a lower inherent risk rating automatically.
steps.action: A. The risk will be assigned a lower inherent risk rating automatically.

steps.title: B. The test procedure will be designed to test against a specific regula…
steps.action: B. The test procedure will be designed to test against a specific regulatory standard rather than substantive financial transactions.

steps.title: C. The risk will only be relevant in US-listed companies subject to SOX.
steps.action: C. The risk will only be relevant in US-listed companies subject to SOX.

steps.title: D. The control will always be a preventive automated control rather than…
steps.action: D. The control will always be a preventive automated control rather than a detective manual control.

steps.title: B2 — Control Types
steps.action: B2 — Control Types

steps.title: Q6. During a Procure-to-Pay process review, you discover that the SAP sy…
steps.action: Q6. During a Procure-to-Pay process review, you discover that the SAP system automatically blocks vendor invoices where the amount exceeds the purchase order value by more than 3% — without any manual review required. This control is best classified as:

steps.title: A. A detective control — it reviews invoices after they are posted to th…
steps.action: A. A detective control — it reviews invoices after they are posted to the ledger.

steps.title: B. A preventive control — the system blocks the erroneous posting before…
steps.action: B. A preventive control — the system blocks the erroneous posting before it completes.

steps.title: C. An ITDM control — a human must review the exception list and approve …
steps.action: C. An ITDM control — a human must review the exception list and approve or reject.

steps.title: D. A corrective control — it reverses postings that were made in error.
steps.action: D. A corrective control — it reverses postings that were made in error.

steps.title: Q7. Your client has a control where a manager receives a weekly SAP-gene…
steps.action: Q7. Your client has a control where a manager receives a weekly SAP-generated report of all vendor master changes made in the prior week, reviews the list for unusual entries, and signs off that all changes were appropriately authorised. Which control classification is most accurate?

steps.title: A. Preventive — the manager reviews changes before they are applied to t…
steps.action: A. Preventive — the manager reviews changes before they are applied to the vendor master.

steps.title: B. Detective ITDM — the system generates the data, and a human reviews a…
steps.action: B. Detective ITDM — the system generates the data, and a human reviews and takes action.

steps.title: C. Configured automated — SAP automatically validates vendor master chan…
steps.action: C. Configured automated — SAP automatically validates vendor master changes against a ruleset.

steps.title: D. Inherent automated — the control is active by default as part of stan…
steps.action: D. Inherent automated — the control is active by default as part of standard SAP functionality.

steps.title: Q8. Ronnie's field insight distinguishes between a 'configured' automate…
steps.action: Q8. Ronnie's field insight distinguishes between a 'configured' automated control and an 'inherent' automated control. What is the primary audit testing implication of this distinction?

steps.title: A. Configured controls are always more reliable than inherent controls a…
steps.action: A. Configured controls are always more reliable than inherent controls and should receive a higher reliance rating.

steps.title: B. Inherent controls require a full configuration review, while configur…
steps.action: B. Inherent controls require a full configuration review, while configured controls only need a "not disabled" check.

steps.title: C. Configured controls require a configuration review to verify paramete…
steps.action: C. Configured controls require a configuration review to verify parameters are appropriate; inherent controls require confirming the functionality has not been switched off.

steps.title: D. There is no audit testing difference — both types are classified as a…
steps.action: D. There is no audit testing difference — both types are classified as automated and receive identical test procedures.

steps.title: Q9. An internal audit team is assessing a quarterly User Access Review p…
steps.action: Q9. An internal audit team is assessing a quarterly User Access Review process. The UAR was performed, but there is no documented evidence that the business process owner took any action on the three flagged exceptions. Which statement best describes the audit conclusion?

steps.title: A. The control is effective — the review was completed and exceptions we…
steps.action: A. The control is effective — the review was completed and exceptions were identified.

steps.title: B. The control is ineffective — for an ITDM, both the system output and …
steps.action: B. The control is ineffective — for an ITDM, both the system output and the human review with documented action must be evidenced. The action element is missing.

steps.title: C. The control is partially effective — the system component (generating…
steps.action: C. The control is partially effective — the system component (generating the UAR report) was effective, which is the primary element for reliance purposes.

steps.title: D. The control cannot be assessed — more information about the exception…
steps.action: D. The control cannot be assessed — more information about the exceptions is required before a conclusion can be drawn.

steps.title: Q10. During an S/4HANA implementation engagement, a client's current-sta…
steps.action: Q10. During an S/4HANA implementation engagement, a client's current-state process uses a paper form that a warehouse manager manually signs to approve each goods receipt. Applying the control nature hierarchy, what is your first design recommendation?

steps.title: A. Retain the manual paper-based control — it provides an independent ph…
steps.action: A. Retain the manual paper-based control — it provides an independent physical audit trail.

steps.title: B. Convert to an ITDM — generate a weekly SAP goods receipt report for t…
steps.action: B. Convert to an ITDM — generate a weekly SAP goods receipt report for the manager to review and sign off.

steps.title: C. Configure an automated system control — set up SAP to enforce goods r…
steps.action: C. Configure an automated system control — set up SAP to enforce goods receipt validation rules automatically, eliminating the need for manual approval in standard transactions.

steps.title: D. Implement a detective control — run a monthly reconciliation of goods…
steps.action: D. Implement a detective control — run a monthly reconciliation of goods received against purchase orders.

steps.title: B3 — Control Nature
steps.action: B3 — Control Nature

steps.title: Q11. An SAP auditor is testing the three-way match control in a client's…
steps.action: Q11. An SAP auditor is testing the three-way match control in a client's Procure-to-Pay process. The control is documented as: "System automatically blocks MIRO invoice postings where the variance between PO, GR, and invoice exceeds the configured OMR6 tolerance." Which test procedure is complete and sufficient for this control?

steps.title: A. Confirm that the three-way match is active in the system and has not …
steps.action: A. Confirm that the three-way match is active in the system and has not been disabled.

steps.title: B. Select a sample of 25 MIRO postings and confirm none were manually ov…
steps.action: B. Select a sample of 25 MIRO postings and confirm none were manually overridden in the period.

steps.title: C. Inspect OMR6 tolerance key settings to confirm the tolerance is ≤3%; …
steps.action: C. Inspect OMR6 tolerance key settings to confirm the tolerance is ≤3%; verify no vendor-specific overrides exist; sample 25 MIRO postings to confirm the system blocked invoices where variance exceeded tolerance.

steps.title: D. Review the MIRO posting log for the period and confirm the total numb…
steps.action: D. Review the MIRO posting log for the period and confirm the total number of blocked invoices matches management's expectation.

steps.title: Q12. A controls review identifies the following: an AP manager generates…
steps.action: Q12. A controls review identifies the following: an AP manager generates a monthly SAP report of all new vendor master records created in the period, reviews the report against the approved vendor creation form, and signs the report as reviewed. During testing, the auditor finds three new vendors flagged as unusual — but finds no follow-up documentation for any of them. What is the correct audit conclusion?

steps.title: A. The control is effective — the review was completed and the signed re…
steps.action: A. The control is effective — the review was completed and the signed report evidences performance.

steps.title: B. The control is ineffective — for an ITDM, a signed report without doc…
steps.action: B. The control is ineffective — for an ITDM, a signed report without documented exception follow-up evidences that a review occurred but not that it was effective.

steps.title: C. The control is partially effective — the system component (generating…
steps.action: C. The control is partially effective — the system component (generating the report) is working correctly, which is sufficient for a medium-reliance ITDM.

steps.title: D. The control cannot be assessed until the auditor interviews the AP ma…
steps.action: D. The control cannot be assessed until the auditor interviews the AP manager about the three exceptions.

steps.title: Q13. Ronnie's insight from Module B2 distinguishes between a configured …
steps.action: Q13. Ronnie's insight from Module B2 distinguishes between a configured automated control and an inherent automated control. In Module B3 we apply this to testing. What is the specific audit test step required for an INHERENT automated control that is NOT required for a configured automated control?

steps.title: A. Inspect the system configuration to verify the control parameters are…
steps.action: A. Inspect the system configuration to verify the control parameters are set to an appropriate threshold.

steps.title: B. Sample a population of transactions to confirm the system enforced th…
steps.action: B. Sample a population of transactions to confirm the system enforced the control during the test period.

steps.title: C. Confirm that the standard SAP functionality has not been switched off…
steps.action: C. Confirm that the standard SAP functionality has not been switched off or overridden in system settings.

steps.title: D. Obtain management's sign-off on the control design documentation for …
steps.action: D. Obtain management's sign-off on the control design documentation for the period under review.

steps.title: Q14. During an S/4HANA implementation engagement, you identify that a cl…
steps.action: Q14. During an S/4HANA implementation engagement, you identify that a client's current goods receipt approval process uses a paper form that the warehouse manager physically signs. Applying the control nature hierarchy and the uplift imperative, what is the correct recommendation sequence?

steps.title: A. Retain the manual control and supplement it with a weekly SAP goods r…
steps.action: A. Retain the manual control and supplement it with a weekly SAP goods receipt report review (adding an ITDM layer).

steps.title: B. First recommend configuring an automated goods receipt tolerance rule…
steps.action: B. First recommend configuring an automated goods receipt tolerance rule in SAP; if that is not feasible, recommend converting the manual process to an ITDM; retain manual only if neither option is feasible.

steps.title: C. Replace the manual control immediately with an ITDM regardless of fea…
steps.action: C. Replace the manual control immediately with an ITDM regardless of feasibility, since ITDMs are always preferable to manual controls.

steps.title: D. Retain the manual control — paper-based approval forms provide an ind…
steps.action: D. Retain the manual control — paper-based approval forms provide an independent physical audit trail that is more reliable than system-generated records.

steps.title: Q15. A practitioner is classifying the following control for an RCM: "At…
steps.action: Q15. A practitioner is classifying the following control for an RCM: "At the end of each month, the Financial Controller reviews a system-generated SAP report of journal entries posted outside the standard approval workflow and signs off that all entries were appropriately authorised. Any exceptions are emailed to Internal Audit." What is the correct control type AND control nature classification?

steps.title: A. Preventive control · Configured automated — the system generates the …
steps.action: A. Preventive control · Configured automated — the system generates the exception list automatically.

steps.title: B. Detective control · ITDM — the system generates the data and a human …
steps.action: B. Detective control · ITDM — the system generates the data and a human reviews and acts on it.

steps.title: C. Detective control · Manual — the Financial Controller performs the re…
steps.action: C. Detective control · Manual — the Financial Controller performs the review without any system involvement.

steps.title: D. Preventive control · ITDM — the review prevents future authorisation …
steps.action: D. Preventive control · ITDM — the review prevents future authorisation failures by identifying the issue.

steps.title: B4 — Why Controls Matter
steps.action: B4 — Why Controls Matter

steps.title: Q16. A programme sponsor asks you: 'Why should we spend budget on a cont…
steps.action: Q16. A programme sponsor asks you: 'Why should we spend budget on a controls workstream during implementation rather than fixing any issues after go-live?' Which answer best represents the business case from Module B4?

steps.title: A. Post-live remediation is technically complex and requires specialist …
steps.action: A. Post-live remediation is technically complex and requires specialist SAP skills that are expensive to source on short notice.

steps.title: B. Prevention during implementation costs a fraction of remediation post…
steps.action: B. Prevention during implementation costs a fraction of remediation post-live — every control gap fixed before go-live avoids rework, audit findings, and business disruption at the most vulnerable moment.

steps.title: C. Regulatory requirements mandate that controls must be in place before…
steps.action: C. Regulatory requirements mandate that controls must be in place before an SAP go-live; there is no legal option to fix them afterwards.

steps.title: D. Controls cannot be retrofitted into SAP after go-live due to technica…
steps.action: D. Controls cannot be retrofitted into SAP after go-live due to technical constraints in the S/4HANA architecture.

steps.title: Q17. The source session describes 'lift-and-shift' as a mindset the cont…
steps.action: Q17. The source session describes 'lift-and-shift' as a mindset the controls workstream must challenge. What does lift-and-shift mean in the context of an S/4HANA transformation, and why is it a problem?

steps.title: A. Physically moving on-premise SAP hardware to a cloud environment — a …
steps.action: A. Physically moving on-premise SAP hardware to a cloud environment — a problem because cloud controls differ from on-premise controls.

steps.title: B. Migrating data from the legacy system to S/4HANA without data cleansi…
steps.action: B. Migrating data from the legacy system to S/4HANA without data cleansing — a problem because dirty data undermines control effectiveness.

steps.title: C. Carrying the old process design directly into the new system without …
steps.action: C. Carrying the old process design directly into the new system without redesign — a problem because it misses the opportunity to build compliance and automation into the future state.

steps.title: D. Transferring documentation from the old system to the new one without…
steps.action: D. Transferring documentation from the old system to the new one without updating it — a problem because outdated documentation creates audit risk.

steps.title: Q18. A client CFO asks: 'How will the controls workstream affect our ext…
steps.action: Q18. A client CFO asks: 'How will the controls workstream affect our external audit cost next year?' Which response from Module B4 is most accurate?

steps.title: A. Controls work happens inside the programme — external auditors conduc…
steps.action: A. Controls work happens inside the programme — external auditors conduct their own independent testing and the two processes do not interact.

steps.title: B. Controls are the inputs for the external audit. Controls designed, do…
steps.action: B. Controls are the inputs for the external audit. Controls designed, documented, and tested from go-live attract higher auditor reliance, require smaller sample sizes, and reduce annual external audit fees.

steps.title: C. The controls workstream cannot guarantee any reduction in external au…
steps.action: C. The controls workstream cannot guarantee any reduction in external audit cost — that depends on the auditor's methodology, not the controls framework.

steps.title: D. External audit cost is driven by the number of entities in scope, not…
steps.action: D. External audit cost is driven by the number of entities in scope, not by control quality, so controls work has no direct impact on audit fees.

steps.title: Q19. Value Driver 4 — Integration and Efficiency — describes what a cont…
steps.action: Q19. Value Driver 4 — Integration and Efficiency — describes what a controls workstream should leave behind when the engagement closes. Which outcome best represents this value driver?

steps.title: A. A comprehensive controls documentation library that the client's Inte…
steps.action: A. A comprehensive controls documentation library that the client's Internal Audit team can use for annual testing.

steps.title: B. Controls that are fully embedded in day-to-day operations, owned by t…
steps.action: B. Controls that are fully embedded in day-to-day operations, owned by the business, automated where possible, and capable of continuous improvement — not just a document set.

steps.title: C. A set of automated SoD rules in SAP GRC Access Control that will cont…
steps.action: C. A set of automated SoD rules in SAP GRC Access Control that will continue to flag conflicts without any manual intervention.

steps.title: D. Integration of the controls workstream outputs into the programme's p…
steps.action: D. Integration of the controls workstream outputs into the programme's project management reporting for ongoing tracking.

steps.title: Q20. The Module B4 practitioner's frame is 'Value Protection, Not Compli…
steps.action: Q20. The Module B4 practitioner's frame is 'Value Protection, Not Compliance Overhead.' In a client conversation, a business process owner pushes back: 'This controls work is slowing down our design workshops and creating extra burden for the team.' How should the practitioner respond using this frame?

steps.title: A. Acknowledge the concern and offer to reduce the controls scope to min…
steps.action: A. Acknowledge the concern and offer to reduce the controls scope to minimise the burden on the design team.

steps.title: B. Explain that compliance is a regulatory requirement and the work cann…
steps.action: B. Explain that compliance is a regulatory requirement and the work cannot be reduced regardless of the burden it creates.

steps.title: C. Reframe: the controls activity during design workshops is protecting …
steps.action: C. Reframe: the controls activity during design workshops is protecting the team's investment — every issue identified now eliminates a more expensive problem post-live, including rework, audit findings, and potential financial loss.

steps.title: D. Escalate the pushback to the programme manager to resolve the schedul…
steps.action: D. Escalate the pushback to the programme manager to resolve the scheduling conflict before the next workshop.

steps.title: B5 — Engagement Types
steps.action: B5 — Engagement Types

steps.title: Q21. You have just joined a controls project. On day one, you are told: …
steps.action: Q21. You have just joined a controls project. On day one, you are told: 'We have identified significant deficiency findings from last year's external audit, and our next audit cycle begins in four months. We need you to overhaul the affected process areas, re-test the controls, and produce an audit-ready evidence package.' Which engagement type are you on?

steps.title: A. Assessment and Recommendation — reviewing the current controls enviro…
steps.action: A. Assessment and Recommendation — reviewing the current controls environment and providing gap findings.

steps.title: B. S/4HANA Transformation — embedded delivery across all four programme …
steps.action: B. S/4HANA Transformation — embedded delivery across all four programme phases.

steps.title: C. Remediation — time-sensitive engagement driven by external audit find…
steps.action: C. Remediation — time-sensitive engagement driven by external audit findings, with a hard deadline before the next audit cycle.

steps.title: D. Controls Testing — testing design effectiveness and operating effecti…
steps.action: D. Controls Testing — testing design effectiveness and operating effectiveness of an existing controls framework.

steps.title: Q22. In an S/4HANA Transformation engagement, the Risk and Controls Matr…
steps.action: Q22. In an S/4HANA Transformation engagement, the Risk and Controls Matrix (RCM) is described as a 'progressively refined' deliverable. What does this mean in practice?

steps.title: A. A new RCM is created from scratch at each phase of the programme, rep…
steps.action: A. A new RCM is created from scratch at each phase of the programme, replacing the previous version.

steps.title: B. The RCM starts as a preliminary draft at solution confirmation, is up…
steps.action: B. The RCM starts as a preliminary draft at solution confirmation, is updated and validated through design and build, and reaches its final tested state by go-live — reflecting increasing detail and certainty at each phase.

steps.title: C. The RCM is written once during the design and build phase and then di…
steps.action: C. The RCM is written once during the design and build phase and then distributed to all stakeholders for their approval.

steps.title: D. The RCM is progressively updated by the client's Internal Audit team,…
steps.action: D. The RCM is progressively updated by the client's Internal Audit team, with the controls workstream reviewing and approving each version.

steps.title: Q23. A controls practitioner on a large SAP programme notices that the s…
steps.action: Q23. A controls practitioner on a large SAP programme notices that the security team has designed several user roles that combine vendor master maintenance and payment run authorisation. The security lead says: 'This is a security design issue — the controls team can deal with it separately.' Is the security lead correct?

steps.title: A. Yes — security role design and controls risk management are independe…
steps.action: A. Yes — security role design and controls risk management are independent workstreams that should not interfere with each other.

steps.title: B. No — a role that creates a SoD conflict is simultaneously a security …
steps.action: B. No — a role that creates a SoD conflict is simultaneously a security design issue and a financial risk. The two workstreams must coordinate, not operate independently.

steps.title: C. Yes — the controls team should document the SoD conflict in the RCM a…
steps.action: C. Yes — the controls team should document the SoD conflict in the RCM as a finding, but the security team is solely responsible for the role design.

steps.title: D. No — the controls team should take over the security role design to r…
steps.action: D. No — the controls team should take over the security role design to resolve the conflict directly.

steps.title: Q24. During the testing phase of an S/4HANA programme, the controls team…
steps.action: Q24. During the testing phase of an S/4HANA programme, the controls team is asked to work with the programme's testing lead to identify which test scripts are relevant from a controls perspective. What is the purpose of this activity?

steps.title: A. To reduce the number of test scripts the testing team needs to execut…
steps.action: A. To reduce the number of test scripts the testing team needs to execute, thereby saving programme time.

steps.title: B. To ensure that the controls the team has identified are actually test…
steps.action: B. To ensure that the controls the team has identified are actually tested in the system — so that only the controls-relevant test scenarios are reviewed for DEF and OEF evidence.

steps.title: C. To replace the testing team's standard test script library with a con…
steps.action: C. To replace the testing team's standard test script library with a controls-specific test approach.

steps.title: D. To validate that the testing team has correctly understood the functi…
steps.action: D. To validate that the testing team has correctly understood the functional requirements documented in the KDDs.

steps.title: Q25. A senior manager describes your team's current engagement as: 'We a…
steps.action: Q25. A senior manager describes your team's current engagement as: 'We are advising the client on their current-state risk and controls environment, identifying gaps, and making recommendations — but we are not directly designing or testing any controls.' Which engagement type and degree-of-engagement position best describes this?

steps.title: A. S/4HANA Transformation engagement, at the design and build phase.
steps.action: A. S/4HANA Transformation engagement, at the design and build phase.

steps.title: B. Controls Testing engagement, at the operating effectiveness testing s…
steps.action: B. Controls Testing engagement, at the operating effectiveness testing stage.

steps.title: C. Assessment and Recommendation engagement, at the advisory (light-touc…
steps.action: C. Assessment and Recommendation engagement, at the advisory (light-touch) end of the degree-of-engagement spectrum.

steps.title: D. Remediation engagement, in the scoping and assessment phase before ov…
steps.action: D. Remediation engagement, in the scoping and assessment phase before overhaul begins.

steps.title: B6 — S/4HANA Lifecycle
steps.action: B6 — S/4HANA Lifecycle

steps.title: Q26. During Solution Confirmation, the controls lead identifies that the…
steps.action: Q26. During Solution Confirmation, the controls lead identifies that the client's current accounts payable process uses a paper approval form. The S/4HANA system implementer is still in early design discussions. What is the correct controls action?

steps.title: A. Document the manual control in the preliminary RACM and plan to test …
steps.action: A. Document the manual control in the preliminary RACM and plan to test it during the testing phase.

steps.title: B. Raise the opportunity to configure an automated approval workflow in …
steps.action: B. Raise the opportunity to configure an automated approval workflow in S/4HANA now — Solution Confirmation is the peak influence window for shaping future state design.

steps.title: C. Wait until Design and Build before making any design recommendations,…
steps.action: C. Wait until Design and Build before making any design recommendations, since Key Design Decisions have not yet been finalised.

steps.title: D. Escalate to the programme manager to determine whether the workflow s…
steps.action: D. Escalate to the programme manager to determine whether the workflow should be included in scope before raising it with the system implementer.

steps.title: Q27. A controls practitioner on a large S/4HANA programme receives a fun…
steps.action: Q27. A controls practitioner on a large S/4HANA programme receives a functional design document describing an interface that transfers purchase requisitions from an external procurement system into SAP. What is the risk-first reading approach for this FD?

steps.title: A. Read the full 21-page document to understand the complete business pu…
steps.action: A. Read the full 21-page document to understand the complete business purpose before identifying any risk implications.

steps.title: B. Skip the FD — interface controls are the system implementer's respons…
steps.action: B. Skip the FD — interface controls are the system implementer's responsibility, not the controls team's.

steps.title: C. First define the relevant risk (e.g. financial completeness of requis…
steps.action: C. First define the relevant risk (e.g. financial completeness of requisition data), then assess whether this interface affects that risk, then extract the error handling mechanism if relevant.

steps.title: D. Check whether the FD has been formally approved by the business proce…
steps.action: D. Check whether the FD has been formally approved by the business process owner before reading its contents.

steps.title: Q28. In the testing phase, a controls practitioner discovers that a test…
steps.action: Q28. In the testing phase, a controls practitioner discovers that a tester has executed a test case but provided only a screenshot of the initial transaction entry screen — without the system confirmation or blocking reason code that the controls team specified as required evidence. What should the practitioner do?

steps.title: A. Accept the evidence — the test was executed and the screenshot proves…
steps.action: A. Accept the evidence — the test was executed and the screenshot proves the tester performed the step.

steps.title: B. Raise a formal defect in the testing tool and escalate to the program…
steps.action: B. Raise a formal defect in the testing tool and escalate to the programme manager immediately.

steps.title: C. Go back to the tester (or the testing captain) and request the specif…
steps.action: C. Go back to the tester (or the testing captain) and request the specific evidence required — the system confirmation or blocking reason code — as agreed in the test plan.

steps.title: D. Re-execute the test case independently without involving the original…
steps.action: D. Re-execute the test case independently without involving the original tester.

steps.title: Q29. At the start of a large S/4HANA programme with approximately 300 co…
steps.action: Q29. At the start of a large S/4HANA programme with approximately 300 controls in scope, the controls team must decide which controls to scope for System Integration Testing (SIT) and which for User Acceptance Testing (UAT). Which scoping decision is correct?

steps.title: A. All 300 controls should be tested in UAT — business users need to con…
steps.action: A. All 300 controls should be tested in UAT — business users need to confirm that every control will work before go-live.

steps.title: B. Configuration controls (automated, no human intervention) → SIT. Work…
steps.action: B. Configuration controls (automated, no human intervention) → SIT. Workflow-driven and report-driven controls requiring human review → UAT.

steps.title: C. High-risk controls → SIT. Medium and low-risk controls → UAT, since U…
steps.action: C. High-risk controls → SIT. Medium and low-risk controls → UAT, since UAT is a less resource-intensive testing environment.

steps.title: D. Controls designed in-house by the controls team → SIT. Controls confi…
steps.action: D. Controls designed in-house by the controls team → SIT. Controls configured by the system implementer → UAT.

steps.title: Q30. At Cutover and Deploy, the controls lead confirms that all controls…
steps.action: Q30. At Cutover and Deploy, the controls lead confirms that all controls in the RACM have been designed, validated, and tested. The team has also prepared training materials for control owners. The programme is ready for the go-live readiness sign-off. Which additional step is required before the go-live date?

steps.title: A. No additional steps are required — design, validation, testing, and t…
steps.action: A. No additional steps are required — design, validation, testing, and training cover all the prerequisites for controls go-live readiness.

steps.title: B. The controls team must re-run the full SoD conflict analysis one fina…
steps.action: B. The controls team must re-run the full SoD conflict analysis one final time to confirm no new conflicts have been introduced during the final system configuration.

steps.title: C. The external auditor must confirm that the controls designed and test…
steps.action: C. The external auditor must confirm that the controls designed and tested are the controls they will rely on in the annual audit — this confirmation is the final gate before go-live.

steps.title: D. The RACM must be re-submitted to all business process owners for a fi…
steps.action: D. The RACM must be re-submitted to all business process owners for a final sign-off round to confirm they have received the training materials.

steps.title: B7 — Reading FD Documents
steps.action: B7 — Reading FD Documents

steps.title: Q31. A controls practitioner on a PetroNova S.A. engagement receives FD-…
steps.action: Q31. A controls practitioner on a PetroNova S.A. engagement receives FD-MM-INT-027 — a 21-page document describing an interface from VANTAGE ERP into SAP S/4HANA. What is the correct first action before opening the document?

steps.title: A. Read the full document from cover to cover before making any judgemen…
steps.action: A. Read the full document from cover to cover before making any judgement about relevance.

steps.title: B. Check whether the FD has been formally approved and signed off by the…
steps.action: B. Check whether the FD has been formally approved and signed off by the business process owner.

steps.title: C. Define the risk being controlled — financial, operational, or regulat…
steps.action: C. Define the risk being controlled — financial, operational, or regulatory — and assess whether this interface could affect that risk if it failed.

steps.title: D. Search the FD for the error handling section first, as that is where …
steps.action: D. Search the FD for the error handling section first, as that is where controls requirements are always found.

steps.title: Q32. Read the following excerpt from FD-MM-INT-027 Section 3.2: "This is…
steps.action: Q32. Read the following excerpt from FD-MM-INT-027 Section 3.2: "This is a unidirectional interface. Data flows from VANTAGE ERP to SAP S/4HANA only. There is no acknowledgement or return data flow from SAP to VANTAGE as part of this interface. Because VANTAGE does not receive confirmation from SAP, any transfer failures must be detected and resolved on the SAP side." What is the controls implication of this excerpt?

steps.title: A. The control must be designed in VANTAGE ERP, since that is where the …
steps.action: A. The control must be designed in VANTAGE ERP, since that is where the data originates.

steps.title: B. No monitoring control is needed — because there is no bidirectional d…
steps.action: B. No monitoring control is needed — because there is no bidirectional data flow, errors are self-correcting.

steps.title: C. Because VANTAGE receives no confirmation, all error detection and mon…
steps.action: C. Because VANTAGE receives no confirmation, all error detection and monitoring controls must be designed and placed at the SAP receiving system.

steps.title: D. A bidirectional interface should be recommended to the client so that…
steps.action: D. A bidirectional interface should be recommended to the client so that VANTAGE can confirm successful transfers.

steps.title: Q33. Read the following excerpt from FD-MM-INT-027 Section 3.3: "Normal …
steps.action: Q33. Read the following excerpt from FD-MM-INT-027 Section 3.3: "Normal Operations: Every 4 hours during business hours: 06:00, 10:00, 14:00, 18:00 WAT." A controls practitioner is designing the monitoring control for this interface. They propose a weekly report review — every Monday morning, the P2P manager reviews a summary of the previous week's interface activity. What is wrong with this design?

steps.title: A. Nothing is wrong — a weekly review is sufficient for a low-risk procu…
steps.action: A. Nothing is wrong — a weekly review is sufficient for a low-risk procurement interface.

steps.title: B. The monitoring frequency (weekly) does not match the interface freque…
steps.action: B. The monitoring frequency (weekly) does not match the interface frequency (every 4 hours). Up to 5 days of transfer failures could accumulate before detection.

steps.title: C. The review should be performed by IT Operations, not the P2P manager,…
steps.action: C. The review should be performed by IT Operations, not the P2P manager, since this is a technical interface.

steps.title: D. A weekly report is not an ITDM control — it must be replaced with an …
steps.action: D. A weekly report is not an ITDM control — it must be replaced with an automated configuration control.

steps.title: Q34. A controls practitioner reviews Section 5 of FD-MM-INT-027 and find…
steps.action: Q34. A controls practitioner reviews Section 5 of FD-MM-INT-027 and finds the following error handling specification: "Hard Errors: SAP logs the error to /PNS/INT_ERR with error code and timestamp. No automated notification is generated. The IT team checks the error log manually during their standard morning review." Is this a complete error handling specification for a 4-hour interface?

steps.title: A. Yes — the error is logged and reviewed by IT, which is sufficient for…
steps.action: A. Yes — the error is logged and reviewed by IT, which is sufficient for a detective ITDM control.

steps.title: B. No — while detection exists (error log), there is no automated alert …
steps.action: B. No — while detection exists (error log), there is no automated alert mechanism, no defined resolution SLA, and the manual morning review creates an exposure window of up to 20+ hours for late-day batch failures.

steps.title: C. Yes — an automated notification is not required as long as the error …
steps.action: C. Yes — an automated notification is not required as long as the error is logged in a system that is reviewed regularly.

steps.title: D. No — error handling for an interface control must always include a co…
steps.action: D. No — error handling for an interface control must always include a configuration testing step, which this specification does not mention.

steps.title: Q35. Using FD-MM-INT-027 as the source document, a controls practitioner…
steps.action: Q35. Using FD-MM-INT-027 as the source document, a controls practitioner has extracted the four parameters: Business Purpose (PR transfer), Direction (unidirectional, SAP-side detection), Frequency (4-hourly), Error Handling (Section 5 complete spec). What is the correct control classification for FIN-P2P-028?

steps.title: A. Preventive control · Configured automated — the system automatically …
steps.action: A. Preventive control · Configured automated — the system automatically blocks failed transfers before they affect the data.

steps.title: B. Detective control · IT-Dependent Manual (ITDM) — the system generates…
steps.action: B. Detective control · IT-Dependent Manual (ITDM) — the system generates the monitoring report (IT component) and the P2P Monitor reviews and signs off (human component).

steps.title: C. Preventive control · IT-Dependent Manual (ITDM) — the daily review pr…
steps.action: C. Preventive control · IT-Dependent Manual (ITDM) — the daily review prevents interface failures from occurring in the first place.

steps.title: D. Detective control · Manual — the P2P Monitor performs the review with…
steps.action: D. Detective control · Manual — the P2P Monitor performs the review without any system involvement.

steps.title: B8 — Testing Phase
steps.action: B8 — Testing Phase

steps.title: Q36. A controls practitioner is reviewing config evidence for the three-…
steps.action: Q36. A controls practitioner is reviewing config evidence for the three-way match control on a major energy sector engagement. The evidence package contains: (1) a screenshot of the SPRO navigation path to the tolerance key, and (2) a screenshot of the OMR6 tolerance screen for company code GC01 showing 3% quantity and price variance. Is this evidence package sufficient?

steps.title: A. Yes — the SPRO path and the tolerance value together constitute suffi…
steps.action: A. Yes — the SPRO path and the tolerance value together constitute sufficient evidence for a configuration test.

steps.title: B. No — the company code cross-check is missing. All company codes must …
steps.action: B. No — the company code cross-check is missing. All company codes must be reviewed, and any that deviate from the standard value must be investigated.

steps.title: C. No — a positive test scenario (invoice processed within tolerance) mu…
steps.action: C. No — a positive test scenario (invoice processed within tolerance) must also be included in the config evidence package.

steps.title: D. Yes — SPRO path and GC01 OMR6 settings are the required two component…
steps.action: D. Yes — SPRO path and GC01 OMR6 settings are the required two components. No further evidence is needed.

steps.title: Q37. A test plan for the payment run SoD control contains the following …
steps.action: Q37. A test plan for the payment run SoD control contains the following test cases: (1) Authorised user executes F110 payment run — payment completes successfully. A controls practitioner reviews the plan before testing starts. What feedback should they give?

steps.title: A. The test plan is complete — the authorised user test confirms the con…
steps.action: A. The test plan is complete — the authorised user test confirms the control is operating correctly.

steps.title: B. The test plan needs a negative scenario: an unauthorised user attempt…
steps.action: B. The test plan needs a negative scenario: an unauthorised user attempting to execute F110 should result in a system block. Without this, the test does not confirm the SoD restriction is functioning.

steps.title: C. The test plan should also include a report test — run the SoD conflic…
steps.action: C. The test plan should also include a report test — run the SoD conflict report and confirm it shows no conflicts for the authorised user.

steps.title: D. The test plan is sufficient if the authorised user successfully execu…
steps.action: D. The test plan is sufficient if the authorised user successfully executes the payment run and the system log captures the execution.

steps.title: Q38. A controls team is scoping a 280-control portfolio across SIT and U…
steps.action: Q38. A controls team is scoping a 280-control portfolio across SIT and UAT for a PetroNova S.A. S/4HANA transformation. The following controls are under discussion: (A) Workflow configuration for purchase order approval thresholds (B) Daily PR interface monitoring report review by the P2P Process Lead (C) MIRO duplicate invoice block (automated system check) (D) Monthly vendor master change report review signed off by Finance Manager Which controls should be scoped for UAT?

steps.title: A. A and C — these are the highest-risk controls and UAT provides the mo…
steps.action: A. A and C — these are the highest-risk controls and UAT provides the most rigorous testing environment.

steps.title: B. All four — UAT is the final testing cycle and all controls should be …
steps.action: B. All four — UAT is the final testing cycle and all controls should be validated with business users present.

steps.title: C. B and D — both require a human to generate a system report and take d…
steps.action: C. B and D — both require a human to generate a system report and take documented action, making UAT the appropriate testing environment.

steps.title: D. A and D — workflow controls always require business user testing in U…
steps.action: D. A and D — workflow controls always require business user testing in UAT to confirm the approval routing is correct.

steps.title: Q39. A controls team has just been told by the programme manager that te…
steps.action: Q39. A controls team has just been told by the programme manager that testing begins in two weeks. The controls team has not yet met the testing team, the test cases have not been reviewed, and evidence requirements have not been communicated. What is the most important immediate action?

steps.title: A. Begin executing controls tests independently, without waiting for the…
steps.action: A. Begin executing controls tests independently, without waiting for the programme testing team, to ensure the testing phase stays on schedule.

steps.title: B. Escalate to the programme sponsor — a two-week lead time is insuffici…
steps.action: B. Escalate to the programme sponsor — a two-week lead time is insufficient and testing should be delayed until the controls team is ready.

steps.title: C. Immediately identify the testing captain(s), review the programme tes…
steps.action: C. Immediately identify the testing captain(s), review the programme test cases, add controls requirements to the test scripts, and agree the evidence requirements before the first test is executed.

steps.title: D. Focus on completing the RACM updates first — the testing team cannot …
steps.action: D. Focus on completing the RACM updates first — the testing team cannot proceed until the RACM is fully finalised.

steps.title: B9 — AI in Controls
steps.action: B9 — AI in Controls

steps.title: Q40. A controls team is working on a large S/4HANA transformation progra…
steps.action: Q40. A controls team is working on a large S/4HANA transformation programme with approximately 400 functional design documents to review in the Design and Build phase.
