49 questions pooled from all 10 modules. A score of 60% or higher passes and marks this prerequisite complete. In the app, questions are presented in random order and the exam can be retaken at any time. The answer key with explanations follows this section.

B1 — Risk Types

Q1. A user in Accounts Payable has authorisation to create vendors using XK01 and also run the automated payment programme via F110. Which risk category does this conflict primarily represent?

A. Operational Risk — the Accounts Payable process is poorly designed.

B. Financial Risk — a Segregation of Duties conflict exists that enables payment fraud.

C. Compliance Risk — the organisation is in breach of GDPR requirements.

D. Change Risk — an unauthorised system configuration change was made.

Q2. An organisation's board states: "We will not tolerate any unmitigated High-risk SoD conflicts in our Financial Accounting module." This statement is best described as:

A. An inherent risk assessment.

B. A risk tolerance threshold.

C. A residual risk rating.

D. A control objective.

Q3. After controls are implemented and tested in a Procure-to-Pay process, the payment run still carries a Medium risk rating. This remaining exposure is referred to as:

A. Inherent risk.

B. Control risk.

C. Residual risk.

D. Detection risk.

Q4. The three-way match in Materials Management (ME21N → MIGO → MIRO) is configured with a tolerance of 95%, allowing invoices to post with up to a 5% discrepancy. A vendor consistently invoices 4.8% above the PO value. This scenario is primarily an example of:

A. Financial Risk — the vendor is committing invoice fraud.

B. Compliance Risk — the configuration violates GDPR Article 5.

C. Operational Risk — a configuration weakness allows material discrepancies to post undetected.

D. Change Risk — the tolerance was altered without approval.

Q5. In building a Risk and Controls Matrix (RCM), a practitioner classifies a risk as Compliance Risk rather than Financial Risk. What is the most significant practical consequence of this classification decision?

A. The risk will be assigned a lower inherent risk rating automatically.

B. The test procedure will be designed to test against a specific regulatory standard rather than substantive financial transactions.

C. The risk will only be relevant in US-listed companies subject to SOX.

D. The control will always be a preventive automated control rather than a detective manual control.

B2 — Control Types

Q6. During a Procure-to-Pay process review, you discover that the SAP system automatically blocks vendor invoices where the amount exceeds the purchase order value by more than 3% — without any manual review required. This control is best classified as:

A. A detective control — it reviews invoices after they are posted to the ledger.

B. A preventive control — the system blocks the erroneous posting before it completes.

C. An ITDM control — a human must review the exception list and approve or reject.

D. A corrective control — it reverses postings that were made in error.

Q7. Your client has a control where a manager receives a weekly SAP-generated report of all vendor master changes made in the prior week, reviews the list for unusual entries, and signs off that all changes were appropriately authorised. Which control classification is most accurate?

A. Preventive — the manager reviews changes before they are applied to the vendor master.

B. Detective ITDM — the system generates the data, and a human reviews and takes action.

C. Configured automated — SAP automatically validates vendor master changes against a ruleset.

D. Inherent automated — the control is active by default as part of standard SAP functionality.

Q8. Ronnie's field insight distinguishes between a 'configured' automated control and an 'inherent' automated control. What is the primary audit testing implication of this distinction?

A. Configured controls are always more reliable than inherent controls and should receive a higher reliance rating.

B. Inherent controls require a full configuration review, while configured controls only need a "not disabled" check.

C. Configured controls require a configuration review to verify parameters are appropriate; inherent controls require confirming the functionality has not been switched off.

D. There is no audit testing difference — both types are classified as automated and receive identical test procedures.

Q9. An internal audit team is assessing a quarterly User Access Review process. The UAR was performed, but there is no documented evidence that the business process owner took any action on the three flagged exceptions. Which statement best describes the audit conclusion?

A. The control is effective — the review was completed and exceptions were identified.

B. The control is ineffective — for an ITDM, both the system output and the human review with documented action must be evidenced. The action element is missing.

C. The control is partially effective — the system component (generating the UAR report) was effective, which is the primary element for reliance purposes.

D. The control cannot be assessed — more information about the exceptions is required before a conclusion can be drawn.

Q10. During an S/4HANA implementation engagement, a client's current-state process uses a paper form that a warehouse manager manually signs to approve each goods receipt. Applying the control nature hierarchy, what is your first design recommendation?

A. Retain the manual paper-based control — it provides an independent physical audit trail.

B. Convert to an ITDM — generate a weekly SAP goods receipt report for the manager to review and sign off.

C. Configure an automated system control — set up SAP to enforce goods receipt validation rules automatically, eliminating the need for manual approval in standard transactions.

D. Implement a detective control — run a monthly reconciliation of goods received against purchase orders.

B3 — Control Nature

Q11. An SAP auditor is testing the three-way match control in a client's Procure-to-Pay process. The control is documented as: "System automatically blocks MIRO invoice postings where the variance between PO, GR, and invoice exceeds the configured OMR6 tolerance." Which test procedure is complete and sufficient for this control?

A. Confirm that the three-way match is active in the system and has not been disabled.

B. Select a sample of 25 MIRO postings and confirm none were manually overridden in the period.

C. Inspect OMR6 tolerance key settings to confirm the tolerance is ≤3%; verify no vendor-specific overrides exist; sample 25 MIRO postings to confirm the system blocked invoices where variance exceeded tolerance.

D. Review the MIRO posting log for the period and confirm the total number of blocked invoices matches management's expectation.

Q12. A controls review identifies the following: an AP manager generates a monthly SAP report of all new vendor master records created in the period, reviews the report against the approved vendor creation form, and signs the report as reviewed. During testing, the auditor finds three new vendors flagged as unusual — but finds no follow-up documentation for any of them. What is the correct audit conclusion?

A. The control is effective — the review was completed and the signed report evidences performance.

B. The control is ineffective — for an ITDM, a signed report without documented exception follow-up evidences that a review occurred but not that it was effective.

C. The control is partially effective — the system component (generating the report) is working correctly, which is sufficient for a medium-reliance ITDM.

D. The control cannot be assessed until the auditor interviews the AP manager about the three exceptions.

Q13. Ronnie's insight from Module B2 distinguishes between a configured automated control and an inherent automated control. In Module B3 we apply this to testing. What is the specific audit test step required for an INHERENT automated control that is NOT required for a configured automated control?

A. Inspect the system configuration to verify the control parameters are set to an appropriate threshold.

B. Sample a population of transactions to confirm the system enforced the control during the test period.

C. Confirm that the standard SAP functionality has not been switched off or overridden in system settings.

D. Obtain management's sign-off on the control design documentation for the period under review.

Q14. During an S/4HANA implementation engagement, you identify that a client's current goods receipt approval process uses a paper form that the warehouse manager physically signs. Applying the control nature hierarchy and the uplift imperative, what is the correct recommendation sequence?

A. Retain the manual control and supplement it with a weekly SAP goods receipt report review (adding an ITDM layer).

B. First recommend configuring an automated goods receipt tolerance rule in SAP; if that is not feasible, recommend converting the manual process to an ITDM; retain manual only if neither option is feasible.

C. Replace the manual control immediately with an ITDM regardless of feasibility, since ITDMs are always preferable to manual controls.

D. Retain the manual control — paper-based approval forms provide an independent physical audit trail that is more reliable than system-generated records.

Q15. A practitioner is classifying the following control for an RCM: "At the end of each month, the Financial Controller reviews a system-generated SAP report of journal entries posted outside the standard approval workflow and signs off that all entries were appropriately authorised. Any exceptions are emailed to Internal Audit." What is the correct control type AND control nature classification?

A. Preventive control · Configured automated — the system generates the exception list automatically.

B. Detective control · ITDM — the system generates the data and a human reviews and acts on it.

C. Detective control · Manual — the Financial Controller performs the review without any system involvement.

D. Preventive control · ITDM — the review prevents future authorisation failures by identifying the issue.

B4 — Why Controls Matter

Q16. A programme sponsor asks you: 'Why should we spend budget on a controls workstream during implementation rather than fixing any issues after go-live?' Which answer best represents the business case from Module B4?

A. Post-live remediation is technically complex and requires specialist SAP skills that are expensive to source on short notice.

B. Prevention during implementation costs a fraction of remediation post-live — every control gap fixed before go-live avoids rework, audit findings, and business disruption at the most vulnerable moment.

C. Regulatory requirements mandate that controls must be in place before an SAP go-live; there is no legal option to fix them afterwards.

D. Controls cannot be retrofitted into SAP after go-live due to technical constraints in the S/4HANA architecture.

Q17. The source session describes 'lift-and-shift' as a mindset the controls workstream must challenge. What does lift-and-shift mean in the context of an S/4HANA transformation, and why is it a problem?

A. Physically moving on-premise SAP hardware to a cloud environment — a problem because cloud controls differ from on-premise controls.

B. Migrating data from the legacy system to S/4HANA without data cleansing — a problem because dirty data undermines control effectiveness.

C. Carrying the old process design directly into the new system without redesign — a problem because it misses the opportunity to build compliance and automation into the future state.

D. Transferring documentation from the old system to the new one without updating it — a problem because outdated documentation creates audit risk.

Q18. A client CFO asks: 'How will the controls workstream affect our external audit cost next year?' Which response from Module B4 is most accurate?

A. Controls work happens inside the programme — external auditors conduct their own independent testing and the two processes do not interact.

B. Controls are the inputs for the external audit. Controls designed, documented, and tested from go-live attract higher auditor reliance, require smaller sample sizes, and reduce annual external audit fees.

C. The controls workstream cannot guarantee any reduction in external audit cost — that depends on the auditor's methodology, not the controls framework.

D. External audit cost is driven by the number of entities in scope, not by control quality, so controls work has no direct impact on audit fees.

Q19. Value Driver 4 — Integration and Efficiency — describes what a controls workstream should leave behind when the engagement closes. Which outcome best represents this value driver?

A. A comprehensive controls documentation library that the client's Internal Audit team can use for annual testing.

B. Controls that are fully embedded in day-to-day operations, owned by the business, automated where possible, and capable of continuous improvement — not just a document set.

C. A set of automated SoD rules in SAP GRC Access Control that will continue to flag conflicts without any manual intervention.

D. Integration of the controls workstream outputs into the programme's project management reporting for ongoing tracking.

Q20. The Module B4 practitioner's frame is 'Value Protection, Not Compliance Overhead.' In a client conversation, a business process owner pushes back: 'This controls work is slowing down our design workshops and creating extra burden for the team.' How should the practitioner respond using this frame?

A. Acknowledge the concern and offer to reduce the controls scope to minimise the burden on the design team.

B. Explain that compliance is a regulatory requirement and the work cannot be reduced regardless of the burden it creates.

C. Reframe: the controls activity during design workshops is protecting the team's investment — every issue identified now eliminates a more expensive problem post-live, including rework, audit findings, and potential financial loss.

D. Escalate the pushback to the programme manager to resolve the scheduling conflict before the next workshop.

B5 — Engagement Types

Q21. You have just joined a controls project. On day one, you are told: 'We have identified significant deficiency findings from last year's external audit, and our next audit cycle begins in four months. We need you to overhaul the affected process areas, re-test the controls, and produce an audit-ready evidence package.' Which engagement type are you on?

A. Assessment and Recommendation — reviewing the current controls environment and providing gap findings.

B. S/4HANA Transformation — embedded delivery across all four programme phases.

C. Remediation — time-sensitive engagement driven by external audit findings, with a hard deadline before the next audit cycle.

D. Controls Testing — testing design effectiveness and operating effectiveness of an existing controls framework.

Q22. In an S/4HANA Transformation engagement, the Risk and Controls Matrix (RCM) is described as a 'progressively refined' deliverable. What does this mean in practice?

A. A new RCM is created from scratch at each phase of the programme, replacing the previous version.

B. The RCM starts as a preliminary draft at solution confirmation, is updated and validated through design and build, and reaches its final tested state by go-live — reflecting increasing detail and certainty at each phase.

C. The RCM is written once during the design and build phase and then distributed to all stakeholders for their approval.

D. The RCM is progressively updated by the client's Internal Audit team, with the controls workstream reviewing and approving each version.

Q23. A controls practitioner on a large SAP programme notices that the security team has designed several user roles that combine vendor master maintenance and payment run authorisation. The security lead says: 'This is a security design issue — the controls team can deal with it separately.' Is the security lead correct?

A. Yes — security role design and controls risk management are independent workstreams that should not interfere with each other.

B. No — a role that creates a SoD conflict is simultaneously a security design issue and a financial risk. The two workstreams must coordinate, not operate independently.

C. Yes — the controls team should document the SoD conflict in the RCM as a finding, but the security team is solely responsible for the role design.

D. No — the controls team should take over the security role design to resolve the conflict directly.

Q24. During the testing phase of an S/4HANA programme, the controls team is asked to work with the programme's testing lead to identify which test scripts are relevant from a controls perspective. What is the purpose of this activity?

A. To reduce the number of test scripts the testing team needs to execute, thereby saving programme time.

B. To ensure that the controls the team has identified are actually tested in the system — so that only the controls-relevant test scenarios are reviewed for DEF and OEF evidence.

C. To replace the testing team's standard test script library with a controls-specific test approach.

D. To validate that the testing team has correctly understood the functional requirements documented in the KDDs.

Q25. A senior manager describes your team's current engagement as: 'We are advising the client on their current-state risk and controls environment, identifying gaps, and making recommendations — but we are not directly designing or testing any controls.' Which engagement type and degree-of-engagement position best describes this?

A. S/4HANA Transformation engagement, at the design and build phase.

B. Controls Testing engagement, at the operating effectiveness testing stage.

C. Assessment and Recommendation engagement, at the advisory (light-touch) end of the degree-of-engagement spectrum.

D. Remediation engagement, in the scoping and assessment phase before overhaul begins.

B6 — S/4HANA Lifecycle

Q26. During Solution Confirmation, the controls lead identifies that the client's current accounts payable process uses a paper approval form. The S/4HANA system implementer is still in early design discussions. What is the correct controls action?

A. Document the manual control in the preliminary RACM and plan to test it during the testing phase.

B. Raise the opportunity to configure an automated approval workflow in S/4HANA now — Solution Confirmation is the peak influence window for shaping future state design.

C. Wait until Design and Build before making any design recommendations, since Key Design Decisions have not yet been finalised.

D. Escalate to the programme manager to determine whether the workflow should be included in scope before raising it with the system implementer.

Q27. A controls practitioner on a large S/4HANA programme receives a functional design document describing an interface that transfers purchase requisitions from an external procurement system into SAP. What is the risk-first reading approach for this FD?

A. Read the full 21-page document to understand the complete business purpose before identifying any risk implications.

B. Skip the FD — interface controls are the system implementer's responsibility, not the controls team's.

C. First define the relevant risk (e.g. financial completeness of requisition data), then assess whether this interface affects that risk, then extract the error handling mechanism if relevant.

D. Check whether the FD has been formally approved by the business process owner before reading its contents.

Q28. In the testing phase, a controls practitioner discovers that a tester has executed a test case but provided only a screenshot of the initial transaction entry screen — without the system confirmation or blocking reason code that the controls team specified as required evidence. What should the practitioner do?

A. Accept the evidence — the test was executed and the screenshot proves the tester performed the step.

B. Raise a formal defect in the testing tool and escalate to the programme manager immediately.

C. Go back to the tester (or the testing captain) and request the specific evidence required — the system confirmation or blocking reason code — as agreed in the test plan.

D. Re-execute the test case independently without involving the original tester.

Q29. At the start of a large S/4HANA programme with approximately 300 controls in scope, the controls team must decide which controls to scope for System Integration Testing (SIT) and which for User Acceptance Testing (UAT). Which scoping decision is correct?

A. All 300 controls should be tested in UAT — business users need to confirm that every control will work before go-live.

B. Configuration controls (automated, no human intervention) → SIT. Workflow-driven and report-driven controls requiring human review → UAT.

C. High-risk controls → SIT. Medium and low-risk controls → UAT, since UAT is a less resource-intensive testing environment.

D. Controls designed in-house by the controls team → SIT. Controls configured by the system implementer → UAT.

Q30. At Cutover and Deploy, the controls lead confirms that all controls in the RACM have been designed, validated, and tested. The team has also prepared training materials for control owners. The programme is ready for the go-live readiness sign-off. Which additional step is required before the go-live date?

A. No additional steps are required — design, validation, testing, and training cover all the prerequisites for controls go-live readiness.

B. The controls team must re-run the full SoD conflict analysis one final time to confirm no new conflicts have been introduced during the final system configuration.

C. The external auditor must confirm that the controls designed and tested are the controls they will rely on in the annual audit — this confirmation is the final gate before go-live.

D. The RACM must be re-submitted to all business process owners for a final sign-off round to confirm they have received the training materials.

B7 — Reading FD Documents

Q31. A controls practitioner on a PetroNova S.A. engagement receives FD-MM-INT-027 — a 21-page document describing an interface from VANTAGE ERP into SAP S/4HANA. What is the correct first action before opening the document?

A. Read the full document from cover to cover before making any judgement about relevance.

B. Check whether the FD has been formally approved and signed off by the business process owner.

C. Define the risk being controlled — financial, operational, or regulatory — and assess whether this interface could affect that risk if it failed.

D. Search the FD for the error handling section first, as that is where controls requirements are always found.

Q32. Read the following excerpt from FD-MM-INT-027 Section 3.2: "This is a unidirectional interface. Data flows from VANTAGE ERP to SAP S/4HANA only. There is no acknowledgement or return data flow from SAP to VANTAGE as part of this interface. Because VANTAGE does not receive confirmation from SAP, any transfer failures must be detected and resolved on the SAP side." What is the controls implication of this excerpt?

A. The control must be designed in VANTAGE ERP, since that is where the data originates.

B. No monitoring control is needed — because there is no bidirectional data flow, errors are self-correcting.

C. Because VANTAGE receives no confirmation, all error detection and monitoring controls must be designed and placed at the SAP receiving system.

D. A bidirectional interface should be recommended to the client so that VANTAGE can confirm successful transfers.

Q33. Read the following excerpt from FD-MM-INT-027 Section 3.3: "Normal Operations: Every 4 hours during business hours: 06:00, 10:00, 14:00, 18:00 WAT." A controls practitioner is designing the monitoring control for this interface. They propose a weekly report review — every Monday morning, the P2P manager reviews a summary of the previous week's interface activity. What is wrong with this design?

A. Nothing is wrong — a weekly review is sufficient for a low-risk procurement interface.

B. The monitoring frequency (weekly) does not match the interface frequency (every 4 hours). Up to 5 days of transfer failures could accumulate before detection.

C. The review should be performed by IT Operations, not the P2P manager, since this is a technical interface.

D. A weekly report is not an ITDM control — it must be replaced with an automated configuration control.

Q34. A controls practitioner reviews Section 5 of FD-MM-INT-027 and finds the following error handling specification: "Hard Errors: SAP logs the error to /PNS/INT_ERR with error code and timestamp. No automated notification is generated. The IT team checks the error log manually during their standard morning review." Is this a complete error handling specification for a 4-hour interface?

A. Yes — the error is logged and reviewed by IT, which is sufficient for a detective ITDM control.

B. No — while detection exists (error log), there is no automated alert mechanism, no defined resolution SLA, and the manual morning review creates an exposure window of up to 20+ hours for late-day batch failures.

C. Yes — an automated notification is not required as long as the error is logged in a system that is reviewed regularly.

D. No — error handling for an interface control must always include a configuration testing step, which this specification does not mention.

Q35. Using FD-MM-INT-027 as the source document, a controls practitioner has extracted the four parameters: Business Purpose (PR transfer), Direction (unidirectional, SAP-side detection), Frequency (4-hourly), Error Handling (Section 5 complete spec). What is the correct control classification for FIN-P2P-028?

A. Preventive control · Configured automated — the system automatically blocks failed transfers before they affect the data.

B. Detective control · IT-Dependent Manual (ITDM) — the system generates the monitoring report (IT component) and the P2P Monitor reviews and signs off (human component).

C. Preventive control · IT-Dependent Manual (ITDM) — the daily review prevents interface failures from occurring in the first place.

D. Detective control · Manual — the P2P Monitor performs the review without any system involvement.

B8 — Testing Phase

Q36. A controls practitioner is reviewing config evidence for the three-way match control on a major energy sector engagement. The evidence package contains: (1) a screenshot of the SPRO navigation path to the tolerance key, and (2) a screenshot of the OMR6 tolerance screen for company code GC01 showing 3% quantity and price variance. Is this evidence package sufficient?

A. Yes — the SPRO path and the tolerance value together constitute sufficient evidence for a configuration test.

B. No — the company code cross-check is missing. All company codes must be reviewed, and any that deviate from the standard value must be investigated.

C. No — a positive test scenario (invoice processed within tolerance) must also be included in the config evidence package.

D. Yes — SPRO path and GC01 OMR6 settings are the required two components. No further evidence is needed.

Q37. A test plan for the payment run SoD control contains the following test cases: (1) Authorised user executes F110 payment run — payment completes successfully. A controls practitioner reviews the plan before testing starts. What feedback should they give?

A. The test plan is complete — the authorised user test confirms the control is operating correctly.

B. The test plan needs a negative scenario: an unauthorised user attempting to execute F110 should result in a system block. Without this, the test does not confirm the SoD restriction is functioning.

C. The test plan should also include a report test — run the SoD conflict report and confirm it shows no conflicts for the authorised user.

D. The test plan is sufficient if the authorised user successfully executes the payment run and the system log captures the execution.

Q38. A controls team is scoping a 280-control portfolio across SIT and UAT for a PetroNova S.A. S/4HANA transformation. The following controls are under discussion: (A) Workflow configuration for purchase order approval thresholds (B) Daily PR interface monitoring report review by the P2P Process Lead (C) MIRO duplicate invoice block (automated system check) (D) Monthly vendor master change report review signed off by Finance Manager Which controls should be scoped for UAT?

A. A and C — these are the highest-risk controls and UAT provides the most rigorous testing environment.

B. All four — UAT is the final testing cycle and all controls should be validated with business users present.

C. B and D — both require a human to generate a system report and take documented action, making UAT the appropriate testing environment.

D. A and D — workflow controls always require business user testing in UAT to confirm the approval routing is correct.

Q39. A controls team has just been told by the programme manager that testing begins in two weeks. The controls team has not yet met the testing team, the test cases have not been reviewed, and evidence requirements have not been communicated. What is the most important immediate action?

A. Begin executing controls tests independently, without waiting for the programme testing team, to ensure the testing phase stays on schedule.

B. Escalate to the programme sponsor — a two-week lead time is insufficient and testing should be delayed until the controls team is ready.

C. Immediately identify the testing captain(s), review the programme test cases, add controls requirements to the test scripts, and agree the evidence requirements before the first test is executed.

D. Focus on completing the RACM updates first — the testing team cannot proceed until the RACM is fully finalised.

B9 — AI in Controls

Q40. A controls team is working on a large S/4HANA transformation programme with approximately 400 functional design documents to review in the Design and Build phase. They have access to an AI agent that can ingest FDs and propose preliminary RACM entries. What is the correct way to describe the agent's role in this workflow?

A. The agent completes the RACM entries, freeing the controls team to focus on stakeholder management and report writing.

B. The agent proposes draft RACM entries — including control description, type, and nature — which the controls team then reviews, challenges, and refines before the RACM is finalised.

C. The agent should only be used for low-risk controls, with high-risk controls reserved for manual RACM drafting by the practitioner.

D. The agent replaces the need for FD review since it extracts all relevant control parameters automatically.

Q41. Which of the following assessment tasks can an AI agent reliably perform in the controls testing phase?

A. Determine whether the evidence provided for FIN-P2P-028 is sufficient for this specific client's external audit requirements.

B. Assess whether the P2P Process Lead's sign-off on a monitoring report represents a genuine review or a perfunctory signature.

C. Cross-reference the RACM against the programme test case library and flag controls with no corresponding test coverage.

D. Evaluate whether a company code's 10% tolerance exception is credible given the client's stated policy rationale.

Q42. A practitioner says: "I've been using an AI agent for gap analysis in Solution Confirmation and it's been great — I've cut my analysis time in half. I now just accept whatever the agent produces." What is the problem with this approach?

A. Gap analysis in SolCon should always be done manually — AI agents are not reliable enough for early-phase work.

B. Passive acceptance of agent outputs removes the practitioner's challenge and scepticism, which means the agent's errors, missed context, and incorrect assumptions will pass into the work product unchecked.

C. The efficiency gain from AI-assisted gap analysis is not recognised by external auditors and should not be used on client-facing engagements.

D. The practitioner should be using the agent for control proposal in Design and Build instead, where it adds more value than in SolCon.

Q43. Under the "augment not replace" frame, which of the following correctly describes what changes in the practitioner's role when AI agents are integrated into the controls workstream?

A. The practitioner's accountability for the work product is shared with the AI agent that produced the initial draft.

B. Information processing decreases in the practitioner's workload; judgement, relationship work, and accountability remain the same or increase.

C. The practitioner becomes primarily responsible for configuring and managing the AI agent rather than performing controls work directly.

D. The practitioner's role is fully preserved — nothing changes about how controls work is performed.

Q44. A controls lead is reviewing an AI agent's output from a current-state to future-state gap analysis. The agent has flagged 12 controls from the current-state framework as having no future-state equivalent. The controls lead reviews the list and notices that 3 of the flagged controls relate to a legacy VANTAGE ERP interface that IS being replaced by a new SAP-native interface with its own control designed earlier in the programme. What does this situation illustrate?

A. The AI agent made a systematic error and its gap analysis output cannot be trusted for this engagement.

B. The controls lead should re-run the gap analysis with better input documents before proceeding.

C. Gap analysis outputs require practitioner review with programme context — the agent identified a gap based on the artefacts it saw, but the practitioner recognises the replacement control exists elsewhere in the programme.

D. The 3 flagged controls should be added to the RACM as gaps since the agent's output takes precedence over the practitioner's recollection.

B10 — Practitioner Capstone

Q45. A controls practitioner is preparing for their first working session with the Order-to-Cash business process team on a new S/4HANA engagement. Before the session, they heard that the team has been struggling with their manual credit limit approval process — it is slow and inconsistently applied. How should the practitioner open the session?

A. Open by presenting the full RACM methodology and explaining how controls will be designed for the O2C process.

B. Lead with the credit limit approval pain point — "I understand you have been having challenges with how credit approvals are processed. Let us start there."

C. Begin by asking the team to walk through their current-state process in full before discussing any controls requirements.

D. Open by explaining the difference between key and non-key controls, since the credit limit approval will need to be classified.

Q46. A controls practitioner has been working on two business process streams simultaneously — P2P and Record-to-Report. In the P2P stream, they agreed that controls evidence would be submitted weekly. In the RTR stream, under time pressure, they agreed to ad hoc submissions. The RTR team has now mentioned that "P2P gets a different standard" and is pushing back on the evidence approach. What does this situation illustrate?

A. Different process streams legitimately require different evidence approaches — the RTR team's pushback is unreasonable.

B. The controls team should have established a consistent evidence approach across both streams before beginning — inconsistency creates noise and unnecessary friction.

C. The RTR team should be managed through the programme manager rather than directly by the controls practitioner.

D. The P2P team's weekly submission standard is the right approach and RTR should be brought into line.

Q47. A controls practitioner is preparing for a cutover review meeting. The go-live is in two weeks. The RACM is finalised, testing is complete, and defects have been resolved. The external auditor has confirmed the control design. What is the most important remaining action before go-live?

A. Run a final pass through the RACM to check for any redundant controls that could be rationalised before go-live.

B. Ensure that the control owners — particularly those responsible for ITDM and manual controls — have been trained on what to do, how often, what evidence to produce, and how to escalate exceptions.

C. Prepare a written summary of the testing results for the programme sponsor before any go-live activities proceed.

D. Schedule a post-go-live review session with the external auditor to confirm that controls are operating as designed.

Q48. A controls practitioner has completed a successful S/4HANA engagement. The RACM is approved, go-live has happened, and the engagement is formally closed. The client's Finance Director mentions that they are struggling with inconsistent control execution six months after go-live — some control owners are performing the reviews, others are not. What is the practitioner's appropriate response?

A. The engagement is complete — post-go-live operational issues are outside the original scope and should be handled by the client's internal team.

B. Engage with the Finance Director to understand the gap, identify what support the controls workstream could provide post-go-live, and position the team as a resource for ongoing improvement.

C. Recommend that the client hire a full-time internal controls manager to address the execution consistency issue.

D. Send the Finance Director a copy of the RACM with a reminder of the control owner responsibilities that were agreed at go-live.

Q49. A controls practitioner receives an incomplete artefact package from the programme team. They have functional design documents for the financial accounting processes but no business process diagrams or end-to-end process flows. What is the correct approach?

A. Request the missing business process diagrams from the programme team and pause RACM development until the complete artefact package is available.

B. Work with the FDs available to develop a preliminary view of the end-to-end, identify the specific gaps in the artefact picture, and pursue those gaps actively while continuing to make progress.

C. Proceed entirely from the FDs and note in the RACM that the risk universe may be incomplete due to missing artefacts.

D. Escalate the incomplete documentation to the programme manager as a risk to the controls workstream delivery timeline.

steps.title: Financial Risk — a Segregation of Duties conflict exists that enables pa…
steps.action: Financial Risk — a Segregation of Duties conflict exists that enables payment fraud.

steps.title: Correct. When a single user can both create the payee (XK01) and authori…
steps.action: Correct. When a single user can both create the payee (XK01) and authorise the payment (F110), no independent check exists — cash can be directed to a fictitious vendor with no oversight. This is a classic Segregation of Duties conflict classified as Financial Risk. It is detected via GRC Access Control Ruleset analysis and is a common driver of SOX 404 material weakness findings.

steps.title: Q2. Answer: B (B1)
steps.action: Q2. Answer: B (B1)

steps.title: A risk tolerance threshold.
steps.action: A risk tolerance threshold.

steps.title: Correct. Risk tolerance is the operational band that translates board-le…
steps.action: Correct. Risk tolerance is the operational band that translates board-level risk appetite into a measurable, enforceable threshold. "Zero unmitigated High-risk SoD conflicts in FA" is a tolerance limit — a specific, testable condition. Risk appetite is the higher-level statement of willingness to accept risk; controls are the mechanisms to stay within tolerance.

steps.title: Q3. Answer: C (B1)
steps.action: Q3. Answer: C (B1)

steps.title: Residual risk.
steps.action: Residual risk.

steps.title: Correct. Residual risk is what remains after controls are designed, impl…
steps.action: Correct. Residual risk is what remains after controls are designed, implemented, and operating effectively. Inherent risk is the starting position — before any controls. Control risk and detection risk are terms from the Audit Risk Model (ISA 315), which is a different framework used in financial statement auditing, not in the risk classification context covered here.

steps.title: Q4. Answer: C (B1)
steps.action: Q4. Answer: C (B1)

steps.title: Operational Risk — a configuration weakness allows material discrepancie…
steps.action: Operational Risk — a configuration weakness allows material discrepancies to post undetected.

steps.title: Correct. This is Operational Risk: a process configuration weakness (tol…
steps.action: Correct. This is Operational Risk: a process configuration weakness (tolerance too wide in OMR6) that allows invoices with material discrepancies to post automatically, with no manual review triggered. It is not necessarily fraud — the question does not state the vendor is acting dishonestly. The risk is in the process design, not the vendor's intent. Operational risk is characterised by process weaknesses that impair accurate, efficient operations.

steps.title: Q5. Answer: B (B1)
steps.action: Q5. Answer: B (B1)

steps.title: The test procedure will be designed to test against a specific regulator…
steps.action: The test procedure will be designed to test against a specific regulatory standard rather than substantive financial transactions.

steps.title: Correct. Risk classification in the RCM directly determines the test app…
steps.action: Correct. Risk classification in the RCM directly determines the test approach. Financial Risk → substantive procedures (transaction testing, balance validation). Compliance Risk → regulatory standard test (test against the specific SOX, GDPR, or FDA requirement). The classification does not automatically determine the inherent rating, the geographic scope, or the control type — those are separate decisions. But it does anchor the entire test design.

steps.title: Q6. Answer: B (B2)
steps.action: Q6. Answer: B (B2)

steps.title: A preventive control — the system blocks the erroneous posting before it…
steps.action: A preventive control — the system blocks the erroneous posting before it completes.

steps.title: Correct. The three-way match tolerance configured in OMR6 is a preventiv…
steps.action: Correct. The three-way match tolerance configured in OMR6 is a preventive control — it stops the erroneous or potentially fraudulent invoice posting from completing without any human action. The system enforces the rule on every transaction. A detective control would identify the discrepancy after the fact; an ITDM would require a human to review a system-generated exception report. This is automated and upstream — the definition of preventive.

steps.title: Q7. Answer: B (B2)
steps.action: Q7. Answer: B (B2)

steps.title: Detective ITDM — the system generates the data, and a human reviews and …
steps.action: Detective ITDM — the system generates the data, and a human reviews and takes action.

steps.title: Correct. This is a Detective ITDM control. It is detective because the v…
steps.action: Correct. This is a Detective ITDM control. It is detective because the vendor master changes have already been made. It is ITDM because it has two components: the system generates the report (IT component) and a human reviews it and takes action (manual component). To test this control, auditors must verify both: that the report is complete and accurate, and that the manager's review is evidenced with exceptions acted upon.

steps.title: Q8. Answer: C (B2)
steps.action: Q8. Answer: C (B2)

steps.title: Configured controls require a configuration review to verify parameters …
steps.action: Configured controls require a configuration review to verify parameters are appropriate; inherent controls require confirming the functionality has not been switched off.

steps.title: Correct. A configured control — like the OMR6 three-way match tolerance …
steps.action: Correct. A configured control — like the OMR6 three-way match tolerance — requires an auditor to inspect the configuration and verify the tolerance parameters are set appropriately. An inherent control — like MIRO's duplicate invoice check — does not need configuration verification, but the auditor must confirm it has not been switched off or overridden. Both types require a specific, different testing step — missing either one results in incomplete audit evidence.

steps.title: Q9. Answer: B (B2)
steps.action: Q9. Answer: B (B2)

steps.title: The control is ineffective — for an ITDM, both the system output and the…
steps.action: The control is ineffective — for an ITDM, both the system output and the human review with documented action must be evidenced. The action element is missing.

steps.title: Correct. The UAR is an ITDM detective control. For an ITDM to be effecti…
steps.action: Correct. The UAR is an ITDM detective control. For an ITDM to be effective, both elements must be evidenced: (1) the system-generated report is complete and accurate, AND (2) a competent person reviewed it and documented their action on exceptions. The absence of documented follow-up means the human component is not evidenced. The control is therefore ineffective for the period — regardless of whether the system output was accurate. This is one of the most common deficiencies found in UAR testing during SOX engagements.

steps.title: Q10. Answer: C (B2)
steps.action: Q10. Answer: C (B2)

steps.title: Configure an automated system control — set up SAP to enforce goods rece…
steps.action: Configure an automated system control — set up SAP to enforce goods receipt validation rules automatically, eliminating the need for manual approval in standard transactions.

steps.title: Correct. The control nature hierarchy places configured/automated contro…
steps.action: Correct. The control nature hierarchy places configured/automated controls at the top — highest reliability, most consistent, least costly to test and maintain. The first design recommendation should always be to automate the control where the system allows it. A manual paper form is the lowest-reliability option and should only be retained when automation is genuinely not feasible. Moving to an ITDM is better than manual, but still requires human action on every cycle. Configuring an automated system control is the strongest option and should be the starting point for future-state design during any S/4HANA implementation.

steps.title: Q11. Answer: C (B3)
steps.action: Q11. Answer: C (B3)

steps.title: Inspect OMR6 tolerance key settings to confirm the tolerance is ≤3%; ver…
steps.action: Inspect OMR6 tolerance key settings to confirm the tolerance is ≤3%; verify no vendor-specific overrides exist; sample 25 MIRO postings to confirm the system blocked invoices where variance exceeded tolerance.

steps.title: Correct. Testing a configured automated control requires three component…
steps.action: Correct. Testing a configured automated control requires three components: (1) configuration inspection — confirm the OMR6 tolerance is set to an appropriate threshold; (2) parameter completeness — verify no overrides bypass the standard tolerance; (3) operating evidence — sample postings to confirm the system actually enforced the control. Option A evidences existence, not appropriateness. Option B tests for manual override but does not verify the configuration. Option D is output-focused but does not verify the control's design is appropriate.

steps.title: Q12. Answer: B (B3)
steps.action: Q12. Answer: B (B3)

steps.title: The control is ineffective — for an ITDM, a signed report without docume…
steps.action: The control is ineffective — for an ITDM, a signed report without documented exception follow-up evidences that a review occurred but not that it was effective.

steps.title: Correct. This is a textbook ITDM deficiency. The control has two require…
steps.action: Correct. This is a textbook ITDM deficiency. The control has two required elements: (1) the system generates a complete and accurate report, and (2) a competent person reviews it and takes documented action on exceptions. The signed report evidences that Element 1 occurred and that a review happened — but the absence of documented follow-up on three flagged exceptions means Element 2 is not evidenced. The control is therefore ineffective for the period. Option A confuses evidence of performance with evidence of effectiveness. Option C is incorrect — the system component alone is not sufficient for an ITDM. Option D is not required — oral testimony cannot substitute for the missing documentary evidence.

steps.title: Q13. Answer: C (B3)
steps.action: Q13. Answer: C (B3)

steps.title: Confirm that the standard SAP functionality has not been switched off or…
steps.action: Confirm that the standard SAP functionality has not been switched off or overridden in system settings.

steps.title: Correct. This is the core of Ronnie's operational distinction. An inhere…
steps.action: Correct. This is the core of Ronnie's operational distinction. An inherent control — like the MIRO duplicate invoice check — is active by default and requires no configuration decision. Its test does not require a configuration review (there is nothing to configure). But the auditor must confirm the standard functionality has not been disabled — some clients switch off standard SAP checks to accommodate process workarounds. A configured control, by contrast, requires inspecting the configuration parameters (e.g. OMR6 tolerance keys) to verify they are set appropriately. Both types also require sampling to confirm operating effectiveness, but that step applies equally to both.

steps.title: Q14. Answer: B (B3)
steps.action: Q14. Answer: B (B3)

steps.title: First recommend configuring an automated goods receipt tolerance rule in…
steps.action: First recommend configuring an automated goods receipt tolerance rule in SAP; if that is not feasible, recommend converting the manual process to an ITDM; retain manual only if neither option is feasible.

steps.title: Correct. The uplift imperative follows the control nature hierarchy: con…
steps.action: Correct. The uplift imperative follows the control nature hierarchy: configured/automated is the first design choice (highest reliability, lowest testing cost), ITDM is the second choice (where full automation is not feasible), and manual is the last resort. The practitioner's recommendation must always start at the top of the hierarchy and work downward only when the process genuinely cannot support automation. Option A adds an ITDM layer but does not recommend the highest option first. Option C assumes ITDM is always feasible without assessing the process. Option D is incorrect — paper forms are the lowest-reliability option and are not preferable to system-generated records.

steps.title: Q15. Answer: B (B3)
steps.action: Q15. Answer: B (B3)

steps.title: Detective control · ITDM — the system generates the data and a human rev…
steps.action: Detective control · ITDM — the system generates the data and a human reviews and acts on it.

steps.title: Correct. This control has two dimensions to classify. Control TYPE: dete…
steps.action: Correct. This control has two dimensions to classify. Control TYPE: detective — the journal entries have already been posted outside the workflow before the control operates. The control identifies what happened after the fact; it does not prevent the unauthorised postings from occurring. Control NATURE: ITDM — the system generates the exception report (IT component), and the Financial Controller reviews it and emails exceptions to Internal Audit (human component). Both elements must be evidenced when testing. Option A is wrong on type (preventive) and nature (the human review is the primary element, not a configuration). steps.action: Correct. Tip 09: do the change management that nobody else is doing. A go-live is not the end of a controls engagement — it is the beginning of an operational reality. The people who will execute these controls from day one may have never heard of the RACM. They need to know what they are responsible for, how often, what a compliant execution looks like, and what to do when something goes wrong. ITDM and manual controls depend entirely on the human element — if the control owner does not know what they are doing on day one, the control is not operating on day one. RACM rationalisation (Option A) should have happened earlier in the process. The programme sponsor summary (Option C) is useful but not the most important action. The post-go-live auditor session (Option D) is a future activity.

steps.action: Correct. Tip 10: go beyond the engagement — position yourself as a trusted advisor. The practitioners who become trusted advisors do not deliver a clean RACM and move on. They stay curious about the client's situation, communicate clearly, and make themselves useful beyond the original scope. The Finance Director has come to them with a real problem six months post-go-live. That is an invitation — not a burden. Understanding what happened, identifying what support could help, and positioning the controls workstream as a long-term resource is exactly the trusted advisor role. Option A treats the engagement boundary as a hard stop on being useful. Option C deflects to a hiring recommendation. Option D sends documentation when the client needs engagement.
