steps.action: Correct. Tip 06: know your artefact landscape — and what you do when it is incomplete. Programmes do not always give you what you need. When that happens, you figure out how much you have to work with and what you need to get from them. You put the pieces together, build a preliminary stance on the end-to-end from what you have, and actively pursue the gaps. You do not wait for complete documentation before forming a view — you will wait indefinitely. Option A pauses progress, which is rarely the right answer on a complex programme. Option C accepts the incomplete picture without pursuing the gaps. Option D escalates as a risk when the practitioner's job is to make progress with imperfect information.

navigation_sections: Q1. Answer: B (B1)
Financial Risk — a Segregation of Duties conflict exists that enables payment fraud.

Correct. When a single user can both create the payee (XK01) and authorise the payment (F110), no independent check exists — cash can be directed to a fictitious vendor with no oversight. This is a classic Segregation of Duties conflict classified as Financial Risk. It is detected via GRC Access Control Ruleset analysis and is a common driver of SOX 404 material weakness findings.
Q2. Answer: B (B1)
A risk tolerance threshold.

Correct. Risk tolerance is the operational band that translates board-level risk appetite into a measurable, enforceable threshold. "Zero unmitigated High-risk SoD conflicts in FA" is a tolerance limit — a specific, testable condition. Risk appetite is the higher-level statement of willingness to accept risk; controls are the mechanisms to stay within tolerance.
Q3. Answer: C (B1)
Residual risk.

Correct. Residual risk is what remains after controls are designed, implemented, and operating effectively. Inherent risk is the starting position — before any controls. Control risk and detection risk are terms from the Audit Risk Model (ISA 315), which is a different framework used in financial statement auditing, not in the risk classification context covered here.
Q4. Answer: C (B1)
Operational Risk — a configuration weakness allows material discrepancies to post undetected.

Correct. This is Operational Risk: a process configuration weakness (tolerance too wide in OMR6) that allows invoices with material discrepancies to post automatically, with no manual review triggered. It is not necessarily fraud — the question does not state the vendor is acting dishonestly. The risk is in the process design, not the vendor's intent. Operational risk is characterised by process weaknesses that impair accurate, efficient operations.
Q5. Answer: B (B1)
The test procedure will be designed to test against a specific regulatory standard rather than substantive financial transactions.

Correct. Risk classification in the RCM directly determines the test approach. Financial Risk → substantive procedures (transaction testing, balance validation). Compliance Risk → regulatory standard test (test against the specific SOX, GDPR, or FDA requirement). The classification does not automatically determine the inherent rating, the geographic scope, or the control type — those are separate decisions. But it does anchor the entire test design.
Q6. Answer: B (B2)
A preventive control — the system blocks the erroneous posting before it completes.

Correct. The three-way match tolerance configured in OMR6 is a preventive control — it stops the erroneous or potentially fraudulent invoice posting from completing without any human action. The system enforces the rule on every transaction. A detective control would identify the discrepancy after the fact; an ITDM would require a human to review a system-generated exception report. This is automated and upstream — the definition of preventive.
Q7. Answer: B (B2)
Detective ITDM — the system generates the data, and a human reviews and takes action.

Correct. This is a Detective ITDM control. It is detective because the vendor master changes have already been made. It is ITDM because it has two components: the system generates the report (IT component) and a human reviews it and takes action (manual component). To test this control, auditors must verify both: that the report is complete and accurate, and that the manager's review is evidenced with exceptions acted upon.
Q8. Answer: C (B2)
Configured controls require a configuration review to verify parameters are appropriate; inherent controls require confirming the functionality has not been switched off.

Correct. A configured control — like the OMR6 three-way match tolerance — requires an auditor to inspect the configuration and verify the tolerance parameters are set appropriately. An inherent control — like MIRO's duplicate invoice check — does not need configuration verification, but the auditor must confirm it has not been switched off or overridden. Both types require a specific, different testing step — missing either one results in incomplete audit evidence.
Q9. Answer: B (B2)
The control is ineffective — for an ITDM, both the system output and the human review with documented action must be evidenced. The action element is missing.

Correct. The UAR is an ITDM detective control. For an ITDM to be effective, both elements must be evidenced: (1) the system-generated report is complete and accurate, AND (2) a competent person reviewed it and documented their action on exceptions. The absence of documented follow-up means the human component is not evidenced. The control is therefore ineffective for the period — regardless of whether the system output was accurate. This is one of the most common deficiencies found in UAR testing during SOX engagements.
Q10. Answer: C (B2)
Configure an automated system control — set up SAP to enforce goods receipt validation rules automatically, eliminating the need for manual approval in standard transactions.

Correct. The control nature hierarchy places configured/automated controls at the top — highest reliability, most consistent, least costly to test and maintain. The first design recommendation should always be to automate the control where the system allows it. A manual paper form is the lowest-reliability option and should only be retained when automation is genuinely not feasible. Moving to an ITDM is better than manual, but still requires human action on every cycle. Configuring an automated system control is the strongest option and should be the starting point for future-state design during any S/4HANA implementation.
Q11. Answer: C (B3)

Inspect OMR6 tolerance key settings to confirm the tolerance is ≤3%; verify no vendor-specific overrides exist; sample 25 MIRO postings to confirm the system blocked invoices where variance exceeded tolerance.

Correct. Testing a configured automated control requires three components: (1) configuration inspection — confirm the OMR6 tolerance is set to an appropriate threshold; (2) parameter completeness — verify no overrides bypass the standard tolerance; (3) operating evidence — sample postings to confirm the system actually enforced the control. Option A evidences existence, not appropriateness. Option B tests for manual override but does not verify the configuration. Option D is output-focused but does not verify the control's design is appropriate.
Q12. Answer: B (B3)
The control is ineffective — for an ITDM, a signed report without documented exception follow-up evidences that a review occurred but not that it was effective.

Correct. This is a textbook ITDM deficiency. The control has two required elements: (1) the system generates a complete and accurate report, and (2) a competent person reviews it and takes documented action on exceptions. The signed report evidences that Element 1 occurred and that a review happened — but the absence of documented follow-up on three flagged exceptions means Element 2 is not evidenced. The control is therefore ineffective for the period. Option A confuses evidence of performance with evidence of effectiveness. Option C is incorrect — the system component alone is not sufficient for an ITDM. Option D is not required — oral testimony cannot substitute for the missing documentary evidence.
Q13. Answer: C (B3)
Confirm that the standard SAP functionality has not been switched off or overridden in system settings.

Correct. This is the core of Ronnie's operational distinction. An inherent control — like the MIRO duplicate invoice check — is active by default and requires no configuration decision. Its test does not require a configuration review (there is nothing to configure). But the auditor must confirm the standard functionality has not been disabled — some clients switch off standard SAP checks to accommodate process workarounds. A configured control, by contrast, requires inspecting the configuration parameters (e.g. OMR6 tolerance keys) to verify they are set appropriately. Both types also require sampling to confirm operating effectiveness, but that step applies equally to both.
Q14. Answer: B (B3)

First recommend configuring an automated goods receipt tolerance rule in SAP; if that is not feasible, recommend converting the manual process to an ITDM; retain manual only if neither option is feasible.

Correct. The uplift imperative follows the control nature hierarchy: configured/automated is the first design choice (highest reliability, lowest testing cost), ITDM is the second choice (where full automation is not feasible), and manual is the last resort. The practitioner's recommendation must always start at the top of the hierarchy and work downward only when the process genuinely cannot support automation. Option A adds an ITDM layer but does not recommend the highest option first. Option C assumes ITDM is always feasible without assessing the process. Option D is incorrect — paper forms are the lowest-reliability option and are not preferable to system-generated records.
Q15. Answer: B (B3)
Detective control · ITDM — the system generates the data and a human reviews and acts on it.

Correct. This control has two dimensions to classify. Control TYPE: detective — the journal entries have already been posted outside the workflow before the control operates. The control identifies what happened after the fact; it does not prevent the unauthorised postings from occurring. Control NATURE: ITDM — the system generates the exception report (IT component), and the Financial Controller reviews it and emails exceptions to Internal Audit (human component). Both elements must be evidenced when testing. Option A is wrong on type (preventive) and nature (the human review is the primary element, not a configuration). Option C is wrong on nature — there is a clear system component. Option D is wrong on type — the postings have already occurred.
Q16. Answer: B (B4)

Prevention during implementation costs a fraction of remediation post-live — every control gap fixed before go-live avoids rework, audit findings, and business disruption at the most vulnerable moment.

Correct. This is the core business case from Module B4. The value of a controls workstream is primarily economic and operational: prevention during implementation is far cheaper than remediation post-live. The comparison is rework cost, audit finding cost, and business disruption cost — all avoidable if controls are embedded before go-live. Option A is a secondary practical point, not the primary business case. Option C overstates the regulatory requirement. Option D is factually incorrect.
Q17. Answer: C (B4)
Carrying the old process design directly into the new system without redesign — a problem because it misses the opportunity to build compliance and automation into the future state.

Correct. Lift-and-shift in the context of an S/4HANA transformation means replicating the legacy process in the new system rather than taking the opportunity to redesign it. The source session is direct: that is not the mindset we should be going with. Transformation is the optimal moment to embed compliance, configure automated controls, and eliminate manual processes. After go-live, that window closes — redesign costs multiples more.
Q18. Answer: B (B4)

Controls are the inputs for the external audit. Controls designed, documented, and tested from go-live attract higher auditor reliance, require smaller sample sizes, and reduce annual external audit fees.

Correct. The source session makes this connection explicit: controls are the inputs for external auditors to conduct their annual audit. When controls are designed, evidenced, and operating from day one, auditors can place higher reliance on them — which translates directly into smaller testing samples, fewer audit hours, and lower fees. Option A is incorrect — external audit is directly dependent on the internal controls framework. Option C and D are inaccurate representations of audit methodology.
Q19. Answer: B (B4)
Controls that are fully embedded in day-to-day operations, owned by the business, automated where possible, and capable of continuous improvement — not just a document set.

Correct. Value Driver 4 is about operational sustainability. The source session frames it as: making sure these controls are fully embedded and operationalised in the client's environment so that they can continue to carry this forward and continuously improve. Option A describes a useful artefact but not operational embedding. Option C describes one specific control type (automated SoD), not the broader embedding concept. Option D describes project reporting, not operational controls maturity.
Q20. Answer: C (B4)

Reframe: the controls activity during design workshops is protecting the team's investment — every issue identified now eliminates a more expensive problem post-live, including rework, audit findings, and potential financial loss.

Correct. The 'value protection' frame is a reframe — it repositions the controls conversation from compliance overhead to investment protection. The correct response is to acknowledge the concern while reframing the activity's purpose: the time spent now eliminates post-live rework and audit exposure that would cost far more. Option A surrenders on scope without a business case response. Option B is a compliance mandate argument — technically correct but not persuasive and not the frame Module B4 teaches. Option D is an escalation, not a stakeholder response.
Q21. Answer: C (B5)
Remediation — time-sensitive engagement driven by external audit findings, with a hard deadline before the next audit cycle.

Correct. The defining characteristics of a remediation engagement are present: external audit findings define the scope, the deadline is the next audit cycle, and time is of essence. The primary deliverables are remediated controls, re-test evidence, and audit-ready packages. The key relationships are the external auditor and CFO. Options A and B describe different starting conditions. Option D describes a testing engagement — the client has controls in place to test; here the controls themselves have failed and must be overhauled.
Q22. Answer: B (B5)

The RCM starts as a preliminary draft at solution confirmation, is updated and validated through design and build, and reaches its final tested state by go-live — reflecting increasing detail and certainty at each phase.

Correct. The transformation engagement's RCM is not created once — it evolves. At solution confirmation, it is a preliminary draft based on early-stage process understanding. Through design and build, controls are validated with business process owners and specifics are refined. During testing, the RCM is updated with test results and evidence. By go-live, it is a fully validated, tested document that reflects the organisation's actual controls environment. Option A is incorrect — the same RCM is refined, not replaced. Option C misses the iterative nature. Option D misidentifies who owns the RCM.
Q23. Answer: B (B5)
No — a role that creates a SoD conflict is simultaneously a security design issue and a financial risk. The two workstreams must coordinate, not operate independently.

Correct. The source session explicitly flags the controls-security integration point as one of the most common failure points on large S/4HANA programmes. A SoD conflict in a user role is simultaneously a security issue (role design) and a financial risk (controls framework). The two workstreams must coordinate — on role design decisions, access approvals, and SoD conflict remediation. Option A is incorrect — independence is the problem, not the solution. Option C describes documentation of a finding, not resolution of the coordination failure. Option D goes too far — the controls team does not take over security design; they coordinate with it.
Q24. Answer: B (B5)
To ensure that the controls the team has identified are actually tested in the system — so that only the controls-relevant test scenarios are reviewed for DEF and OEF evidence.

Correct. The source session describes this precisely: the testing programme will test everything in the system; the controls team is only focused on the controls that have been identified and ensuring those are tested. The activity of working with the testing team to identify control-relevant test scripts is about making sure DEF and OEF evidence is captured for each control in the RCM — not about reducing scope or replacing the test approach. Option A misframes the objective. Option C mischaracterises what the controls team does with testing. Option D describes a different activity (requirements validation).
Q25. Answer: C (B5)
Assessment and Recommendation engagement, at the advisory (light-touch) end of the degree-of-engagement spectrum.

Correct. The description matches an Assessment and Recommendation engagement precisely: reviewing the current environment, identifying gaps, making recommendations — without direct design or testing involvement. This places the team at the advisory, light-touch end of the degree-of-engagement spectrum. The primary deliverable is a findings and recommendations report. The primary relationship is with Internal Audit or the Compliance function. Options A and B involve active design or testing work. Option D involves an audit-finding-driven scope and urgency not present in this description.
Q26. Answer: B (B6)
Raise the opportunity to configure an automated approval workflow in S/4HANA now — Solution Confirmation is the peak influence window for shaping future state design.

Correct. Solution Confirmation is the peak influence window — the optimal moment to identify manual controls that could be automated in the future state and raise them with the programme. The source session is explicit: it is better to have a workflow designed and built now than to try to get it built later in the programme. Once Key Design Decisions are finalised, influencing the design becomes progressively harder and more expensive. Option A accepts the status quo instead of advocating for improvement. Option C waits too long. Option D adds an unnecessary escalation step.
Q27. Answer: C (B6)
First define the relevant risk (e.g. financial completeness of requisition data), then assess whether this interface affects that risk, then extract the error handling mechanism if relevant.

Correct. The three-step risk-first reading approach from Module B6: (1) What risk am I concerned about? Define this before opening the document — it is your filter. (2) Does this FD affect that risk? If incomplete requisition data could cause a financial misstatement or liability issue, the FD is relevant. (3) If relevant — extract the error handling mechanism: how does the system detect, alert, and resolve interface failures? That mechanism is the control. Option A reads the whole document without a filter — inefficient. Option B misunderstands the controls team's responsibility for interface controls in the RACM. Option D focuses on approvals rather than risk analysis.
Q28. Answer: C (B6)
Go back to the tester (or the testing captain) and request the specific evidence required — the system confirmation or blocking reason code — as agreed in the test plan.

Correct. The source session provides a field example directly on this point: when the evidence coming back is inadequate, go back and ask for the specific evidence required. The preferred route on large programmes is through the testing captain — the coordinator who manages a group of testers — rather than chasing individual testers directly. The test plan should already specify exactly what screenshots or system outputs are required, so the request is grounded in pre-agreed expectations. Option A accepts insufficient evidence — this would result in an incomplete controls test. Option B is disproportionate for a standard evidence rework situation. Option D bypasses the programme's testing process.
Q29. Answer: B (B6)
Configuration controls (automated, no human intervention) → SIT. Workflow-driven and report-driven controls requiring human review → UAT.

Correct. The SIT vs UAT scope decision is based on control nature, not risk rating or design ownership. Configuration controls — automated, no human intervention — belong in SIT, where the system itself is being validated. Workflow-driven and report-driven controls — those requiring human review and action — belong in UAT, where business users are in the system and can demonstrate they can perform the required human element. This approach distributes effort across testing cycles and matches each control type with the most appropriate testing environment. The source session notes that on a programme with hundreds of controls, testing everything in every cycle is not feasible — the SIT/UAT split is the efficiency mechanism.
Q30. Answer: C (B6)
The external auditor must confirm that the controls designed and tested are the controls they will rely on in the annual audit — this confirmation is the final gate before go-live.

Correct. The external auditor confirmation gate is an explicit prerequisite for go-live readiness in Module B6. Even when controls are designed, validated, tested, and control owners trained, the external auditor must confirm that the controls the programme has built are the ones they will rely on in the annual external audit. This confirmation is the final gate. If the auditor has concerns — about design, evidence quality, or coverage — those must be resolved before go-live, not after. Option A omits the auditor gate entirely. Option B describes a valid activity but is not the primary missing step. Option D is a useful activity but does not represent the final gate the source session identifies.
Q31. Answer: C (B7)
Define the risk being controlled — financial, operational, or regulatory — and assess whether this interface could affect that risk if it failed.

Correct. The risk filter is applied before reading the document — not after. Define the risk type first (financial, operational, or regulatory), then assess whether this interface could cause that risk to materialise if it failed. Only if the answer is yes do you proceed to parameter extraction. Option A reads everything without a filter — inefficient. Option B focuses on approvals rather than risk analysis. Option D goes directly to error handling without first confirming the FD is relevant to the risk being controlled.
Q32. Answer: C (B7)
Because VANTAGE receives no confirmation, all error detection and monitoring controls must be designed and placed at the SAP receiving system.

Correct. This is the key controls implication of a unidirectional interface. Because the sending system (VANTAGE) receives no acknowledgement from the receiving system (SAP), it has no visibility of what happened after transmission. This means the monitoring control must be placed entirely on the SAP side — error detection, alerts, resolution tracking, and the daily sign-off report must all be SAP-based. Option A incorrectly places the control in VANTAGE, which has no visibility of the transfer outcome. Option B is incorrect — a unidirectional interface creates a higher monitoring requirement, not zero. Option D is a system design recommendation, not a controls response.
Q33. Answer: B (B7)
The monitoring frequency (weekly) does not match the interface frequency (every 4 hours). Up to 5 days of transfer failures could accumulate before detection.

Correct. Frequency directly determines the exposure window — the period during which undetected errors accumulate before the monitoring cycle runs. An interface that runs every 4 hours during business hours could generate 20 batch cycles in a 5-day week. A weekly review means up to 5 days of transfer failures, missing records, or data corruption could go undetected before the control fires. The control design must match or exceed the transfer frequency. A daily monitoring report — as specified in FD-MM-INT-027 Section 5.3 — is appropriate. A weekly review creates an unacceptable exposure window.
Q34. Answer: B (B7)

No — while detection exists (error log), there is no automated alert mechanism, no defined resolution SLA, and the manual morning review creates an exposure window of up to 20+ hours for late-day batch failures.

Correct. A complete error handling specification must cover: (1) automatic detection ✓ (error logged), (2) notification mechanism ✗ (no automated alert), (3) resolution SLA ✗ (not defined), (4) reconciliation/sign-off ✗ (not mentioned). The manual morning review also creates a significant exposure window: a batch failure at 18:00 WAT will not be detected until the following morning — more than 12 hours of exposure. Compared to FD-MM-INT-027's full specification (email alert within 15 minutes, 4-hour SLA, re-submission log, daily sign-off), this is materially incomplete. Option A accepts a detection-only specification as sufficient. Option C accepts no notification as acceptable. Option D introduces a testing step requirement that is not part of the error handling completeness assessment.
Q35. Answer: B (B7)
Detective control · IT-Dependent Manual (ITDM) — the system generates the monitoring report (IT component) and the P2P Monitor reviews and signs off (human component).

Correct. Two dimensions must be classified: Type and Nature. Control TYPE: Detective. The interface errors have already occurred before the control fires — the monitoring report identifies what went wrong after the fact and triggers remediation. It does not prevent the transfer failure from occurring. Control NATURE: ITDM (IT-Dependent Manual). The system automatically generates the monitoring report from /PNS/INT_ERR and /PNS/INT_WARN (IT component). The P2P Interface Monitor reviews the report, investigates exceptions, and signs off (human component). Both elements are required and must be evidenced. Option A misclassifies as preventive and automated — the control does not stop errors from occurring. Option C is wrong on type — reviewing a report after errors have occurred is detection, not prevention. Option D misclassifies as manual — there is a clear IT component generating the monitoring data.
Q36. Answer: B (B8)
No — the company code cross-check is missing. All company codes must be reviewed, and any that deviate from the standard value must be investigated.

Correct. The evidence package covers two of the three required components for config testing: the SPRO navigation path and the tolerance value. The third component — the company code cross-check — is missing. All relevant company codes must be reviewed. On the major energy sector engagement described in the source session, reviewing all company codes revealed one at 10% when all others were at 2–3%. That exception required a policy justification or a correction before go-live. A practitioner who checks only GC01 would miss this. Option A accepts two components as sufficient. Option C confuses transactional testing requirements with configuration testing requirements — these are separate test steps. Option D is incorrect — there are three required components, not two.
Q37. Answer: B (B8)
The test plan needs a negative scenario: an unauthorised user attempting to execute F110 should result in a system block. Without this, the test does not confirm the SoD restriction is functioning.

Correct. This test plan contains only a positive scenario — an authorised user executing successfully. It does not prove that the SoD restriction blocks an unauthorised user. The negative scenario is required: attempt the F110 execution with a user who has SoD conflicts, and confirm the system blocks the transaction. A SoD control that only has a positive test result is not fully validated — you need both the "works correctly" evidence and the "blocks correctly" evidence. Option A accepts a positive-only test as complete. Option C introduces a report test as a substitute for the negative transactional scenario — these are different test types addressing different questions. Option D confuses successful execution logging with evidence of SoD restriction.
Q38. Answer: C (B8)
B and D — both require a human to generate a system report and take documented action, making UAT the appropriate testing environment.

Correct. The SIT vs UAT split is based on control nature, not risk rating. Controls B and D are both ITDM controls: the system generates a report (IT component) and a human reviews and signs off (human component). UAT is the appropriate environment because business users — the P2P Process Lead and Finance Manager — need to be in the system to demonstrate they can perform the review and sign-off steps. Controls A and C are automated/configuration controls: the system enforces the control automatically without human intervention. These belong in SIT. A is a workflow configuration test (confirm approval routing is set correctly); C is a duplicate invoice block (confirm the system-level check is operating). Option A applies a risk-based scoping logic — incorrect. Option B re-runs all controls in UAT — unnecessary and wasteful. Option D misclassifies workflow configuration testing as requiring UAT.
Q39. Answer: C (B8)
Immediately identify the testing captain(s), review the programme test cases, add controls requirements to the test scripts, and agree the evidence requirements before the first test is executed.

Correct. The source session is explicit on this point: the testing captain model and the integration of controls requirements into programme test cases must be set up before testing begins — not after. With two weeks until testing starts, the immediate priority is: (1) identify the testing captain(s), (2) review the programme test cases and map controls to them, (3) add controls testing requirements directly to the test scripts, (4) publish evidence requirements and agree them with the testing captain. Setting this up now prevents the most common testing phase problems: inconsistent evidence, re-test chasing, and evidence packages that arrive incomplete. Option A bypasses the programme structure entirely. Option B is an escalation response, not an action that resolves the setup gap. Option D creates a sequential dependency where none is required — RACM updates and testing integration can happen in parallel.
Q40. Answer: B (B9)
The agent proposes draft RACM entries — including control description, type, and nature — which the controls team then reviews, challenges, and refines before the RACM is finalised.

Correct. The agent proposes — the practitioner decides. The agent produces a structured draft RACM entry from the FD, which the practitioner then reviews, challenges, and refines. Some proposals will be accepted largely as drafted; others will need significant rework if the agent missed a nuance in the error handling specification or proposed a manual control where the FD supports an automated one. The value is that the practitioner starts from a structured draft rather than a blank page — not that the agent replaces the review process. Option A misrepresents the agent's role as completing rather than proposing. Option C invents a risk-based scoping rule that does not exist in the module. Option D removes FD review entirely, which is incorrect.
Q41. Answer: C (B9)
Cross-reference the RACM against the programme test case library and flag controls with no corresponding test coverage.

Correct. The AI agent's strength in the testing phase is cross-referencing at scale — mapping controls to test cases, identifying gaps, and flagging inconsistencies between evidence requirements and control types. This is structured pattern-matching across large volumes, which agents handle well. The other three options represent the limits of AI capability: Option A requires professional judgement about sufficiency for a specific engagement context. Option B requires scepticism about whether a formal action represents substantive review — agents can see the sign-off, not the absence of genuine review behind it. Option D requires evaluating the credibility of a client's explanation using relationship knowledge and business judgement that an agent does not have.
Q42. Answer: B (B9)

Passive acceptance of agent outputs removes the practitioner's challenge and scepticism, which means the agent's errors, missed context, and incorrect assumptions will pass into the work product unchecked.

Correct. The module distinguishes between two stances: passive acceptance (receives agent outputs, accepts without challenge) and critical engagement (develops working understanding, reviews with scepticism, applies professional judgement). Passive acceptance is the problem described — the efficiency gain is real, but so is the risk that errors, missed programme context, and incorrect control classifications pass through unchallenged. The practitioner's value in AI-assisted workflows is exactly this critical review. Option A incorrectly dismisses agent use in SolCon entirely. Option C introduces an auditor recognition constraint that does not exist in the module. Option D misconstrues the module's position on where agents add value — they add value across all three phases.
Q43. Answer: B (B9)
Information processing decreases in the practitioner's workload; judgement, relationship work, and accountability remain the same or increase.

Correct. The attention-shift framework from the module: Information Processing = Less (agent handles triage and first drafts); Judgement = More (validating, challenging, contextualising agent outputs); Relationship Work = More (client credibility cannot be automated); Accountability = Same (professional sign-off cannot be delegated to an agent). The practitioner's role shifts in emphasis — less time on volume processing, more time on the judgements that matter. Option A incorrectly suggests accountability is shared — it is not. Professional accountability remains with the practitioner who signs off on the work. Option C reframes the practitioner as an AI manager, which misrepresents the model. Option D denies any change, which is also incorrect.
Q44. Answer: C (B9)

Gap analysis outputs require practitioner review with programme context — the agent identified a gap based on the artefacts it saw, but the practitioner recognises the replacement control exists elsewhere in the programme.

Correct. This scenario illustrates exactly why practitioner review of agent outputs is essential. The agent performed its task correctly based on what it could see in the artefacts it was given — if the new SAP-native interface control was documented separately or not yet formally linked to the legacy gap, the agent would correctly flag the gap based on available information. The practitioner's value here is programme context: knowing that the replacement control exists and is already in the design. The agent's first-cut analysis is valuable — it raised 12 potential gaps, 9 of which may be genuine. The practitioner's review, not the agent's output alone, produces the reliable final picture. Option A overreacts — one miss does not invalidate the analysis. Option B adds unnecessary rework. Option D inverts the correct hierarchy: agent outputs are proposals, not decisions.
Q45. Answer: B (B10)
Lead with the credit limit approval pain point — "I understand you have been having challenges with how credit approvals are processed. Let us start there."

Correct. Tip 01: always start with pain points. When you connect to something the business team is already worried about, you become relevant immediately. The credit limit approval problem gives you an opening that is theirs — not a controls framework they were not expecting. The conversation you planned becomes one they want to have. Option A leads with methodology, which is less engaging than the team's actual concern. Option C delays addressing the pain point in favour of process mapping. Option D opens with classification theory when the team wants to solve a real problem.
Q46. Answer: B (B10)
The controls team should have established a consistent evidence approach across both streams before beginning — inconsistency creates noise and unnecessary friction.

Correct. Tip 02: establish consistency across all teams from day one. The source session is direct: if you tell one team one thing and another team something different, they will compare notes. That creates unnecessary noise you will then have to manage on top of everything else. Consistency is a form of credibility — when every team gets the same standard, there is nothing to push back against. The practitioner's error here was making a different deal under time pressure. Option A accepts the inconsistency as reasonable. Option C escalates when direct resolution is the right move. Option D picks a winner rather than establishing a consistent standard.
Q47. Answer: B (B10)
Ensure that the control owners — particularly those responsible for ITDM and manual controls — have been trained on what to do, how often, what evidence to produce, and how to escalate exceptions.

Correct. Tip 09: do the change management that nobody else is doing. A go-live is not the end of a controls engagement — it is the beginning of an operational reality. The people who will execute these controls from day one may have never heard of the RACM. They need to know what they are responsible for, how often, what a compliant execution looks like, and what to do when something goes wrong. ITDM and manual controls depend entirely on the human element — if the control owner does not know what they are doing on day one, the control is not operating on day one. RACM rationalisation (Option A) should have happened earlier in the process. The programme sponsor summary (Option C) is useful but not the most important action. The post-go-live auditor session (Option D) is a future activity.
Q48. Answer: B (B10)
Engage with the Finance Director to understand the gap, identify what support the controls workstream could provide post-go-live, and position the team as a resource for ongoing improvement.

Correct. Tip 10: go beyond the engagement — position yourself as a trusted advisor. The practitioners who become trusted advisors do not deliver a clean RACM and move on. They stay curious about the client's situation, communicate clearly, and make themselves useful beyond the original scope. The Finance Director has come to them with a real problem six months post-go-live. That is an invitation — not a burden. Understanding what happened, identifying what support could help, and positioning the controls workstream as a long-term resource is exactly the trusted advisor role. Option A treats the engagement boundary as a hard stop on being useful. Option C deflects to a hiring recommendation. Option D sends documentation when the client needs engagement.
Q49. Answer: B (B10)
Work with the FDs available to develop a preliminary view of the end-to-end, identify the specific gaps in the artefact picture, and pursue those gaps actively while continuing to make progress.

Correct. Tip 06: know your artefact landscape — and what you do when it is incomplete. Programmes do not always give you what you need. When that happens, you figure out how much you have to work with and what you need to get from them. You put the pieces together, build a preliminary stance on the end-to-end from what you have, and actively pursue the gaps. You do not wait for complete documentation before forming a view — you will wait indefinitely. Option A pauses progress, which is rarely the right answer on a complex programme. Option C accepts the incomplete picture without pursuing the gaps. Option D escalates as a risk when the practitioner's job is to make progress with imperfect information.
