steps.title: PRIMARY LAB
steps.action: PRIMARY LAB
steps.narration:
II · IT General Controls: Change & Operations — Change Management Testing

Control question: Verify that all transports imported into the production system during the testing period were authorised, tested, and approved before migration, and that the ability to migrate was restricted to appropriate personnel.

Systems / tools: STMS, SE01, SCC4

The Story

I opened Lab 2 with one discipline: I wrote the control assertion in plain English before opening SAP. The question was not “Can I run the report?” It was whether the evidence could support this statement: Verify that all transports imported into the production system during the testing period were authorised, tested, and approved before migration, and that the ability to migrate was restricted to appropriate personnel.

Priya: “Before you touch the system, tell me the population, the period, and what would count as an exception.”

I wrote those three items at the top of my workpaper. That small habit prevents one of the most common failures in controls testing: allowing the available report to define the test instead of allowing the control objective to define the report.

I then moved into the system. SAP GUI command field > /nSTMS > Import Overview > select the target system > Import History > set the testing period and retain both selection and result evidence. SAP GUI command field > /nSE01 > enter/open the transport request > Display > inspect object list and request attributes. SAP GUI command field > /nSCC4 > select the production client > Display > record client change/transport settings; do not edit.

Before execution, I recorded the system/client or source application, test period, population definition, report parameters, preparer and evidence date. If the menu path differed from the training wording, I documented the actual path rather than pretending the environment looked exactly like the manual.

My execution notes read like a trail another consultant could follow:

Re-read the objective and define the exact control assertion, population, period and exception condition before opening the report.

Pulled the full production import population from STMS Import History for the testing period, capturing transport number, owner, import date/time, and return code for every entry.

Opened SE01 for a sample of transports and reviewed the actual objects contained in each — programs, table entries, and configuration objects.

Matched every transport in the population to its change ticket, classifying every exception into one of three categories: no ticket at all; approval date after the import date; or import by a user outside the authorised Basis group.

Confirmed via SCC4 that the production client is configured to restrict changes and transports for client-specific objects.

Reconcile the extracted population/result to the scope used in the completed example. Investigate differences; do not force your result to match the sample.

After the system work, I reconciled the extracted population to the defined scope, investigated differences rather than forcing the result to match the completed example, traced each exception to its underlying evidence, and completed the evidence index before drafting the conclusion.

The Moment the Test Changed

The first result was not the conclusion. It was the point where the case became interesting.

Six production imports in the period had no matching approved change ticket.

All six were imported over a single weekend, by the same user, outside business hours.

Review of transport contents found no unauthorised functional change; one transport contained an unrelated configuration change, which management explained as incidental.

Maya: “So what does that actually tell us? Is this a failed control, a documentation problem, a design issue, or simply something we still need to investigate?”

That question forced me to stop describing the screen and start analyzing the control. I separated the observed condition from management’s explanation, then asked what additional evidence would prove or disprove the explanation.

The Rookie Mistake I Would Warn You About

Do not accept a ticket number as proof of control performance. Compare approval time, migration/import time, emergency classification and evidence creation time.

A second rookie mistake is to crop evidence too aggressively. A screenshot that proves the number but hides the system, date, user, parameters or surrounding context may look clean in a slide deck and still be weak audit evidence.

Building the Evidence Trail

I treated the evidence package as part of the test, not as administration after the test. My rule was simple: selection criteria first, result second, raw export preserved separately, analysis performed only on a working copy.

THORNFIELD-B02-CH-01_SystemStatus.png

THORNFIELD-B02-CH-01_STMS_ImportHistory.png — selection screen and result, date range visible

THORNFIELD-B02-CH-01_SE01_ObjectList_[TransportID].png — one per sampled transport

THORNFIELD-B02-CH-01_SCC4_ClientSettings.png

THORNFIELD-B02-CH-01_ExceptionClassification.xlsx — Tab "Reconciliation"

For every file I recorded the source, system/client, period, extraction criteria, filename, preparer, date and workpaper cross-reference. That is what turns a folder of screenshots into an evidence trail.

The Reviewer Challenge

Elena: “Ilse states she raised tickets for all six on the following Monday. This workpaper treats retrospective ticket creation as documentation after the fact, not as evidence of approval before migration, and flags that framing for reviewer discussion rather than accepting it as resolving the exception.”

I answered by going back to the source evidence rather than defending my first interpretation. Reviewer challenge is not an interruption to the work; it is part of the control-testing process. If the conclusion survives challenge, it becomes stronger. If it changes, the workpaper has done its job.

My Conclusion

The change management control did not operate for six production imports during the period, all arising from a single out-of-hours incident for which no emergency change procedure existed. Recommendation: define an emergency change procedure with retrospective approval inside a defined window, a mandatory business justification, and a post-implementation review.

I deliberately avoided writing beyond the evidence. Where a cause had not been proven, I called it a reviewer question or an investigation item rather than turning an assumption into a finding.

What This Lab Is Really Teaching

A change ticket is useful only when its timing and approvals support the control assertion. Documentation created after migration cannot retroactively become pre-implementation approval.

The technical transaction or report is only the visible part of the work. The professional skill is deciding what evidence is sufficient, recognizing when the population or control design makes a “clean” result misleading, and documenting the reasoning so that someone who was not in the room can follow it.

Before Leaving the Lab

✓ Correct system/source, client/entity and period are documented.

✓ Population completeness and report parameters are evidenced.

✓ Required screenshots and raw exports are saved and readable.

✓ Every exception is traced to underlying evidence.

✓ Sample exhibit/analysis reconciles to the workpaper.

✓ Conclusion is supported by the evidence and does not rely only on the completed example.

✓ Evidence filenames and workpaper cross-references are complete.

✓ Reviewer discussion items are clearly separated from resolved findings.

Field-journal close: I did not leave Lab 2 when the report finished running. I left when the evidence, workpaper, exception logic and conclusion told the same story.

steps.title: PRIMARY LAB
steps.action: PRIMARY LAB
steps.narration:
II · IT General Controls: Change & Operations — Computer Operations Testing

Control question: Verify that financial data can be restored if lost or corrupted — both that backups execute as scheduled and that restoration is tested periodically.

Systems / tools: SM37

The Story

I opened Lab 18 with one discipline: I wrote the control assertion in plain English before opening SAP. The question was not “Can I run the report?” It was whether the evidence could support this statement: Verify that financial data can be restored if lost or corrupted — both that backups execute as scheduled and that restoration is tested periodically.

Priya: “Before you touch the system, tell me the population, the period, and what would count as an exception.”

I wrote those three items at the top of my workpaper. That small habit prevents one of the most common failures in controls testing: allowing the available report to define the test instead of allowing the control objective to define the report.

I then moved into the system. SAP GUI command field > /nSM37 > enter job name/user/status/date range > Execute > open job log/spool as required and retain the population/result. Before executing, record the system/client or source application, test period, population definition, report parameters, preparer and evidence date. If the configured menu path differs from the wording in this lab, document the actual client path used rather than guessing.

Before execution, I recorded the system/client or source application, test period, population definition, report parameters, preparer and evidence date. If the menu path differed from the training wording, I documented the actual path rather than pretending the environment looked exactly like the manual.

My execution notes read like a trail another consultant could follow:

Re-read the objective and define the exact control assertion, population, period and exception condition before opening the report.

Wrote down the expected number of backup executions for the period before opening any screen (e.g. 365 nights = 365 expected runs).

Reviewed the DB13 backup calendar for the full period, scanning for gaps in the pattern rather than reading individual entries in isolation.

Pulled the DB12 backup log for the same period, recorded the actual execution count, and compared it to the expected count from step one.

Searched for evidence of a restoration test within SAP and, finding none, documented that as a finding rather than a testing limitation.

Reviewed SM37 for the wider job picture, noting that a "Finished" status confirms a job ran to completion, not that it processed any records.

After the system work, I reconciled the extracted population to the defined scope, investigated differences rather than forcing the result to match the completed example, traced each exception to its underlying evidence, and completed the evidence index before drafting the conclusion.

The Moment the Test Changed

The first result was not the conclusion. It was the point where the case became interesting.

364 of 365 expected backup executions completed successfully in the period; one scheduled execution is missing from the log on a specific, named date.

No evidence of any restoration test exists anywhere in SAP for the period.

Maya: “So what does that actually tell us? Is this a failed control, a documentation problem, a design issue, or simply something we still need to investigate?”

That question forced me to stop describing the screen and start analyzing the control. I separated the observed condition from management’s explanation, then asked what additional evidence would prove or disprove the explanation.

The Rookie Mistake I Would Warn You About

Do not accept a ticket number as proof of control performance. Compare approval time, migration/import time, emergency classification and evidence creation time.

A second rookie mistake is to crop evidence too aggressively. A screenshot that proves the number but hides the system, date, user, parameters or surrounding context may look clean in a slide deck and still be weak audit evidence.

Building the Evidence Trail

I treated the evidence package as part of the test, not as administration after the test. My rule was simple: selection criteria first, result second, raw export preserved separately, analysis performed only on a working copy.

THORNFIELD-B18-OPS-01_ExpectedCount_Note.xlsx

THORNFIELD-B18-OPS-01_DB13_Calendar.png

THORNFIELD-B18-OPS-01_DB12_Log.png

THORNFIELD-B18-OPS-01_SM37_Selection_Result.png

THORNFIELD-B18-OPS-01_RestorationTestSearch_Note.docx

For every file I recorded the source, system/client, period, extraction criteria, filename, preparer, date and workpaper cross-reference. That is what turns a folder of screenshots into an evidence trail.

The Reviewer Challenge

Elena: “364 clean backup-completion reports were the starting point handed to the tester. Flagged for reviewer discussion on what the next question should be when evidence looks uniformly clean — i.e. what the reports do not show, rather than accepting what they do show.”

I answered by going back to the source evidence rather than defending my first interpretation. Reviewer challenge is not an interruption to the work; it is part of the control-testing process. If the conclusion survives challenge, it becomes stronger. If it changes, the workpaper has done its job.

My Conclusion

Design deficiency — the control as designed monitors backup execution only and does not include restoration testing, so it cannot provide assurance that data is actually recoverable, independent of the one missed execution noted above. Recommendation: Introduce periodic, documented restoration testing with a defined scope and frequency, in addition to the existing execution monitoring.

I deliberately avoided writing beyond the evidence. Where a cause had not been proven, I called it a reviewer question or an investigation item rather than turning an assumption into a finding.

What This Lab Is Really Teaching

A change ticket is useful only when its timing and approvals support the control assertion. Documentation created after migration cannot retroactively become pre-implementation approval.

The technical transaction or report is only the visible part of the work. The professional skill is deciding what evidence is sufficient, recognizing when the population or control design makes a “clean” result misleading, and documenting the reasoning so that someone who was not in the room can follow it.

Before Leaving the Lab

✓ Correct system/source, client/entity and period are documented.

✓ Population completeness and report parameters are evidenced.

✓ Required screenshots and raw exports are saved and readable.

✓ Every exception is traced to underlying evidence.

✓ Sample exhibit/analysis reconciles to the workpaper.

✓ Conclusion is supported by the evidence and does not rely only on the completed example.

✓ Evidence filenames and workpaper cross-references are complete.

✓ Reviewer discussion items are clearly separated from resolved findings.

Field-journal close: I did not leave Lab 18 when the report finished running. I left when the evidence, workpaper, exception logic and conclusion told the same story.

steps.narration:
II · IT General Controls: Change & Operations — Interface Control Testing

Control question: Verify that all transactions transmitted by the Warehouse Management System are completely and accurately recorded in SAP, and that failures are identified and resolved on time.

Systems / tools: SM58, SMQ1, SMQ2

The Story

I opened Lab 19 with one discipline: I wrote the control assertion in plain English before opening SAP. The question was not “Can I run the report?” It was whether the evidence could support this statement: Verify that all transactions transmitted by the Warehouse Management System are completely and accurately recorded in SAP, and that failures are identified and resolved on time.

Priya: “Before you touch the system, tell me the population, the period, and what would count as an exception.”

I wrote those three items at the top of my workpaper. That small habit prevents one of the most common failures in controls testing: allowing the available report to define the test instead of allowing the control objective to define the report.

I then moved into the system. SAP GUI command field > /nSM58 > scope transactional RFC entries to the period/interface in question > Execute > retain status/error evidence. SAP GUI command field > /nSMQ1 > use Display/report mode for the scope described in this lab > retain the selection criteria and output. SAP GUI command field > /nSMQ2 > use Display/report mode for the scope described in this lab > retain the selection criteria and output.

Before execution, I recorded the system/client or source application, test period, population definition, report parameters, preparer and evidence date. If the menu path differed from the training wording, I documented the actual path rather than pretending the environment looked exactly like the manual.

My execution notes read like a trail another consultant could follow:

Re-read the objective and define the exact control assertion, population, period and exception condition before opening the report.

Obtained the source system's transmitted transaction count for the period before reconciling anything in SAP.

Reviewed the SM58 tRFC error queue, sorted by date, and recorded the count and age of the oldest item in error.

Checked SMQ1/SMQ2 outbound and inbound queue counts.

Filtered WE02 for IDoc error statuses (51, 64) for the period and recorded the error population.

Reconciled the source transmission count to the SAP posting count, converted the unit difference to value, and assessed whether the difference was concentrated by day, plant, or material type, or scattered.

After the system work, I reconciled the extracted population to the defined scope, investigated differences rather than forcing the result to match the completed example, traced each exception to its underlying evidence, and completed the evidence index before drafting the conclusion.

The Moment the Test Changed

The first result was not the conclusion. It was the point where the case became interesting.

The source system reported 41,206 goods movements for the quarter; SAP recorded 41,192 — a gap of 14 units.

The 14-unit gap, converted to value and assessed by composition, was concentrated rather than scattered evenly across days, plants, and material types.

Aged items remained in the SM58 error queue beyond the control's target resolution window.

Maya: “So what does that actually tell us? Is this a failed control, a documentation problem, a design issue, or simply something we still need to investigate?”

That question forced me to stop describing the screen and start analyzing the control. I separated the observed condition from management’s explanation, then asked what additional evidence would prove or disprove the explanation.

The Rookie Mistake I Would Warn You About

Do not accept a ticket number as proof of control performance. Compare approval time, migration/import time, emergency classification and evidence creation time.

A second rookie mistake is to crop evidence too aggressively. A screenshot that proves the number but hides the system, date, user, parameters or surrounding context may look clean in a slide deck and still be weak audit evidence.

Building the Evidence Trail

I treated the evidence package as part of the test, not as administration after the test. My rule was simple: selection criteria first, result second, raw export preserved separately, analysis performed only on a working copy.

THORNFIELD-B19-OPS-02_SourceCount_Reference.xlsx

THORNFIELD-B19-OPS-02_SM58_Selection_Result.png

THORNFIELD-B19-OPS-02_WE02_ErrorPopulation.png

THORNFIELD-B19-OPS-02_Reconciliation_ValueAnalysis.xlsx

For every file I recorded the source, system/client, period, extraction criteria, filename, preparer, date and workpaper cross-reference. That is what turns a folder of screenshots into an evidence trail.

The Reviewer Challenge

Elena: “The client's position that a 0.03% difference is "within tolerance" is noted but not accepted without disaggregating the difference by composition first — a percentage alone does not establish immateriality when the underlying items are concentrated rather than scattered. Flagged for reviewer discussion.”

I answered by going back to the source evidence rather than defending my first interpretation. Reviewer challenge is not an interruption to the work; it is part of the control-testing process. If the conclusion survives challenge, it becomes stronger. If it changes, the workpaper has done its job.

My Conclusion

A reconciliation gap exists between the source system and SAP. Because the gap is concentrated rather than scattered, it is treated as indicative of a systematic failure rather than immaterial noise, regardless of the small percentage the 14 units represent of the total population.

I deliberately avoided writing beyond the evidence. Where a cause had not been proven, I called it a reviewer question or an investigation item rather than turning an assumption into a finding.

What This Lab Is Really Teaching

A change ticket is useful only when its timing and approvals support the control assertion. Documentation created after migration cannot retroactively become pre-implementation approval.

The technical transaction or report is only the visible part of the work. The professional skill is deciding what evidence is sufficient, recognizing when the population or control design makes a “clean” result misleading, and documenting the reasoning so that someone who was not in the room can follow it.

Before Leaving the Lab

✓ Correct system/source, client/entity and period are documented.

✓ Population completeness and report parameters are evidenced.

✓ Required screenshots and raw exports are saved and readable.

✓ Every exception is traced to underlying evidence.

✓ Sample exhibit/analysis reconciles to the workpaper.

✓ Conclusion is supported by the evidence and does not rely only on the completed example.

✓ Evidence filenames and workpaper cross-references are complete.

✓ Reviewer discussion items are clearly separated from resolved findings.

Field-journal close: I did not leave Lab 19 when the report finished running. I left when the evidence, workpaper, exception logic and conclusion told the same story.

1. /nBD87. Look at it. Understand that it reprocesses IDocs and changes production data. Press nothing. Close it.

steps.action: PRIMARY LAB
steps.narration:
III · Record to Report — Manual Journal Entry Review Testing

Control question: Verify that manual journal entries meeting the policy risk threshold were routed for, and received, independent review and approval before posting.

Systems / tools: FBL3N, SE16N, FB03, SWI1, BP

The Story

I opened Lab 3 with one discipline: I wrote the control assertion in plain English before opening SAP. The question was not “Can I run the report?” It was whether the evidence could support this statement: Verify that manual journal entries meeting the policy risk threshold were routed for, and received, independent review and approval before posting.

Priya: “Before you touch the system, tell me the population, the period, and what would count as an exception.”

I wrote those three items at the top of my workpaper. That small habit prevents one of the most common failures in controls testing: allowing the available report to define the test instead of allowing the control objective to define the report.

I then moved into the system. SAP GUI command field > /nFBL3N > enter company code/G/L account and period criteria > Execute > retain selection and result/export. SAP GUI command field > /nSE16N > enter the table named in the procedure > set the exact filters/period > Execute > retain selection criteria and result/export. SAP GUI command field > /nFB03 > enter document/company code/fiscal year > Display > review header, line items and available change/workflow references.

Before execution, I recorded the system/client or source application, test period, population definition, report parameters, preparer and evidence date. If the menu path differed from the training wording, I documented the actual path rather than pretending the environment looked exactly like the manual.

My execution notes read like a trail another consultant could follow:

Re-read the objective and define the exact control assertion, population, period and exception condition before opening the report.

Confirmed with Finance which document types represent manual journal entries under this client's configuration, rather than assuming.

Pulled all manual journal entries posted in the period via FBL3N (supplemented by SE16N on BKPF/BSEG where needed), explicitly documenting whether posting date or entry date defined the testing period.

Opened a sample document directly in FB03 to record entered-by, entry date/time, document type, and posting date.

Pulled the workflow log via SWI1 for the sample, recording the approver and the approval timestamp against the posting timestamp.

Separately obtained the current workflow routing threshold and its change history across the testing period — a distinct procedure from the operating-effectiveness sample.

After the system work, I reconciled the extracted population to the defined scope, investigated differences rather than forcing the result to match the completed example, traced each exception to its underlying evidence, and completed the evidence index before drafting the conclusion.

The Moment the Test Changed

The first result was not the conclusion. It was the point where the case became interesting.

The workflow routing threshold was configured at $100,000 against a documented policy threshold of $10,000, from 3 January to 6 June.

412 manual journal entries totalling $18.4 million posted above the policy threshold without workflow routing during that window.

A sample of 25 entries above the (incorrectly configured) threshold all showed correct approval — but this sample could not have failed, since only entries the broken configuration actually routed were eligible for selection.

Maya: “So what does that actually tell us? Is this a failed control, a documentation problem, a design issue, or simply something we still need to investigate?”

That question forced me to stop describing the screen and start analyzing the control. I separated the observed condition from management’s explanation, then asked what additional evidence would prove or disprove the explanation.

The Rookie Mistake I Would Warn You About

Do not write the conclusion while you are still collecting evidence. Finish the evidence index, reconcile the population, and separate facts from explanations before deciding what the result means.

A second rookie mistake is to crop evidence too aggressively. A screenshot that proves the number but hides the system, date, user, parameters or surrounding context may look clean in a slide deck and still be weak audit evidence.

Building the Evidence Trail

I treated the evidence package as part of the test, not as administration after the test. My rule was simple: selection criteria first, result second, raw export preserved separately, analysis performed only on a working copy.

THORNFIELD-B03-BP-01_FBL3N_Selection_Result.png

THORNFIELD-B03-BP-01_FB03_DocumentHeader.png

THORNFIELD-B03-BP-01_SWI1_WorkflowLog.png

THORNFIELD-B03-BP-01_ThresholdConfig_ChangeHistory.xlsx

THORNFIELD-B03-BP-01_ApprovalPostingGap_Calc.xlsx

For every file I recorded the source, system/client, period, extraction criteria, filename, preparer, date and workpaper cross-reference. That is what turns a folder of screenshots into an evidence trail.

The Reviewer Challenge

Elena: “The original operating-effectiveness sample was drawn only from entries the mis-configured workflow actually routed. Flagged for reviewer discussion on whether that sample can support any conclusion about the control's true population.”

I answered by going back to the source evidence rather than defending my first interpretation. Reviewer challenge is not an interruption to the work; it is part of the control-testing process. If the conclusion survives challenge, it becomes stronger. If it changes, the workpaper has done its job.

My Conclusion

The routing configuration did not reflect policy for the stated period, and the population most relevant to the control objective — entries between $10,000 and $100,000 — was never exposed to the original sampling approach, because it was never routed in the first place. Recommendation: Correct the configuration, retest a sample drawn from the previously-unrouted population, and quantify the approval-to-posting timing gap going forward rather than only noting its presence.

I deliberately avoided writing beyond the evidence. Where a cause had not been proven, I called it a reviewer question or an investigation item rather than turning an assumption into a finding.

What This Lab Is Really Teaching

A clean sample cannot rescue a flawed population. First prove that the population contains the transactions that could actually violate the policy; only then does sampling mean anything.

The technical transaction or report is only the visible part of the work. The professional skill is deciding what evidence is sufficient, recognizing when the population or control design makes a “clean” result misleading, and documenting the reasoning so that someone who was not in the room can follow it.

Before Leaving the Lab

✓ Correct system/source, client/entity and period are documented.

✓ Population completeness and report parameters are evidenced.

✓ Required screenshots and raw exports are saved and readable.

✓ Every exception is traced to underlying evidence.

✓ Sample exhibit/analysis reconciles to the workpaper.

✓ Conclusion is supported by the evidence and does not rely only on the completed example.

✓ Evidence filenames and workpaper cross-references are complete.

✓ Reviewer discussion items are clearly separated from resolved findings.

Field-journal close: I did not leave Lab 3 when the report finished running. I left when the evidence, workpaper, exception logic and conclusion told the same story.

steps.title: PRIMARY LAB
steps.action: PRIMARY LAB
steps.narration:
IV · SAP GRC Platform Modules — GRC Process Control (CCM) Testing

Control question: Verify that the automated monitoring rule executed as scheduled, evaluated its intended population, and correctly identified exceptions.

Systems / tools: SE16N, BP

The Story

I opened Lab 14 with one discipline: I wrote the control assertion in plain English before opening SAP. The question was not “Can I run the report?” It was whether the evidence could support this statement: Verify that the automated monitoring rule executed as scheduled, evaluated its intended population, and correctly identified exceptions.

Priya: “Before you touch the system, tell me the population, the period, and what would count as an exception.”

I wrote those three items at the top of my workpaper. That small habit prevents one of the most common failures in controls testing: allowing the available report to define the test instead of allowing the control objective to define the report.

I then moved into the system. SAP GUI command field > /nSE16N > enter the table named in the procedure > set the exact filters/period > Execute > retain selection criteria and result/export. SAP GUI command field > /nBP > use Display/report mode for the scope described in this lab > retain the selection criteria and output. Before executing, record the system/client or source application, test period, population definition, report parameters, preparer and evidence date. If the configured menu path differs from the wording in this lab, document the actual client path used rather than guessing.

Before execution, I recorded the system/client or source application, test period, population definition, report parameters, preparer and evidence date. If the menu path differed from the training wording, I documented the actual path rather than pretending the environment looked exactly like the manual.

My execution notes read like a trail another consultant could follow:

Re-read the objective and define the exact control assertion, population, period and exception condition before opening the report.

Opened the rule definition in GRC Process Control and recorded the data source, filter condition, and deficiency criteria, comparing them against the control's description in the control matrix.

Pulled the rule's execution history for the period, recording every scheduled execution and its result.

Pulled the rule's change history, recording when the definition was last modified, by whom, and with what approval.

Independently identified, via SE16N and the relevant transactional data, a transaction meeting the rule's condition, and confirmed whether the rule actually flagged it (injection test).

Reconcile the extracted population/result to the scope used in the completed example. Investigate differences; do not force your result to match the sample.

After the system work, I reconciled the extracted population to the defined scope, investigated differences rather than forcing the result to match the completed example, traced each exception to its underlying evidence, and completed the evidence index before drafting the conclusion.

The Moment the Test Changed

The first result was not the conclusion. It was the point where the case became interesting.

The rule's data source was changed during the period; from that date the rule evaluated an empty or incorrect population and returned a clean result for six consecutive weeks.

The injection test confirmed the rule did not flag a transaction independently known to meet its condition, following the data source change.

The change to the rule's configuration was not subject to documented review or approval.

Maya: “So what does that actually tell us? Is this a failed control, a documentation problem, a design issue, or simply something we still need to investigate?”

That question forced me to stop describing the screen and start analyzing the control. I separated the observed condition from management’s explanation, then asked what additional evidence would prove or disprove the explanation.

The Rookie Mistake I Would Warn You About

Do not write the conclusion while you are still collecting evidence. Finish the evidence index, reconcile the population, and separate facts from explanations before deciding what the result means.

A second rookie mistake is to crop evidence too aggressively. A screenshot that proves the number but hides the system, date, user, parameters or surrounding context may look clean in a slide deck and still be weak audit evidence.

Building the Evidence Trail

I treated the evidence package as part of the test, not as administration after the test. My rule was simple: selection criteria first, result second, raw export preserved separately, analysis performed only on a working copy.

THORNFIELD-B14-BP-03_RuleDefinition.png

THORNFIELD-B14-BP-03_ExecutionHistory.png

THORNFIELD-B14-BP-03_ChangeHistory.png

THORNFIELD-B14-BP-03_InjectionTest_Evidence.png

THORNFIELD-B14-BP-03_RuleVsDescription_Comparison.xlsx

For every file I recorded the source, system/client, period, extraction criteria, filename, preparer, date and workpaper cross-reference. That is what turns a folder of screenshots into an evidence trail.

The Reviewer Challenge

Elena: “Six weeks of "no exceptions" was initially treated internally as a clean result rather than investigated. Flagged for reviewer discussion on whether "no exceptions" and "the rule is not executing correctly" were being adequately distinguished before this test.”

I answered by going back to the source evidence rather than defending my first interpretation. Reviewer challenge is not an interruption to the work; it is part of the control-testing process. If the conclusion survives challenge, it becomes stronger. If it changes, the workpaper has done its job.

My Conclusion

Two findings, one root cause. The automated monitoring control did not operate effectively from the date of the data source change. Separately, changes to monitoring rule configuration are not subject to review or approval, meaning this failure mode could recur, undetected, in any other rule — remediating only the first finding leaves the second exposed.

I deliberately avoided writing beyond the evidence. Where a cause had not been proven, I called it a reviewer question or an investigation item rather than turning an assumption into a finding.

What This Lab Is Really Teaching

The consultant’s job is not to reproduce a sample answer. It is to build a defensible chain from scope, to population, to evidence, to exception, to conclusion — with enough clarity that another reviewer can reperform the work.

The technical transaction or report is only the visible part of the work. The professional skill is deciding what evidence is sufficient, recognizing when the population or control design makes a “clean” result misleading, and documenting the reasoning so that someone who was not in the room can follow it.

Before Leaving the Lab

✓ Correct system/source, client/entity and period are documented.

✓ Population completeness and report parameters are evidenced.

✓ Required screenshots and raw exports are saved and readable.

✓ Every exception is traced to underlying evidence.

✓ Sample exhibit/analysis reconciles to the workpaper.

✓ Conclusion is supported by the evidence and does not rely only on the completed example.

✓ Evidence filenames and workpaper cross-references are complete.

✓ Reviewer discussion items are clearly separated from resolved findings.

Field-journal close: I did not leave Lab 14 when the report finished running. I left when the evidence, workpaper, exception logic and conclusion told the same story.

Part A — Fact one: what does it actually evaluate?

1. Open GRC. Navigate to Rule Setup → Continuous Monitoring → Business Rules. Open one rule's definition.

2. Read three things: the data source, the filter condition, and the deficiency criteria. Read the condition out loud.

3. Find the control description — what the control matrix says this rule does — and compare it to the rule definition. A description is a claim; the rule definition is the fact. When they disagree, the rule wins.

Part B — Fact two: when did it last run?

1. Open the execution history / job monitor for that rule (Assessments → Monitoring Scheduler, or the job monitor). Set your date range.

2. Record every execution: date and result. "Scheduled" is not "executed" — a rule can sit scheduled and never fire.

3. Six weeks of "no exceptions" and six weeks of "did not run" produce the same silence — only this screen tells them apart. Screenshot.

Part C — Fact three: when was it last changed?

1. Open the rule's change history. Record when the definition was last modified, by whom, and with what approval.

2. A rule correct all year and modified in November is two different controls — your conclusion must cover both periods separately. Screenshot.

1. Independently identify a transaction that meets the rule's condition using SE16N or the relevant transactional report, not the rule itself.

3. Six weeks of "no exceptions" and six weeks of "did not run" produce the same silence — only this screen tells them apart. Screenshot.

Part C — Fact three: when was it last changed?

1. Open the rule's change history. Record when the definition was last modified, by whom, and with what approval.

2. A rule correct all year and modified in November is two different controls — your conclusion must cover both periods separately. Screenshot.

Part D — The injection test

Before you start: This is the strongest evidence available and juniors never think of it.

1. Independently identify a transaction that meets the rule's condition using SE16N or the relevant transactional report, not the rule itself.

2. Confirm the rule flagged it. You are testing whether the report is capable of not being empty, not whether it is empty.

If there is no GRC Process Control

1. /nSM37. Enter the job name for the equivalent monitoring job. Set the date range. Execute — that is fact two.

2. Open the job → Step list — it shows the program it runs — that is fact one.

3. /nSE16N on the relevant configuration table, with change documents if available — that is fact three.

4. Say the substitution out loud in your workpaper — the tool changes at every client, the three questions do not.

What to capture: The rule definition showing data source and condition; execution history for the period; change history with dates and who; your one-line statement of what the rule evaluates, in your own words; evidence of the injection test, if you ran one.

Evaluation | The rule's data source was changed. From that date it evaluated an empty or wrong population and returned clean — six weeks of meaningless clean results. A control description is a claim; the rule definition is the fact.

Conclusion (write yours first, then reveal the model in-app) | The automated monitoring control did not operate effectively from [date] to [date]. Separately: changes to monitoring rule configuration were not subject to review or approval, so the failure could recur without detection. Two findings, one root cause — remediating only the first fixes this rule and leaves every other rule exposed.

Reviewer challenge | "You have told me the rule produced no exceptions. How do you know it would have produced one if there had been one?"

Common errors to avoid | Testing the output instead of the rule — an empty report and a broken rule look identical. Assuming scheduled means executed. Not checking when the rule was last changed. Never attempting an injection test — it is the strongest evidence available and juniors never think of it.

Gate — facilitator-led discussion (model answer reveals for facilitators only) | Six weeks of clean results from an automated rule. Is that good news?

steps.title: PRIMARY LAB
steps.action: PRIMARY LAB
steps.narration:
V · Governance, Disclosure & Executive Reporting — Supporting a Disclosure Controls Review

Control question: Verify that security incidents meeting defined escalation criteria reached the disclosure committee without unreasonable delay, and that materiality determinations were documented.

Systems / tools: STMS, SM20, SM21, BP

The Story

I opened Lab 12 with one discipline: I wrote the control assertion in plain English before opening SAP. The question was not “Can I run the report?” It was whether the evidence could support this statement: Verify that security incidents meeting defined escalation criteria reached the disclosure committee without unreasonable delay, and that materiality determinations were documented.

Priya: “Before you touch the system, tell me the population, the period, and what would count as an exception.”

I wrote those three items at the top of my workpaper. That small habit prevents one of the most common failures in controls testing: allowing the available report to define the test instead of allowing the control objective to define the report.

I then moved into the system. SAP GUI command field > /nSTMS > Import Overview > select the target system > Import History > set the testing period and retain both selection and result evidence. SAP GUI command field > /nSM20 > use the approved security audit log selection for the defined user/time period > Execute > retain selection and result. SAP GUI command field > /nSM21 > use Display/report mode for the scope described in this lab > retain the selection criteria and output.

Before execution, I recorded the system/client or source application, test period, population definition, report parameters, preparer and evidence date. If the menu path differed from the training wording, I documented the actual path rather than pretending the environment looked exactly like the manual.

My execution notes read like a trail another consultant could follow:

Re-read the objective and define the exact control assertion, population, period and exception condition before opening the report.

Reviewed SM21 and the SM20/SM19 security audit log configuration for the incident period, establishing what was actually being captured and the log's retention period.

Obtained the incident record from the security incident management system — not the disclosure committee's minutes — and recorded detection, containment, and escalation timestamps.

Cross-referenced the incident date against STMS production import history to check for any related emergency production change.

Obtained the documented escalation criteria and assessed whether they were specific enough to be actionable at the point of use, rather than general guidance.

Reconcile the extracted population/result to the scope used in the completed example. Investigate differences; do not force your result to match the sample.

After the system work, I reconciled the extracted population to the defined scope, investigated differences rather than forcing the result to match the completed example, traced each exception to its underlying evidence, and completed the evidence index before drafting the conclusion.

The Moment the Test Changed

The first result was not the conclusion. It was the point where the case became interesting.

Twenty-three days elapsed between detection/containment and the incident reaching the disclosure committee, against a documented "without unreasonable delay" standard.

No related production change was identified via the cross-reference check for this incident.

Escalation criteria on file were broadly worded ("escalate significant incidents") rather than stated as specific, actionable thresholds.

Maya: “So what does that actually tell us? Is this a failed control, a documentation problem, a design issue, or simply something we still need to investigate?”

That question forced me to stop describing the screen and start analyzing the control. I separated the observed condition from management’s explanation, then asked what additional evidence would prove or disprove the explanation.

The Rookie Mistake I Would Warn You About

Do not write the conclusion while you are still collecting evidence. Finish the evidence index, reconcile the population, and separate facts from explanations before deciding what the result means.

A second rookie mistake is to crop evidence too aggressively. A screenshot that proves the number but hides the system, date, user, parameters or surrounding context may look clean in a slide deck and still be weak audit evidence.

Building the Evidence Trail

I treated the evidence package as part of the test, not as administration after the test. My rule was simple: selection criteria first, result second, raw export preserved separately, analysis performed only on a working copy.

THORNFIELD-B12-BP-02_SM21_Extract.png

THORNFIELD-B12-BP-02_SM20_Result.png

THORNFIELD-B12-BP-02_SM19_Configuration.png

THORNFIELD-B12-BP-02_IncidentRecord.pdf

THORNFIELD-B12-BP-02_STMS_CrossReference.png

For every file I recorded the source, system/client, period, extraction criteria, filename, preparer, date and workpaper cross-reference. That is what turns a folder of screenshots into an evidence trail.

The Reviewer Challenge

Elena: “IT Security's position that the incident had no material impact, and therefore did not require escalation, is noted but not adopted here — materiality determination sits with the disclosure committee, informed by Legal and Finance, not with the team that detected the incident. Flagged for reviewer discussion.”

I answered by going back to the source evidence rather than defending my first interpretation. Reviewer challenge is not an interruption to the work; it is part of the control-testing process. If the conclusion survives challenge, it becomes stronger. If it changes, the workpaper has done its job.

My Conclusion

The escalation control did not operate within the standard implied by policy for this incident. Whether a disclosure obligation was in fact triggered is a legal determination outside the scope of this test and is referred to Legal and the disclosure committee; this workpaper's finding is limited to the elapsed time and the criteria's lack of specificity.

I deliberately avoided writing beyond the evidence. Where a cause had not been proven, I called it a reviewer question or an investigation item rather than turning an assumption into a finding.

What This Lab Is Really Teaching

The consultant’s job is not to reproduce a sample answer. It is to build a defensible chain from scope, to population, to evidence, to exception, to conclusion — with enough clarity that another reviewer can reperform the work.

The technical transaction or report is only the visible part of the work. The professional skill is deciding what evidence is sufficient, recognizing when the population or control design makes a “clean” result misleading, and documenting the reasoning so that someone who was not in the room can follow it.

Before Leaving the Lab

✓ Correct system/source, client/entity and period are documented.

✓ Population completeness and report parameters are evidenced.

✓ Required screenshots and raw exports are saved and readable.

✓ Every exception is traced to underlying evidence.

✓ Sample exhibit/analysis reconciles to the workpaper.

✓ Conclusion is supported by the evidence and does not rely only on the completed example.

✓ Evidence filenames and workpaper cross-references are complete.

✓ Reviewer discussion items are clearly separated from resolved findings.

Field-journal close: I did not leave Lab 12 when the report finished running. I left when the evidence, workpaper, exception logic and conclusion told the same story.

Part A — The system log

1. /nSM21. Set the date and time range. Execute, or click Reread system log.

2. Ask the retention question: how far back does this log actually go?

3. Screenshot, with the date range visible.

Part B — The security audit log

1. /nSM20 (SM20N on some releases — check which yours is). Set your period. Execute.

2. Record what you get — including if you get nothing.

Part C — The most important step in this Book

1. /nSM19 — the configuration behind SM20; shows what is actually being captured, and since when. Display only.

2. An empty security audit log has two completely different explanations: nothing happened, or nothing was being recorded. SM19 tells you which.

3. If security audit logging is not enabled on a production financial system, that is a serious finding in its own right, entirely separate from what you were testing.

4. Screenshot the SM19 configuration.

Part D — The cross-reference nobody makes

1. Take the incident date. /nSTMS → Import Overview → production → Import History. Set the date range to the days around the incident.

2. Look for production imports made in response to the incident.

3. An incident that triggered an unapproved emergency production change is two findings and one story — neither team will tell you, because each sees only their half.

4. Screenshot.

What to capture: SM21 extract with the date range and retention period; SM20 result, even if empty; SM19 configuration; production import history around the incident date; one sentence on what this log tells you, and what it does not.

Evaluation | For each incident meeting escalation criteria, the elapsed time from detection to escalation — twenty-three days against a "without unreasonable delay" standard is the finding. An empty security audit log has two completely different explanations: nothing happened, or nothing was being recorded.

Conclusion (write yours first, then reveal the model in-app) | State the elapsed time. State the criterion it breached. State whether a disclosure obligation was triggered — and if that is a legal determination, say it requires legal assessment rather than concluding it yourself.

Reviewer challenge | "The incident turned out to be immaterial. What exactly is your finding?"

Common errors to avoid | Building the population from the disclosure committee's minutes. Reading an empty SM20 as "nothing happened." Concluding on materiality yourself — that determination belongs to the disclosure committee, informed by Legal and Finance. Missing the cross-reference between the incident and any related production change.

Gate — facilitator-led discussion (model answer reveals for facilitators only) | IT Security says the incident had no material impact, so escalation was not required.
